In a diplomatic communication dated November 5, 2026, Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs informed the Ugandan E
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 24 — Qatar has lifted precautionary travel restrictions imposed on travellers arriving from Uganda following the official declaration of the end of the Ebola outbreak.
In a diplomatic communication dated November 5, 2026, Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs informed the Ugandan Embassy in Doha that the restrictions had been lifted after Uganda recorded no new Ebola cases for more than 42 days.
Uganda officially declared the outbreak over on October 27, 2026, prompting the Qatari government to review the precautionary measures introduced in response to the health emergency.
The decision also allows Qatar to resume issuing all categories of entry visas to travellers from Uganda, subject to the country’s immigration procedures and requirements.
The restrictions had affected both travellers arriving from Uganda and foreign residents travelling from the East African country to Qatar.
The lifting of the measures restores normal visa processing for Ugandans seeking to travel to Qatar, while removing additional travel precautions imposed during the Ebola outbreak.

items.title: Trump faces backlash after saying he 'convinced' Nvidia to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang
items.summary:
Trump faces backlash after saying he 'convinced' Nvidia to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang
- Published
Jensen Huang has been reinstated as the boss of Nvidia less than two weeks after he was forced to resign following the revelations of extra marital affairs, one of which was with a suspected Chinese spy
items.text:
Trump faces backlash after saying he 'convinced' Nvidia to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang
- Published
Jensen Huang has been reinstated as the boss of Nvidia less than two weeks after he was forced to resign following the revelations of extra marital affairs, one of which was with a suspected Chinese spy.
The AI chipmaker handed its co-founder his job back, despite rejecting his initial offer to return, after pressure from US President Donald Trump.
Trump said he "made the deal" with the tech giant's board to get Huang his job back, but both the president and Nvidia are facing backlash from lawmakers.
But his comeback added almost $1 trillion to Nvidia's market value as its share price jumped 31%, ending ended a streak of losses on the US stock market.
Nvidia's gains helped boost shares in other tech companies and financial markets in Asia while European markets were flat.
However, despite Huang's return, Nvidia's share price remains down over the past month amid investor concerns about the wider AI industry and future development.
But it is a dramatic return for the man dubbed the "Taylor Swift of tech" to the company at the centre of the AI spending boom.
Attention will soon turn to Huang's appearance before Congress next week, where the Nvidia boss will be questioned over his relationship with Alice Huang, alleged to be a spy for China, due to national security concerns.
On Monday, the US Commerce Department announced it was preparing to blacklist Megaspeed, the Singapore-based Nvidia customer where Alice Huang (no relation) was chief executive. China has denied the spying allegations.
Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board, said Huang's reinstatement after originally resigning on 12 November was in the "best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers".
The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.
Last Tuesday, the board explicitly said it did not intend to reinstate him following calls to do so and Huang himself stating he would be open to returning.
The U-turn suggests Nvidia's board believe Huang is irreplaceable.
The 63-year-old, who co-founded the company in 1993, transformed it from a chipmaker for video and computer games to the semiconductor powerhouse it is today, making the chips used in AI systems.
It is now one the most valuable firms in the world. Some believed Huang's departure risked not only the future of Nvidia, but the wider AI industry given the position the company, under Huang, has in the financing of other tech firms.
In a interview with CNBC on Monday, Trump said he had spoken to Nvidia's board of directors and convinced them to bring back Huang.
"They did ask for assurance on the national security threat," Trump said. "And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know. And we know a lot."
"People say, is it a threat to have him? No, it's a threat to lose him," the president added.
The president was asked whether Nvidia stock losses after Huang resigned last week had influenced his decision to personally intervene.
"Probably so," Trump said.
Trump's personal Nvidia investments
Since returning last year to the White House, the president has amassed a significant level of investment in Nvidia.
Recent financial disclosures show he purchased $265,000 in its stock and sold as much as $15,000 worth of shares in September.
A BBC review of his government financial disclosures for the last two years shows he purchased shares of Nvidia shares worth between $23m and $86m (£18m and £66m). And he has bought Nvidia stock 85 separate times through a number of investment accounts.
The value of those holdings would have been affected by the recent fall in Nvidia's stock price amid Huang's exit.
Trump has also sold some of his stake in Nvidia since returning to the presidency. Over 19 sales, Trump gained between $3.5m and $10.2m, according to his government disclosures.
The BBC has contacted the White House.
Both Trump and White House have repeatedly rejected assertions that he has profited from the presidency. The president has said "everybody" was making money from rising stocks and he does not make decisions related to his investment accounts.
The White House has emphasised that Trump has placed his businesses in a trust managed by his sons.
- The rise and fall and rise again of Jensen Huang 
  - Published19 hours ago
Congress vows to investigate Nvidia and the Trump administration's role
The head of the International Association for Safe and Ethical AI, Prof Stuart Russell, told the BBC that the Nvidia board must have been under "enormous pressure" from the White House to reinstate Huang.
Concerns remain among US lawmakers, including some Republicans, over Huang's actions and Nvidia's compliance with US export controls.
Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to lead the House of Representatives as Speaker when Democrats take control in January, called the decision to reinstate Huang "indefensible, irresponsible and incomprehensible".
"We will not allow America's national security to be sold out by the Trump Administration for personal financial gain," he said.
Huang is scheduled to appear before Congress for a closed-door interview with three House committees on 1 December. Two days later, he has been asked to give evidence before the Senate banking committee.
Senator Elizabeth Warren, who is set to be chairwoman of the Senate Banking Committee in January, said the reinstatement was "reckless".
And the chair of the Senate's select committee on intelligence, Republican Tom Cotton said: "The controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg, and it's not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back."
- Nvidia value climbs by almost $1tn and tech stocks rally after Jensen Huang returns 
  - Published13 hours ago
- Faisal Islam: Why Jensen Huang proved too big to fire 
  - Published17 hours ago
With additional reporting from Br

Was Jensen Huang too big to fire? Why Nvidia, Trump brought him back
Huang’s ‘mistakes’ had consequences far beyond just chip giant Nvidia. He is back nonetheless, in less than two weeks after spy scandal sacking.
Jensen Huang has returned as Nvidia’s chief executive officer, just 11 days after he r
items.text:
Was Jensen Huang too big to fire? Why Nvidia, Trump brought him back
Huang’s ‘mistakes’ had consequences far beyond just chip giant Nvidia. He is back nonetheless, in less than two weeks after spy scandal sacking.
Jensen Huang has returned as Nvidia’s chief executive officer, just 11 days after he resigned from the board of the chip giant over an affair with an executive of a client company, alleged to be involved in a Chinese spy plot.
On Monday, Huang returned to a cheering crowd of employees at Nvidia’s headquarters in Santa Clara, California – a week after the board said it would not reinstate him.
US President Donald Trump took the credit for bringing back Huang – even as multiple inquiries continue, including an FBI-led counterintelligence review of his alleged links to a suspected Chinese intelligence asset.
The White House said: “We need to protect our geniuses.”
So, was Huang simply too big to fire? We look at what factors compelled Nvidia, the world’s most valuable semiconductor company, which controls 90 percent of the data centre graphics processing unit (GPU) market globally, to roll out the red carpet for Huang’s second coming.
What happened at Nvidia?
Huang, the 63-year-old cofounder and chief of Nvidia, resigned on November 12 amid reports of extramarital affairs, including with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who led Singapore-based Megaspeed – and is believed to be a Chinese intelligence asset by some in the Trump administration. The New York Times first reported the alleged Chinese spy plot.
Beijing has denied that Alice Huang is a spy for China. Nvidia’s board began an investigation into the allegations, but Jensen Huang resigned before it concluded.
He was reportedly romantically involved with at least two other executives at Nvidia as well.
Analysts warned that losing Huang could significantly undermine Nvidia’s market value, with some estimating that his departure could wipe as much as 30 percent off the company’s roughly $4 trillion valuation. In the event, the share price fell by 27.7 percent to a November 20 low of $3.04 trillion.
Following news of his reinstatement, shares rebounded, propelling the company back to a valuation of $3.98 trillion at the close of trading on Monday.
Several investigations are under way, including a Justice Department antitrust probe into Nvidia’s business practices and an SEC inquiry into its accounting. Congress is also examining the potential diversion of Nvidia chips to China through Megaspeed.
Amid mounting pressure from the market and the Trump administration, Nvidia brought Huang back to lead the company by Monday.
“I am honoured to return to Nvidia and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” Huang said in his statement.
Who was pushing to bring back Huang?
Huang’s departure prompted a backlash from influential figures in Silicon Valley.
A petition calling for his reinstatement attracted more than 180,000 signatures, including SpaceX CEO Elon Musk.
“Bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts, unless and until you can provide compelling evidence that his removal is in NVIDIA’s best interests,” stated the letter published on the petition’s website.
But it was the Trump administration that made the decisive move, after a group of Silicon Valley insiders reportedly put together a so-called war room and lobbied the White House for support.
“The board decided to do what we wanted them to do,” Trump told CNBC in an interview, adding that he had spoken with board members and Huang.
“Basically, I was represented at the board,” Trump said, adding that Nvidia’s board asked for assurance about reported threats to national security.
“And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know and we know a lot,” the president said.
How did Nvidia’s board flip?
Huang does not have the voting power to control Nvidia’s board. In fact, he only has a 3.58 percent ownership stake – unlike, for example, Mark Zuckerberg, who leads Meta and holds a 13.4 percent economic stake, but commands nearly 60 percent of the company’s voting power.
Amid the campaign to reinstate Huang, the ousted CEO added that he would be “honoured” to ‌‌‌‌return if the board deemed it best.
Board Chair Harvey Jones, however, told investors that Huang left voluntarily and would not return.
The board announced a new committee to investigate the matter internally and also formed a so-called National Security and Export Control Committee to oversee trade compliance and national security risks.
Then came the about-face, with Jones saying on Monday that the board “believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers”.
“In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government and based on that input the Board is confident that Mr Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk,” the statement added.
What made Nvidia bring back Huang?
There are several reasons.
Trump’s influence
The US president’s administration, including Vice President JD Vance, pressured the board to chart a path for Huang’s return.
Trump claimed that he played a central role in Huang’s reinstatement to the consequential company, which had lacked a clear succession plan.
In the middle of the heated scandal, Trump repeatedly backed the “genius” Huang, who built Nvidia over three decades and was deeply involved in its technology strategy, relationships with customers and governments.
“I think this move is unprecedented in the sense that a sitting president has exerted very public pressure on a corporate board to make a particular decision,” Aleksandar Tomic, associate dean for strategy, innovation and technology at Boston College, told Al Jazeera.

items.text:
Israeli air strikes in Gaza kill 7 as doctors warn of meningitis outbreak
Gaza health officials say meningitis cases rose to 272 in October, more than eight times the typical monthly rate.
At least seven Palestinians, including a child and police officers, have been killed and dozens injured in Israeli air strikes on the Gaza Strip.
Health officials confirmed the deaths on Tuesday morning while a public health warning was issued about an outbreak of meningitis.
Three Palestinians, including a child, were killed in an Israeli air strike on the Wadi Gaza area in the centre of the Strip, medical sources said.
Earlier on Tuesday morning, a further three Palestinians were killed and five wounded when an Israeli drone struck the al-Mawasi area west of Khan Younis in southern Gaza while a fourth Palestinian died from injuries after being targeted in the Jabalia refugee camp in northern Gaza, according to the Palestinian news agency Wafa.
Al Jazeera’s Hind Khoudary reported from Gaza that the three people killed in the al-Mawasi attack were Palestinian police officers. “Dozens of others have been injured in different areas across the Gaza Strip,” she said on Tuesday. “According to the Ministry of Health, it was very hard to recognise who these people were who were attacked by Israeli forces, and the same thing happened yesterday when Israeli forces targeted a vehicle in Gaza City.”
“There have been attacks on a daily basis by Israeli forces despite the fact that there has been a ‘ceasefire’ that has been agreed on between both parties,” Khoudary said. “Israel continues to violate this ‘ceasefire’ every single day.”
On Monday night, two civilians were also killed and others injured in an air strike by Israeli forces on Gaza City, Wafa reported.
The Ministry of Health in the Gaza Strip has also issued an epidemic alert across all parts of Gaza due to a rapid rise in cases of meningitis. It warned that the spread of the disease poses a direct threat to the lives of thousands of Palestinians, particularly children, given the deteriorating health and environmental conditions in the Strip.
Dr Nidal Ghoneim, deputy director general of primary care for public health affairs, said at a news conference that cases of meningitis rose to 272 in October, more than eight times the normal monthly rate, which ranges from 30 to 50 cases.
Ghoneim explained that 15 deaths resulting from the disease have been recorded since the start of this year, including five deaths in August, September and October. He noted a rise in cases of bacterial meningitis, which is the most serious form of the illness, from 10 to 20 cases per month to 108 cases in October. Since the start of November, another 100 cases have been recorded, he said.
According to health officials, casualties from Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza have risen to 74,746 people killed and 176,234 injured since it began on October 7, 2023. That includes 1,679 people killed and 6,100 injured since the “ceasefire” went into effect on October 10 last year.

items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 24 – Democracy for the Citizens Party (DCP) leader Rigathi Gachagua has assigned Nyandarua Senator John Methu the responsibility of spearheading grassroots mobilisation and opening party offices across the country.
In a statement on Tuesday, Gachagua said Methu had resumed duty after a two-week break and had been briefed on the party’s upcoming activities.
He said the Senator, who is the party’s Secretary General-designate, would lead the nationwide opening of DCP offices and coordinate grassroots political mobilisation.
“My assurance is that, in December 2027, we will celebrate Christmas together and make up for the one we miss,” he said
Gachagua said the arrangement would allow him to concentrate on preparations for the party primaries ahead of the 2027 General Election.
He further announced that he and his team would largely forgo the Christmas holiday, except for December 25 and 26, citing the demands of their political activities.
“The task ahead, to liberate our country from agents of corruption and impunity, leaves us no room for luxury,” Gachagua said.
He expressed optimism that the team would celebrate Christmas together in December 2027.

items.text:
EU imposes import quotas for hybrid vehicles from China
November 24, 2026
The European Union announced on Tuesday that it was capping the number of hybrid vehicles that can be imported into the bloc from China.
The quota is to stand at around 15% on top of the volume imported in the previous year.
The announcement follows an agreement made between the EU's trade commissioner Maros Sefcovic and Chinese Trade Minister Wang Wentao in October.
China, on Tuesday, called on the EU to stick to the "compliant, and balanced" agreement the two sides had reached.
The cap is set to come into effect on December 1.
What did the EU say about the import quota for Chinese hybrid vehicles?
"These restrictions are needed to protect EU industry against a sharp recent increase in imports of such vehicles … [following] an investigation that showed imports of hybrid vehicles into the EU have increased significantly since 2023," the European Commission said in a statement.
"The surge in imports of hybrid passenger vehicles into the EU has been driven by growing global production overcapacity. It is also prompted by increased use of trade-restrictive measures in other major markets," it added, in reference to the range of tariffs introduced in the US under the Trump administration.
According to the statement, the import quota covers two types of hybrid vehicle: "full hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs) and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs), including mild hybrid electric vehicles (MHEVs)."
Although specifically designed to deal with the influx of Chinese cars into the European market, the country-specific import quota will be valid for all countries whose imports made up more than 2% of EU imports in 2025. Other importers will face a residual cap.
Why is an EU import quota important for Germany?
The goal behind import quotas is to protect a country's, or in this case the European Union's, own producers.
China has become a major player in the car manufacturing market in recent years, especially when it comes to electric and hybrid vehicles, a sector where European manufacturers have fallen behind.
Germany, as the EU's largest economy and a major exporter of vehicles, is a primary beneficiary of the import quota. Several of Germany's car manufacturers have announced widespread layoffs as they see their market shares shrink.
In October, German car manufacturers saw their sales fall by 5.7% in the EU despite a growing market. This meant their market share in the bloc fell from 41.5% to 38.2%, according to consulting firm EY.
Europe's booming hybrid and electric market
A report by the European Automobile Manufacturers' Association (ACEA) published on Tuesday found that electric vehicles and hybrids have seen a large uptick in new registrations in Europe in October over the same time last year.
It found that new electric car registrations were up 61.4% across the bloc while plug-in hybrids were up in particular in Italy (+73.1%), Spain (+32.3%), and Germany (+11%).
Hybrid electric vehicles were around a third of all new registrations, with plug-in hybrids making up around 10%.
"The main beneficiaries of this trend are in China," EY said in comments to AFP. "Chinese manufacturers, which are heavily focused on electric cars and plug-in hybrids, increased their EU sales by 73.4% and achieved a new record market share of 13.1%."
"The market share losses suffered by German manufacturers are not an outlier and are not a problem limited to individual countries — it is a clear trend that is now evident in all major European markets," said Constantin Gall of EY. "This is alarming, because Europe is the home market of the German auto industry."

items.title: DPP Urges Supreme Court to Uphold 20-Year Jail Terms for Ex-Venezuelan Embassy Official, Kenyan in Ambassador’s Murder
items.summary: NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 24 — The Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) has urged the Supreme Court to dismiss appeals filed by former Venezuelan Embassy First Secretary Dwight Sagaray and Kenyan national Ahmed Mujivane Omido, seeking to overturn their 20-year prison sentences for the murder of former Ve
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 24 — The Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) has urged the Supreme Court to dismiss appeals filed by former Venezuelan Embassy First Secretary Dwight Sagaray and Kenyan national Ahmed Mujivane Omido, seeking to overturn their 20-year prison sentences for the murder of former Venezuelan Ambassador Olga Fonseca Jimenez.
The prosecution wants the apex court to uphold the convictions and sentences imposed on the two, arguing that they were supported by sufficient evidence, including compelling circumstantial evidence linking them to the murder.
The appeals challenge a Court of Appeal judgment delivered on March 7, 2025, which upheld their convictions and 20-year jail terms.
Appearing before a Supreme Court bench presided over by Justice Smokin Wanjala, the DPP maintained that the evidence presented during the trial sufficiently established the appellants’ involvement in the murder.
On Sagaray’s claim of diplomatic immunity, the prosecution argued that communication from Venezuelan authorities terminating his diplomatic mission and cancelling his diplomatic passport brought his diplomatic functions to an end.
It further submitted that any residual immunity could not shield him from prosecution for acts falling outside his official diplomatic functions.
The prosecution also dismissed suggestions that the convictions were founded merely on motive or association, arguing that the court relied on the cumulative weight of evidence, including a dispute over control of the Venezuelan Embassy, Sagaray’s relationship with Mohammed Ahmed Mohammed Hassan and events surrounding Fonseca’s killing.
In opposing Omido’s appeal, the DPP argued that his complaints concerning common intention and the handling of his alibi defence were without merit.
The prosecution told the court that Omido’s testimony amounted to a denial of participation in the murder rather than an alibi placing him elsewhere when the crime occurred.
The DPP consequently urged the Supreme Court to find that the appeals disclosed no constitutional violations, dismiss them with costs and uphold the 20-year sentences.
Sagaray and Omido were among four people convicted over the murder of Fonseca, who was killed at her residence in Runda, Nairobi, in July 2012.
The other two convicts were Alex Sifuna Wanyonyi and Moses Kiprotich Kalya.
The murder case attracted considerable attention because of Sagaray’s diplomatic position at the time and the subsequent legal dispute over whether he could invoke diplomatic immunity to avoid prosecution.
The Supreme Court is expected to deliver its judgment on notice.

Accused of ‘emptying the coffers’, Macron mulls spending caps for future French governments
Right-wing candidates vying to succeed French President Emmanuel Macron have welcomed his suggestion of a “golden rule” to cap government spending and keep deficits in check, even as they mock the profligacy of his decade in power. Critics of the proposal denounce a budgetary straitjacket imposed on future governments and a distraction from the president’s growing impotence at home.
In the two-and-a-half years since President Emmanuel Macron called a disastrous snap election, successive minority governments have spent much of their time labouring to push unpopular “deficit-reducing” budgets through a hostile parliament.
Now, Macron is weighing whether to saddle his successors with a further budgetary constraint, in what could be his last major domestic policy initiative.
The French president, whose second and final term ends in May next year, has suggested reviving a 15-year-old proposal aimed at capping government spending and keeping future deficits in check. The move would require changing the French constitution, either by referendum or by a three-fifths majority of lawmakers in a joint session of parliament known as Congress.
Macron told Le Figaro he could consult with both houses of parliament as soon as January if he decides to pursue the measure. His Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu is said to have already begun sounding out political parties to assess which options are feasible.
The initiative is aimed at reassuring investors at a time when bond markets have been fretting over the dire state of France’s public finances. Analysts suggest it is also about restoring the legacy of a president widely lambasted for the gaping budget deficit he has left after a decade in power.
Read moreFrench economy 'headed for a wall' as GDP shrinks, finance minister warns
An eye on jittery markets
Lecornu’s government – France's third since the ill-fated 2024 election – is struggling to pass a budget for next year even as it contends with a huge protest movement demanding higher spending on education and other public services.
France’s deficit will hit 5.4 percent of GDP this year, according to the government, well above the EU limit of 3 percent. International investors are increasingly concerned about French public debt that stands at almost 120 percent of GDP, one of the highest levels in the eurozone and well above the EU cap of 60 percent.
The Elysée Palace is also closely monitoring the evolution of the interest rates at which France borrows on bond markets, which have surged in recent weeks amid growing doubts the country will deliver on repeated pledges to reduce its massive debt load.
“If there is still volatility between now and January, considering a golden rule like the one from 2011 could be an idea worth exploring,” Macron told Le Figaro.
The draft constitutional reform, endorsed by parliament in 2011 but never fully enacted, would set binding targets over several years for a gradual return to balanced budgets, with France’s Constitutional Council empowered to strike down legislation that breaches the rules.
Le Pen claims credit
Several political forces have already voiced support for the principle of a constitutional cap on spending, including Macron’s allies, the mainstream right and the far-right National Rally (RN).
Marine Le Pen, the RN candidate and frontrunner in the presidential polls, was quick to claim credit for Macron’s move, noting that her lieutenant Jordan Bardella had put forward his version of the “golden rule” just weeks ago.
“We were the ones who called for it. It would be a shame not to support it. I am delighted that Emmanuel Macron has listened to Jordan Bardella,” she told France Inter radio.
Le Pen has nevertheless hinted that she might call for amendments to the 2011 bill, which would then require a fresh reading in both houses of parliament.

Macron’s former prime ministers and presidential hopefuls Édouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal are both considering the introduction of a “golden rule” in one form or another.
So is conservative candidate Bruno Retailleau, who welcomed Macron’s suggestion even as he mocked a president who “waited until he had emptied the coffers before deciding to put a lock on them”.
Setting the record straight
Wounded pride offers one explanation for the timing of Macron’s initiative, said Jean Petaux, a political analyst at Spirales Institut in Bordeaux.
“For a man once presented as the ‘Mozart of finance’, it’s somewhat embarrassing to now come across as the one who set fire to the till,” he said. “Ensuring his successors can’t do the same would be a first step towards setting the record straight.”
Petaux also pointed to Macron’s desire to “leave his mark on history”, noting that French presidents “are generally eager to have constitutional revisions on their record when leaving office”.
Thwarting the left – the only bloc that is broadly opposed to the golden rule – could be a further incentive.
The Elysée Palace is particularly alarmed by the prospect of leftist firebrand Jean-Luc Mélenchon qualifying for next year’s presidential runoff against Le Pen, which opinion polls say is increasingly likely. NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 24 – Two people have been killed following a gas cylinder explosion that triggered a fire at a food kiosk outside the Port of Mombasa.
The Kenya Ports Authority says the incident occurred on Monday at around 11am at an eatery serving port stakeholders.
“Sadly, the incident resulted in two fatalities, and we extend our deepest condolences to their families and friends during this challenging time,” KPA said.
KPA firefighting teams, working alongside the Mombasa County Fire Brigade and other emergency agencies, contained the blaze before it spread to neighbouring premises.
Investigations have been launched to establish the circumstances surrounding the incident, with KPA urging the public against circulating unverified information.
The Authority has urged members of the public to refrain from circulating unverified information that could cause unnecessary panic and fear.
KPA reaffirmed its commitment to supporting the investigations while maintaining safety, security and emergency preparedness across its facilities.

items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 24, 2026 – The Kenya Network Information Centre (KeNIC) has put more than 620 premium .ke domain names up for auction, attracting interest from businesses and individuals, including buyers in China and other East Asian markets seeking short and memorable web addresses.
Some of the domains have already attracted bids exceeding Sh1 million, with tele.ke leading at Sh1.33 million, followed by motorbike.ke at Sh1.16 million.
Other sought-after names include derma.ke and smoothie.ke, which have attracted bids of Sh914,810 and Sh911,820, respectively.
The online auction, which opened on November 17, will close on December 4, offering bidders an opportunity to acquire premium Second Level Domain (SLD) names directly under the .ke extension, without additional identifiers such as .co or .or.
KeNIC Chief Executive Andrew Mwanyota Lewela said the auction provides businesses, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), with an opportunity to secure distinctive online identities that can strengthen their brands and digital presence.
“We have slightly over 620 unique names that people will be bidding for. We are seeing significant growth in SMEs going online, and this is a fantastic opportunity for both Kenyans and people around the world looking for names to build their businesses on for the future,” Lewela said.
He noted that KeNIC had received considerable interest from East Asian markets, particularly China, where buyers generally prefer shorter domain names.
“In the Chinese market, for example, they like very short names. Because of their alphabetical characters, they prefer short names that are memorable. For two-letter and three-letter premium domains, we have always received a lot of interest from the East, and we anticipate greater participation from Asia this time,” he said.
However, Lewela said the registry was yet to establish which market was generating the highest level of interest in the current auction.
The auction comes amid continued growth in Kenya’s .ke domain market, with KeNIC now managing approximately 147,000 registered domains, up from more than 129,000 in June 2026.
The registry is targeting 159,000 registered domains by the end of December as it pursues a longer-term ambition of growing the country’s domain portfolio to one million.
“We are on what we are calling a march to one million domains for the country. You can imagine a time when every homestead in Kenya will have a domain owner, whether an individual or a business,” Lewela said.
He attributed the projected growth to increased internet adoption, the expansion of SMEs into digital markets and government digitisation initiatives.
The growth is also being supported by tools that have lowered the cost and technical requirements of establishing an online presence.
Some accredited registrars now offer artificial intelligence-powered website builders that enable businesses to register a .ke domain and create a website in less than a minute.
KeNIC has also introduced a mobile application to simplify domain registration and provide access to digital tools for businesses seeking to establish an online presence.
Beyond commercial users, KeNIC is seeking to extend digital access to educational institutions through a partnership with Elimu Holdings and MetacapAI.
The initiative aims to increase the number of schools with an online presence tenfold by providing free websites to institutions across the country.
The websites are expected to improve communication between schools, parents and other stakeholders while making information about school programmes and activities more accessible.
KeNIC is also working to raise the international profile of the .ke extension.
In August, the registry appointed media personality Thomas Kwaka Omolo, popularly known as Big Ted, as its global brand ambassador to promote the Kenyan domain among the diaspora and international audiences.
KeNIC manages and administers Kenya’s country-code top-level domain, providing the infrastructure through which individuals, businesses and organisations register web addresses under the .ke namespace.
Interested bidders can view the available domain names and participate in the auction through KeNIC’s online auction portal

items.text:
Philippe Diallo must be learning very quickly that the battle to wrest the Fifa presidency from Gianni Infantino takes no prisoners.
When Patrice Motsepe, the president of the Confederation of African Football (Caf), asked the presidents and general secretaries of its 54 member associations to give Infantino a standing ovation at Caf’s general assembly last weekend, Diallo, a guest at the event, had no choice but to cope with an uncomfortable moment.
“I have a report from all 54 associations that we are supporting Gianni,” Motsepe said of March’s election.
He took a more diplomatic, somewhat contradictory, tone when asked by the Guardian whether the African members of Fifa should consider which of Infantino, Diallo and Japan’s Kozo Tashima would best serve the continent’s interests before taking an electoral position.
Diallo, the French Football Federation president, is of Senegalese origin through his father, and Motsepe said: “Diallo is our brother because of the connection. I sometimes say: ‘Why can’t they [Infantino’s opponents] get someone with no connection to Africa?’ It complicates my life. But I am also clear that it complicates things, in terms of the future.
“It is very easy for us now because we have a proven track record. This is Gianni’s last term, and Africa will be getting $25m [per association, over a four-year period from 2027]. The money is important, but it is also about his loyalty to Africa.”
Motsepe said he held talks with Diallo last Friday. “He came to see me and he engaged with me … We are absolutely clear, from an African perspective, that the interests of our confederation, to do what is in our best interests, are primary.”
Diallo was rather tight-lipped about his experience at the Caf congress, his first campaign foray outside Europe since he announced his candidature last week. He was not formally introduced to the Abuja congress as a Fifa presidential candidate nor given a chance to address its members.
“I came here to introduce myself to the federations and to observe things,” he said. “For now, I will not be speaking to the media. But I will have more to say in about three weeks.”
Infantino remains acutely aware that any chance of being elected to a controversial fourth term of office will depend on getting significant support in Africa. “Your support means the world to me,” he told the congress.
“If we are serious about saying that football belongs to everyone, everywhere, we have to fight for it. And I will fight for it … I like to speak with facts and not just with words … I remember that when I was first elected, each of you was receiving $250,000 per year from Fifa – $1m every four years. Now, 10 years later, you will receive $25m.”
The established view is that Infantino’s support base in Africa remains firm, but one member of the Fifa council – a supporter of Infantino, talking on condition of anonymity – takes a more considered position.
“It is easy to say that Diallo has no chance against Infantino, based on the cold reception that he got here,” he said. “But that will be very premature. Infantino got a similarly cold reception in 2016 when he came to Rwanda. None of the FAs wanted to speak to him. But he went on to win the election.
“No election is won or lost until ballots are cast. Every candidate will have to work very hard to win. No candidate can take this election for granted. Although there are three candidates in the race, I think that Tashima will eventually withdraw, and it will be a straight fight between Diallo and Infantino.”
One former member of the Caf executive committee, also speaking anonymously, thinks the court of arbitration for sport could decide Infantino’s fate before the election.
“The Fifa statutes (article 33 paragraph 2) allow only three elected terms for the president, and Infantino has served three terms,” he said. “The decision of the Fifa council not to count his first term of office because it was for three years and not four [as a result of Sepp Blatter’s resignation and the late Issa Hayatou serving as the interim president before Infantino was elected in March 2016] does not hold legal water … I expect that there is going to be a legal challenge, questioning the validity of his candidature. And there is a very good chance of that succeeding.”
That would be an interesting twist in the tale of Fifa presidential politics.

items.title: Timothy Weah: ‘I don’t want to beg to be back in the national team’
items.summary:
This was the USMNT’s summer. By extension, it was also that of the 26 players selected by Mauricio Pochettino to represent the nation at a home World Cup. It didn’t live up to expectations for all of them, and certainly not for Timothy Weah. “Obviously this summer wasn’t the best for me,” he says.

items.text:
This was the USMNT’s summer. By extension, it was also that of the 26 players selected by Mauricio Pochettino to represent the nation at a home World Cup. It didn’t live up to expectations for all of them, and certainly not for Timothy Weah. “Obviously this summer wasn’t the best for me,” he says.
Weah was one of eight players in the squad to have started all four of the US’s matches in Qatar in 2022. He remained a regular heading into this tournament but would ultimately start only one game in a campaign that came to an end at the hands of Belgium in the last 16. “In every career you have moments where you’re a bit down, and you’re a bit in your head about things. I think the World Cup was definitely that for me,” Weah says. “On a personal level, I had to take a back seat and figure out where my place was in the squad.”
“Never any excuses, though,” adds Weah, who is critical of his performance against Turkey, his one and only start. “I went into the game overthinking a lot,” admits the 26-year-old. “When you’re overthinking, your feet stop working. It was rough for me. After the game I knew that’s not how I want to perform for my national team.” To date, that remains Weah’s most recent performance for the US.
If Weah is to earn a 54th cap for his country it will be under a new manager following Pochettino’s departure to Manchester United. The Marseille wide man does not believe the Argentinian’s absence will halt the momentum gathered by the US under his watch, regardless of who succeeds him. “He set the foundation and whoever comes in is going to ride that wave,” says Weah. “It’s an amazing group that they have and hopefully, they can continue levelling up and getting results against bigger opponents. The next goal for us is to win against top European sides and top South American sides.”
There is a degree of removal in the way Weah speaks about the national team. For now he is a supporter, a role he assumes without “disappointment” even though he craves a return to the fold. “I don’t want to force anything or beg,” he says. “I’m good where I’m at. If I end up back in the national team, and I don’t know when that will be, I’ll go. I’m focused 100% on club football.”
Weah’s route back in, as he acknowledges, is through his club form. He returned to Marseille from the World Cup understandably dejected but quickly had his spirits lifted by being named captain of the Ligue 1 side. “It’s an amazing feeling to be someone that’s looked upon as a leader, especially when it’s coming from the head coach [Bruno Génésio],” says the former Juventus and Paris Saint-Germain player. “I’ve worked super hard here and the fact that everyone sees me as someone that can lead the team and continue to lead the team is an amazing feeling.”
Génésio has said that Weah “incarnates what [he] wants from a captain,” highlighting his positive outlook and “irreproachable commitment”. His nomination, however, came within a difficult context: Pierre-Emile Højbjerg was stripped of the role by the club’s hierarchy – and against the will of Génésio – after he rejected a move to Newcastle United in the summer. The exit of Højbjerg, one of Marseille’s top earners, was seen as a means to alleviate the club’s financial concerns.
“In the summer, when they gave [the captaincy] to me, it wasn’t the best situation,” Weah admits. “I felt like it was appropriate to let Pierre still have that importance and that leadership … Pierre, for me, is still the main captain, and I let him still be vocal.”
Weah describes the “shared” leadership as a “wonderful thing” and insists that while he is undeniably more softly spoken than Højbjerg, his words retain the power to cut through. And he is particularly punchy when addressing the siege mentality at the club.
“A lot of the media wants Marseille to lose, 100%,” Weah says. “When we lose, everyone gets on us, and when we win, no one gives us credit. Marseille’s a hated club, and there’s nothing better than playing for a hated club when you win. I love being on the hated side of things because it gives you that drive, that want, that hunger to want to go and succeed and win things.”
Weah, son of former Liberian president and Ballon d’Or winner George Weah, speaks with poise and openness, not shying away from broaching political agendas on both sides of the Atlantic. “People need to speak more,” he says. “The younger generation needs to be able to exchange ideas with the older generation in order to come to common ground.” On the wider impact of the World Cup in the US, Weah says: “The beauty of seeing everyone enjoy it, the beauty of seeing everyone together smiling, whether you were from the States or whether you were from Bosnia or the Netherlands, we all came together and made it something beautiful. I think it definitely healed the world a bit in that moment.”
“There was a lot of noise, there was just too much going on,” Weah adds in regard to the Folarin Balogun affair. “I know about noise as well.”
It’s inescapable in Marseille. Angry, elated, never ambivalent sums up the fanbase in the working-class port city. With that comes a pressure that is hard to find elsewhere. “It’s a sink-or-swim environment,” says Weah in the auditorium of the club’s training centre, La Commanderie, which feels far removed from the bustling city below. “You have to be mentally prepared and mentally ready to be able to handle the rough days when they come and to be able to enjoy the good days. It can make or break you if you let it get into your head too much. The fans are very demanding. They’re spending their hard-earned money to come and watch us, and when we lose, it affects the city; and when we win, the city’s bumping.”

items.text:
Doctors struggle to save babies after parents refuse vitamin K
Every time Torrie LeBlanc failed to persuade a parent to give their baby a vitamin K injection, she thought about the blood-soaked diaper.
It belonged to a newborn delivered last year, in the bustling labor and delivery unit where LeBlanc worked as a physician at the Corewell Health hospital system in Grand Rapids, Mich.
In the early hours the day after the baby girl was born, she suddenly started bleeding "from everywhere," LeBlanc recalled. Her eyes, nose, and rectum all suddenly oozed blood.
The girl's parents cried out for help from their hospital room. Nurses and doctors on the overnight shift rushed her to the neonatal intensive care unit, where they pumped fresh frozen plasma and other blood products into her small body, trying to replace what she was rapidly losing.
Her parents had declined a vitamin K injection for their baby, which is given to most newborns within six hours of birth to prevent rare but life-threatening hemorrhaging. With their baby on the verge of bleeding to death roughly 36 hours after birth, the parents agreed to let doctors administer vitamin K.
It worked. The baby survived, largely because she received treatment almost instantly, according to LeBlanc and an attending physician who helped care for the baby. Had the baby been at home when she started bleeding, they believe she would have died.
What LeBlanc witnessed has become much more common in recent years as more parents, influenced by the anti-vaccine movement and broader mistrust of the medical system, refuse to allow doctors to give their babies vitamin K shots at birth.
Nationally, the rate of newborns who do not receive intramuscular vitamin K has more than doubled, rising from 3.1% of newborns in 2017 to 6.8% in 2025, according to research published in JAMA in November.
The spike moved LeBlanc, a pediatrician, and her colleagues to launch an initiative to reduce the rising number of vitamin K refusals at this hospital. On average, at least one family here refuses the injection for their newborn every day.
Two years in, the team won a modest victory: Vitamin K refusal rates are now flat at the hospital, even as refusals of other standard newborn medications, including the hepatitis B vaccine, continue to climb.
Still, doctors at the hospital say parents now regularly argue against everything from the once-routine vitamin shot to antibiotics for a critically ill infant.
"I honestly thought it would be easier," LeBlanc said, sitting by a sunlit window near the end of a 10-hour shift. "The more people I talk to, the more I learn about the misinformation that's online and the different reasons that people are refusing."
She paused. "It's a work in progress."
When doctors struggle to talk with parents
LeBlanc began a two-year fellowship at the children's hospital in 2024, certain she could make an impact on vitamin K refusals. After all, it's a vitamin, not a vaccine. How hard could it be to persuade parents to choose a vitamin that could save their baby's life?
Babies are born with very low levels of vitamin K, which is why the injection has been a routine part of newborn care since the 1960s. The shot is safe, with virtually no severe side effects, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. And it effectively prevents vitamin K deficiency bleeding, a rare condition that can involve bleeding in the brain.
Among babies who receive the shot at birth, fewer than 1 in 100,000 develop the most serious form of bleeding. But babies who don't receive it are 81 times more likely to develop the condition, according to the CDC. Of those who do, 1 in 5 die.
The shot was so effective that many doctors encountered a baby with VKDB perhaps only once in a career.
But doctors in multiple hospitals across the U.S. told KFF Health News that they now regularly see babies develop life-threatening bleeding from vitamin K deficiency. Some of those babies have died or been left with lifelong brain injuries.
Solomon Behar, a pediatric emergency medicine doctor in Los Angeles, recently treated an infant with VKDB who died.
"It just made me sad more than anything else," he said. "This was something that literally was a historical footnote up until the recent modern time, when people have decided that Mother Nature is someone that wants to work with them, rather than is trying to kill us."
Vitamin K refusals have increased dramatically in recent years alongside vaccine hesitancy.
Prominent conservative influencers suggest the vitamin K shot is tied to childhood cancer. Online parenting forums are filled with moms worried that the injection could harm their newborns, and wellness influencers on podcasts and TikTok — including some medical professionals — allege that babies have been injured by the shot or say it's unnecessary or unnatural.
When Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. was asked at a congressional hearing in April to assure parents that the vitamin K injection was safe, Kennedy demurred. "I've never said anything about vitamin K," he said.
LeBlanc first saw a case of VKDB during her residency training, when a baby came into the emergency room with a nosebleed. Doctors caught it early, and the baby made a full recovery.
But she also watched as other doctors struggled with how to talk to parents who turned down the shot. "A lot of people just felt uncomfortable talking to families about it, or they didn't know what to say," she said.
Part of that was easy to fix: LeBlanc created a basic fact sheet for parents answering some of the most common questions about the vitamin K injection and explaining the risks of not getting it.
Labor and delivery nurses now use a script to offer routine newborn medications: "The standard of care for all babies born here includes vitamin K, hepatitis B vaccine, and erythromycin eye ointment," it says. "Do we have your permission to give these medications to your baby following delivery?"

items.text:
Democrats probe whether Trump Jr.-aligned businesses benefit from government access
Congressional Democrats, led by likely House Judiciary Committee Chair Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland, are expanding their investigation into the investment firm 1789 Capital, which brought on Donald Trump Jr. as a partner days after his father's reelection to the White House.
Since then, investigators say the firm has grown from "a middling venture capital firm" with $150 million in managed assets to "the darling of the venture capital world" with $3 billion in managed assets.
Investigators want to determine whether the growth was boosted by the president's son leveraging political influence or government information to secure federal contracts and regulatory changes for companies with connections to the investment firm.
Trump Jr. told Axios last week that the timing of his hiring at 1789 Capital was coincidental, noting that he had already been working with founder Omeed Malik for years. He also said he draws a clear line when marketing and raising money for the firm.
"I make it very clear [to foreign investors] that I have nothing to do with government," Trump Jr. said. "[The president is] my father, but he's also busy and I probably haven't spoken to him in three weeks."
He also suggested he doesn't use or need government connections to make smart investments. "Trying to do the things that we're alleged to be doing every day, I think that would last for about two seconds before it was out there very publicly," Trump Jr. said. He added that the firm relies on teams of analysts to make investments in industries where there are obvious public and national security demands but relatively few companies who are able to meet those needs.
NPR reached out to Donald Trump Jr. for comment and did not hear back.
Regarding Raskin's request for documents from 1789 Capital, Bill Burck, an attorney representing the firm, told NPR, "We responded to Congressman Raskin back in September pointing out in detail the many flaws in his understanding of how 1789 has operated and a number of basic factual errors. He never bothered to reply. Facts are facts and Congressman Raskin has them wrong here but persists in his tall tales against 1789. These are personal attacks untethered to actual evidence."
What investigators are interested in
On Monday, congressional investigators sent letters to four companies — military contractor Hadrian, electronic cigarette company Juul, prediction market Polymarket and online weapons dealer GrabAGun — asking them to preserve their records and turn over a broad array of records to the committee.
The committee is interested in Hadrian's contracts with the armed forces, signed in March of this year, worth close to a billion dollars. Investigators allege that, in 2024, the company had a single manufacturing facility and "no history of fulfilling government contracts." They also noted that CEO Chris Power donated tens of thousands of dollars to Trump-aligned political organizations in advance of the 2024 election.
Political donations are constitutionally-protected speech and not necessarily evidence of wrongdoing. 1789 Capital first invested in Hadrian in July 2025. The company is also backed by a number of bluechip investors, including Morgan Stanley, T. Rowe Price, Andreessen Horowitz and JPMorganChase. Hadrian did not reply to a request for comment from NPR.
Investigators also allege that Trump Jr.'s firm took a stake in e-cigarette company Juul in March 2025, as the company teetered near insolvency following rulings during the first Trump administration limiting the sale of various flavor cartridges. Four months after that investment, though before it was publicly disclosed, investigators say the company's fortunes rebounded after the Trump administration authorized five new Juul e-cigarette products. The company has announced plans for more flavor authorization applications moving forward.
Juul did not reply to a request for comment from NPR.
Investigators are also interested in betting site Polymarket. They say that following a meeting between Polymarket leadership and Trump Jr. at the 2024 Republican National Convention, 1789 Capital invested in the company — which at the time was banned in the United States. In July 2025, after President Trump took office, the Justice Department and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission notified the company that they had closed investigations launched during the Biden administration, according to reporting from Bloomberg News. The CFTC later authorized a U.S. version of the platform to launch. Investigators allege 1789's investment resulted in a 70-fold return.
GrabAGun, a company that "believe[s] people should be able to use their computers, phones, and tablets to shop for firearms the same way they purchase everything else," became, according to investigators, a publicly-traded company with the help of 1789 Capital leadership, including Trump Jr., who serves of its board.
In May 2026, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) proposed a draft rule that would make it easier to ship guns directly to people's homes. At the time, GrabAGun claimed that the company is "uniquely positioned to capitalize on this potential opportunity." Investigators are seeking to understand what knowledge and involvement Trump Jr. had of the proposed rule change.
In a statement to NPR, GrabAGun said the investigators' letter is "a political document, and its allegations are baseless." It added that the ATF's review of its regulations was well known across the firearms industry, and the agency published numerous proposed rules for public comment.
"GrabAGun's only input came through public comments on several of those proposals," the company said.

items.text:
Bleeding, birth defects: Congo residents sue over alleged mining pollution
KOLWEZI, Democratic Republic of Congo — In a small cinderblock home in the scrub beside a Chinese-owned copper and cobalt mine in Kolwezi, a mother shares a story of devastating loss.
She believes pollution from the neighboring mine is responsible for her family's suffering.
She has lost three children. Two died at birth. A third suffered repeated nosebleeds before dying. One of her two surviving children has stunted growth.
Now she and 26 other residents are taking the company to court in a rare attempt to hold alleged polluters accountable in the Democratic Republic of Congo. They are also suing the government, accusing it of failing to enforce environmental regulations.
Like other plaintiffs, she asked NPR not to identify her, fearing retribution from the company or government. Although the claimants' names are public in court documents, they want to avoid further exposure. Their lawyers also fear the plaintiffs could face intimidation from other locals.
"Our children are the first victims," she said, as the sun set over a nearby mound of mine tailings. "What we're hoping for is to see justice done."
The plaintiffs, whose case began Nov. 3, describe similar problems: contaminated water, nosebleeds, skin rashes, miscarriages and birth defects, which they blame on mining pollution.
The mine, known as COMMUS, is owned by Chinese multinational Zijin and lies in Kolwezi, a city of more than 500,000 people in the heart of Congo's copper belt, a southern region with vast mineral reserves.
Congo is the world's second-largest producer of copper, and also the source of over 70% of the world's cobalt, a metal that is critical to the electric-vehicle revolution because of its use in rechargeable batteries.
Last year, the U.S. signed a sweeping economic partnership with Congo aimed at attracting American investment and challenging the dominance of Chinese companies in the country's mining industry
Despite the global importance of Congo's copper and cobalt mines, however, environmental pollution from the industry has received comparatively little scrutiny.
In Kolwezi, pollution is severe. Neighborhoods near mines are often filled with an acrid smell that residents attribute to the sulfuric acid used to process minerals. A study published in June by environmental research organization Source International — carried out with the advocacy groups RAID and Afrewatch, and scientists from Congo's University of Lubumbashi — also highlighted the scale of the contamination.
Researchers found that levels of fine particulate matter, known as PM2.5, in Kolwezi were three to six times the World Health Organization's air quality guideline. The highest concentrations were recorded near the COMMUS mine.
These tiny particles can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream. Exposure poses health risks generally, but is particularly dangerous for pregnant women and young children.
The researchers also tested dust samples and found residue of copper, cobalt and manganese, which they said pointed to mining waste as the main source. When the study was released, Source International's executive director, Flaviano Bianchini, said that "these are among the most concerning air quality results we have documented in years of monitoring pollution at industrial mining sites around the world."
The study did not examine health impacts directly, and the authors recommended formal epidemiological research. Residents and health workers in Kolwezi nonetheless point to a string of ailments that they blame on a polluted environment.
In a dilapidated health clinic in the shadow of a mountain of waste from the COMMUS mine, nurse Héritier Bukassa said that people routinely break out in itchy hives. "Some sick people scratch themselves with knives to relieve itching," he explained.
Bukassa added that women in the area also suffer from high rates of miscarriage, and that he had referred four babies born with congenital malformations — mostly cleft palates — to hospitals this year alone.
Respiratory illnesses are common too, Bukassa said, especially in otherwise healthy babies who develop breathing problems a few weeks after birth. "No one from the [mining] company has ever come to talk to us about this," the nurse said.
Zijin, the owner of COMMUS, did not respond to emailed requests for comment. Neither did Congo's mining and environment ministries.
The Cobalt Institute, an industry lobby, said that understanding environmental pollution requires "an evidence-based approach that considers all potential sources and contributors." It added that companies perform environmental monitoring and carry out mitigation measures.
RAID, which is supporting the plaintiffs alongside Afrewatch, described the case this month as one of "the most ambitious legal challenges yet brought by Congolese residents over industrial mining pollution."
The suit is an important test case that could lead to communities challenging other mines in the future, it added.
The plaintiffs are seeking $1.3 million in compensation for health problems and medical expenses, as well as $5 million to restore the environment. Their lawyers say they worry their clients might come under pressure or intimidation to withdraw their testimony.
The mother, however, said she had no such fears. "We have a right to a clean environment," she said, "and to health."
