items.text:
Meet Colombia's fuzzy 'water guardians'
Meet Colombia's fuzzy 'water guardians'
MONGUÍ, Colombia — Moisés Moreno greets visitors at his greenhouse 10,000 feet high in the Andes Mountains. Underneath the plastic roof, he nurtures tiny seedlings that can grow to be 30-feet tall.
"Do you know anything about frailejons?" Moreno asks his visitors, who are mostly clueless.
Related to the sunflower, frailejons are the iconic flora of Colombia's high mountain wetlands, which are known as páramos, and are vital for the country's water supply.
The wooly fuzz on their leaves protect frailejons from the cold and absorb water from the cloud cover. This helps maintain moisture in the páramos, which are the source of major rivers, and much of Colombia's water.
But frailejons and the páramos where they grow face a growing array of threats, including farmers, cattle ranchers and coal miners who are gradually pushing higher into the Andes. In addition, climate change is warming the mountains, allowing invasive species to survive at higher altitudes and disrupt their fragile ecosystems.
Of the nearly 150 species of frailejons, two-thirds are at risk and 17 are endangered, says Mauricio Diazgranados, a Colombian expert on the plant who is chief science officer at the New York Botanical Garden.
"They are a keystone species for maintaining the páramos and play a key role in water production," he says. "But most frailejons are in trouble,"
When explorers first spotted the shrubs mysteriously protruding from the mountain fog centuries ago, they reminded them of hooded monks. Hence the name frailejon, which is Spanish for "big friar."
The long, thin leaves of some species bend toward the sky and resemble palm fronds. Many are stout in the middle because, rather than falling to the ground, their dying leaves slump down to form a brownish outer shell to their trunks.
The Muisca Indians, who once populated the area, considered frailejons to be sacred guardians of the water. When he first came across the plants as a teenager in Colombia, Diazgranados says: "I became completely captivated."
By contrast, Moreno, 53, who runs the frailejon greenhouse, used to be one of the plant's predators. Growing up on a mountainside farm near the central Colombian town of Monguí, Moreno and neighboring farmers knew little about them and chopped them down to make way for potato fields and cow pastures.
"We viewed them as a nuisance," Moreno says.
Later, while employed by a coal mine, he was injured during a cave-in and vowed to work above ground in the fresh mountain air.
On his own he began studying páramo ecosystem that he'd grown up in, started his greenhouse and began leading tourists and volunteers on expeditions to replace the frailejons that had been wiped out.
"I felt inspired to do something to protect the páramos," he says.
Elsewhere, Colombia's National Parks agency and even its armed forces have gotten involved in reforestation campaigns after wildfires scorched thousands of acres of frailejons.
Yet many average Colombians have learned about the plant's importance through an enormously popular cartoon character called Ernesto Pérez. Shaped like a frailejon, he exhorts people to conserve the flora and fauna of the Andes, similar to the way Smokey Bear promotes forest fire prevention in the U.S.
In fact, several of the volunteers Moreno is guiding up the mountain say the cartoon and its earworm theme song introduced them to the frailejon.
"The song is very contagious," says Nicolás Coronado, 25, who works for a Bogotá-based plastics company, and is carrying a 6-inch frailejon that he will plant in the páramo.
The hike takes the group up to an altitude of 11,000 feet, past streams, waterfalls and lagoons. Underfoot, the ground is damp and spongy. The area is a state park and frailejons dot the landscape. But there are also barbed-wire fences erected by farmers and a half dozen cows grazing on the mountainside.
Moreno and his assistants show the volunteers how to dig shallow holes, then add a bit of shredded tobacco as fertilizer, before nestling the tiny frailejons into the soil.
Their survival is no sure thing. Many die in the cold, harsh climate and those that take hold grow just a few inches per year.
To help them along, the volunteers hold an impromptu ceremony, with one member reciting a prayer to connect with the mountain spirits and another blowing on a conch shell.
By now, some volunteers have grown attached to the frailejons that they've carried up the mountain and have bestowed names on them. Among them is biologist Julieta Barba has baptized hers "Gerry," in honor of her mother.
After patting some dirt around the plant's roots, she says: "I'm very excited for her future here in the páramo."

items.title: Black travelers on Route 66 weren't welcome at most gas stations — except this one
items.summary:
Black travelers on Route 66 weren't welcome at most gas stations — except this one
During the Jim Crow Era, Black families traveling Route 66, the historic highway that ran more than 2,000 miles from Chicago to Los Angeles, needed to carry food and gas with them. Most restaurants, gas stations and m
items.text:
Black travelers on Route 66 weren't welcome at most gas stations — except this one
During the Jim Crow Era, Black families traveling Route 66, the historic highway that ran more than 2,000 miles from Chicago to Los Angeles, needed to carry food and gas with them. Most restaurants, gas stations and motels wouldn't serve them.
But there was one place they were guaranteed to find respite: a small, family-owned business just east of Oklahoma City that offered fuel, food and a place to stop for the night. The Threatt Filling Station, according to the National Trust for Historic Preservation, was the only known Black-owned and operated gas station along the famous Mother Road.
"Grandpa took care of whatever they needed to have," said Linda Fisher, the granddaughter of the station's founder, Allen Threatt Sr. Her family still owns the station and the 150 acres around it.
"If they didn't have any food, they fed them," she said. "If they needed some kind of shelter or blankets or those types of things, Grandpa and Grandma made sure they got those kinds of things."
Threatt moved from Alabama to the farming community of Luther, Okla., in the early 1900s as part of the Great Migration. His father had been born into slavery, and Threatt and his wife, Alberta, seeking stability and refuge, wanted their own farm.
At the time, Oklahoma was a place where Black migrants could own land and form their own towns. Between 1865 and 1920, Black Americans settled more than 50 "all-Black" municipalities in Oklahoma, the largest number of any state.
But Oklahoma also had its issues — by the time of the Great Depression, many of those all-Black towns had ceased to exist. And there was a rise in "sundown towns": all-white communities that warned non-white people to get out before dark, or they would face violence or police harassment. There was a sundown town on either side of the filling station during the Jim Crow era, Fisher said.
But at the Threatt Filling Station, "everyone was welcome," Fisher said.
The building, which closed to the public in the 1970s, is now on the National Register of Historic Places.
A century of welcome
Allen Threatt Sr. built the original filling station in 1915, when he started to notice people driving by a corner of his property on what was then the Ozark Trail.
In 1926, Route 66 was founded, and the trickle of cars became a steady stream. When the old wooden building burned down, Threatt replaced it with a charming sandstone one, built like a small, welcoming house.
Eventually, the station and the property surrounding it became a community hub. There were dances in the restaurant next door, social club meetings, barbecues. Occasionally, players from the Negro Leagues would have a game on the baseball diamond.
Allen and Alberta Threatt had 11 living children, and a couple of them took over the running of the station in the 1950s.
But the building of the Interstate Highway System, launched under the Eisenhower administration, led to dwindling traffic on Route 66, and by the mid-'70s, the station had closed.
A half-century later later, the building was derelict. In 2021, the National Trust for Historic Preservation listed the station as one of America's 11 Most Endangered Historic Places.
But hope was around the corner: A few years earlier, a trio of Allen Threatt Sr.'s grandchildren decided to restore the property. Now, thanks to nonprofit grants and a lot of cousin elbow grease, the filling station has a restored exterior.
Ceramic Conoco gas pumps from the 1940s stand proudly outside; new signs inside detail the history of the family, the gas station and Route 66, and visitors can talk to the Threatts themselves and buy a T-shirt.
Eventually, the family is planning to build an RV park, a restaurant and perhaps even a new baseball diamond.
"We're all standing on Grandpa's shoulders — Grandpa and Grandma's shoulders," said Edward Threatt, another grandchild of Allen Threatt Sr. who is one of the leaders of the restoration.
"We have this property today because of Grandpa, and so we represent him, we represent our mothers, our fathers. And we're just trying to do them proud, that's all."
Broadcast and digital story edited by Steven Drummond; audio mixed by Chloee Weiner. Photo editing by Emily Bogle.

items.title: For workplace culture champions, Jensen Huang's return is 'unfathomable'
items.summary:
For workplace culture champions, Jensen Huang's return is 'unfathomable'
Sign up for NPR's Up First morning newsletter for the stories you need to start your day.
On Monday morning, a couple hours after Nvidia's board announced it had reinstated co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO, President Trump shared
items.text:
For workplace culture champions, Jensen Huang's return is 'unfathomable'
Sign up for NPR's Up First morning newsletter for the stories you need to start your day.
On Monday morning, a couple hours after Nvidia's board announced it had reinstated co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO, President Trump shared an AI-generated image on social media.
It's based on that striking photo of the president from 2024, just after he survived an assasination attempt. Surrounded by Secret Service agents, his face bloodied, Trump hoists a defiant fist in the air.
In the doctored photo, instead of Trump, it's Huang. An Nvidia flag flies behind him. And in his hoisted fist, he holds a red bra.
"I was absolutely flabbergasted," says Bo Young Lee, who worked as chief diversity officer at Uber for five years starting in 2018.
To Lee, it seems Trump is suggesting that the Nvidia CEO is as important to the country as he is.
"But then also the red bra is an indication that it's open hunting season for women," she says. "It stirs up all sorts of stereotypes and misogynistic perspectives about women."
To others, the image drives home the idea that in Silicon Valley, as long as you're successful, anything goes.
The White House has not responded to NPR's questions about what Trump was trying to say with the image.
Spy intrigue overshadows workplace transgressions
Even as Huang's return to Nvidia has been cheered by investors, some employees and Trump, it has sparked shock and disbelief among others, including those who have long worked to improve workplace culture in Silicon Valley.
"It's actually unfathomable to me," says Lee, who now serves as an adviser to AI4ALL, a nonprofit dedicated to increasing diversity, inclusion, and responsible practices in artificial intelligence.
After The New York Times revealed that Huang had engaged in an extramarital affair with a woman the U.S government believes is a Chinese intelligence asset, Lee watched as the broader conversation was dominated by concerns about national security, corporate governance and Nvidia's stock price.
That scandal overshadowed allegations of other problematic behavior in the workplace, specifically Huang's alleged affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, one of Huang's many direct reports.
"Everyone is minimizing that alleged relationship there because of who she is," says Lee.
The fact that Powell is herself a senior leader who makes a lot of money shouldn't matter, Lee says. She argues that people in subordinate roles, even powerful ones, can't properly consent, "simply for the fact that there is this power differential."
Nvidia's board did find that Huang's behavior was "inconsistent" with the company's code of conduct. By Monday morning, that didn't seem to matter.
"The Board of Directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang's candor and ability to lead Nvidia," the board said in a statement.
Lee says that response sends a message to Nvidia employees and all of Silicon Valley that it's OK to break the rules as long as you come clean.
"'Just be transparent with us,'" she imagines the board saying.
Nvidia did not respond to NPR's questions about Lee's concerns.
A deepening of "tech bro" culture in Trump's second term
In Silicon Valley, there have been private conversations about Huang's alleged workplace transgressions and the power dynamics at play, but women don't appear eager to speak publicly.
NPR reached out to two dozen women who work in the tech space. Freada Kapor Klein was one of the few willing to talk. The social impact investor says conversations about workplace behavior are much quieter than they have been in other eras, such as in 2017 and 2018, when a number of venture capitalists resigned amid allegations they were sexually harassing female entrepreneurs.
In 2017, Kapor Klein and her husband, Mitch Kapor, used their positions as early investors in Uber to publicly call out the company over its toxic culture, one they said tolerated bullying and harassment. The co-founder and CEO Travis Kalanick ended up resigning. Kapor Klein hoped it'd be a teachable moment.
But now, she feels Silicon Valley has gone backwards.
"Tech bro culture is stronger now than I have seen it in decades," she says, adding that Trump's attacks on DEI have amplified that culture.
Among women and people of color in Silicon Valley, she says there's now real trepidation about the anti-DEI sentiment — the axing of programs, chief diversity officers and employee resource groups.
"All of the supports or mechanisms have been pretty much stripped away," she says.
"All that matters is money"
To be clear, Huang has not been accused of predatory behavior. Still, Kapor Klein says his swift comeback is troubling.
"It is a resounding message that all that matters is money," she says. "If you are thought of as a singular talent, you can violate corporate policy, you can possibly threaten national security, you can make up your own rules as you go, you can create toxic workplace culture — as long as you bring in the money."
By the end of last week, Nvidia's stock had fallen almost 49% from its peak in October, and about 27% from before Huang's resignation. On Monday, it rebounded significantly.
Lee says Silicon Valley has always had an unhealthy relationship with its "genius founders."
"We elevate these leaders to god-like levels, and that's been done to Mark Zuckerberg, and that's being done to Sam Altman, and that's definitely [been] done to Jensen Huang," says Lee. "You become untouchable at that point."
Kapor Klein says what's unfolded at Nvidia has made abundantly clear that AI companies need guardrails for their CEOs, not just for the tools they're creating.
"We see a board that ignored that," she says. "There are no guardrails on this CEO's behavior."
NPR's Scott Horsley contributed to this story.

items.title: CS Murkomen Orders Crackdown on Illegal Guns After Deadly Isiolo-Garissa Border Clashes
items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 24 – Interior Cabinet Secretary Kipchumba Murkomen has ordered an intelligence-led security operation to recover illegal firearms in Isiolo and Garissa counties following deadly inter-communal clashes that left several people dead and property destroyed.
Murkomen announced the me
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 24 – Interior Cabinet Secretary Kipchumba Murkomen has ordered an intelligence-led security operation to recover illegal firearms in Isiolo and Garissa counties following deadly inter-communal clashes that left several people dead and property destroyed.
Murkomen announced the measures after convening a consultative meeting with leaders from the two counties to assess the security situation, identify gaps and agree on interventions to restore peace.
In a statement shared on Tuesday, the CS said the government would intensify security operations while strengthening local peace initiatives to prevent further violence.
He directed the Inspector General of Police Douglas Kanja to organise an intensive operation targeting illegal firearms in the two counties.
The National Police Service will also undertake a comprehensive assessment of security deployments and reposition police installations while increasing personnel in areas affected by the violence.
Murkomen further directed the Inspector General to assess the mobility needs of security officers in the region, with Isiolo and Garissa prioritised in the upcoming allocation of police vehicles.
The government will also review the operations of National Police Reservists (NPR) in the two counties, including vetting and retraining officers.
Murkomen said those found to be misusing their firearms would be replaced as part of efforts to strengthen accountability and restore public confidence in security operations.
The CS also announced plans to strengthen and resource peace committees in the two counties to promote peaceful coexistence and establish mechanisms for sharing natural resources.
The government will convene public meetings involving political leaders, National Government Administrative Officers (NGAOs), elders and religious leaders to address tensions, recover stolen livestock and resolve outstanding disputes.
Murkomen said the government would engage telecommunications companies to improve mobile network coverage in the affected areas to enhance communication and security coordination.
He added that the allocation of funds for constructing security roads in the region would be fast-tracked to improve access and facilitate the movement of security personnel.
The Interior CS also announced plans to visit the affected areas next month to hold peace meetings and assess the implementation of the agreed security interventions.
He called on residents to remain calm as security agencies pursue those responsible for the killings and destruction of property.
Murkomen condemned the violence and expressed condolences to families who lost loved ones, noting that communities along the Isiolo-Garissa border had historically maintained peaceful relations and shared cultural ties, trade networks and natural resources.

items.title: Death of Nahel: French police officer who shot dead a teenage boy to stand trial for murder
items.summary:
Death of Nahel: French police officer who shot dead a teenage boy to stand trial for murder
A French police officer who shot and killed 17-year-old Nahel Merzouk during a traffic stop in June 2023 will stand trial for murder following a ruling by the Versailles appeals court. Merzouk's death at the
items.text:
Death of Nahel: French police officer who shot dead a teenage boy to stand trial for murder
A French police officer who shot and killed 17-year-old Nahel Merzouk during a traffic stop in June 2023 will stand trial for murder following a ruling by the Versailles appeals court. Merzouk's death at the hands of the police sparked intense riots in the sprawling suburbs surrounding Paris.
A French appeals court on Tuesday ruled that the police officer who fatally shot a teenage boy of North African descent in June 2023 during a traffic stop should be tried for murder. The police killing of 17-year-old Nahel Merzouk set off days of riots in Paris’s poorer suburbs.
The Versailles court of appeals found that there was “sufficient evidence” against the defendant and rejected the “mitigating circumstance raised by the defence”, it explained. The decision may be subject to further appeals.
Mobile phone footage of police officer Florian M. shooting Nahel point-blank inside a car during a traffic stop on a busy street went viral following the boy’s death, sparking days of protests.
The police initially alleged that Nahel had driven his car at the officer – a story contradicted by the video evidence, which showed two officers standing by a stationary car, one of them pointing his gun at its driver.
Read moreFrench suburbs: Fresh protests against police violence rooted in decades of harassment, inequality
Tuesday’s ruling is only the latest in a series of competing judicial rulings over a case that has for many become a symbol of police brutality in France.
The police officer, who spent five months in pre-trial detention before being released in November 2023, had initially been set to be tried for murder before appealing the decision.
The appeals court in March ruled that he should instead be tried for the lesser charge of violence leading to death in a court without a jury.
That decision was then overruled by France’s highest court in June, opening the path for the police officer to stand trial for murder.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

items.title: Why S Korea issued air raid alert after Russian jets flew near its airspace
items.summary:
Why S Korea issued air raid alert after Russian jets flew near its airspace
South Korean authorities issue air raid warnings after several Russian jets were on verge of entering its airspace.
South Korea has scrambled fighter jets and issued brief air raid warnings for residents of an island after R
items.text:
Why S Korea issued air raid alert after Russian jets flew near its airspace
South Korean authorities issue air raid warnings after several Russian jets were on verge of entering its airspace.
South Korea has scrambled fighter jets and issued brief air raid warnings for residents of an island after Russian military planes approached its airspace over waters between the Korean Peninsula and Japan.
Russian jets on Tuesday briefly entered South Korea’s air defence identification zone (ADIZ), an aerial buffer area between countries, South Korea’s military said, adding that “multiple” Russian aircraft were “on the verge” of entering the country’s airspace over Ulleung Island.
“Airspace intrusion was anticipated. Therefore, to protect the safety of our people, we issued a warning pre-emptively,” Jang Do-young, a spokesperson for the Joint Chiefs of Staff, said.
Authorities had earlier issued an alert that a North Korean plane had made an incursion, which would have been a significant escalation in tensions between the two Koreas, which remain technically at war after the 1950-1953 Korean War ended with an armistice and not a peace treaty. South Korea later issued a correction saying no North Korean jet was involved.
Here’s everything we know about the incident:
Why did South Korea tell residents to take shelter?
According to the Joint Chiefs of Staff, about five Russian military aircraft entered South Korea’s ADIZ on Tuesday morning. There was no intrusion of South Korea’s airspace by the Russian aircraft in the end, the South Korean military said.
Jang said the aircraft came “very close” to the airspace above Ulleung Island, which is home to 9,000 people and lies 120km (75 miles) off the northeastern coast of South Korea. South Korean fighter jets conducted “tactical manoeuvres” to prevent any incident, the Joint Chiefs of Staff said.
But confusion ensued over the alert and who was responsible for the intrusion.
The government of North Gyeongsang province, which includes Ulleung, sent out an alert saying the jets were suspected to be North Korean, which it later corrected.
Still, the Ministry of the Interior and Safety issued the shelter warning at 7:52am (22:52 GMT on Monday) and lifted the alert three minutes later after the aircraft had left the area.
The last time the island in the East Sea, also known as the Sea of Japan, was sent into panic was in 2022 after North Korea fired more than 20 missiles into the sea during a period of heightened inter-Korean tensions. After one missile headed towards Ulleung, it triggered air raid sirens and led to residents evacuating.
What has South Korea said about Russia?
South Korea’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said it had conveyed its regret over the incident to Russia and called for measures to prevent a recurrence, South Korea’s Yonhap News Agency reported.
The ministry also sent the message to the Russian embassy in Seoul but stopped short of summoning the Russian ambassador, diplomatic sources told the agency.
Still, the Ministry of National Defence called in Russia’s military attache, Nikolai Marchenko, to lodge a formal complaint.
Russian military aircraft have entered South Korea’s ADIZ five times so far this year.
Last week, South Korea announced Russian military aircraft had temporarily entered the ADIZ.
On the same day, Japan protested to Moscow after also saying two suspected Russian aircraft had entered its airspace off its southwestern coast.
In 2019, South Korean fighter jets had fired warning shots after a Russian A-50 early warning aircraft, flying alongside Russian and Chinese bombers in a joint patrol, entered its territorial airspace near the island of Dokdo.
At the time, Moscow denied violating South Korean airspace.
What has Russia said about the incident?
So far, Moscow has not commented.
Russia does not recognise South Korea’s authority over its ADIZ and has argued it has no basis in international law.
What is the status of Russian-South Korean relations?
The two countries have fairly strained relations.
Moscow has a close relationship with North Korea, and Pyongyang deployed troops to help Russia’s soldiers during its war in Ukraine. Meanwhile, Seoul has joined Western sanctions against Russia due to its invasion of Ukraine.
However, recently, the leaders of the two countries have signalled interest in restoring ties.
Last week, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung and Russian President Vladimir Putin held a 10-minute meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit and agreed to pursue cooperation where possible while also working to ease tensions on the Korean Peninsula, an official in Seoul told reporters on the condition of anonymity, Yonhap reported.

items.summary:
Russian strike kills two in Ukraine, days after ship attack off Libya
Russian attack on Zaporizhzhia destroyed a house and damaged a five-storey apartment building, Ukrainian officials said.
A Russian air attack on Zaporizhzhia in Ukraine has killed two people and wounded more than 40, including an
items.text:
Russian strike kills two in Ukraine, days after ship attack off Libya
Russian attack on Zaporizhzhia destroyed a house and damaged a five-storey apartment building, Ukrainian officials said.
A Russian air attack on Zaporizhzhia in Ukraine has killed two people and wounded more than 40, including an infant, the day after Kyiv said its drones sank a Russian warship in a Libyan port far from the front lines of the war.
Russia’s dawn raid on the city in southeast Ukraine destroyed a house and damaged a five-storey apartment building, regional officials said on Tuesday.
It came as the two warring sides continued long-range attacks, launching hundreds of drones overnight.
Russia’s Ministry of Defence said air defences intercepted and destroyed 699 Ukrainian drones over seven regions, occupied Crimea and the Black Sea.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 355 drones flew towards the capital overnight and 63 were shot down as they approached.
Reporting from Moscow, Al Jazeera’s Amin Dorghami said it had been a “long time” since Moscow had been targeted with as many drones.
Ukraine’s Air Force said Russia launched 96 drones overnight, with hits at 13 locations and 73 shot down or jammed.
Russia’s Defence Ministry said its forces hit an electricity substation in Pryluky, in Ukraine’s Chernihiv region, which it said powered Ukraine’s military. Russian forces also hit a dry cargo ship southwest of Odesa that the ministry said was carrying military supplies.
“This too could be considered routine, since Russia is enforcing a blockade on Ukraine’s Black Sea ports,” Dorghami said.
Late on Monday, the Polish military said a Russian drone briefly entered Poland’s airspace during an attack on western Ukraine but was not shot down because of the risk to civilians. Deputy Defence Minister Pawel Zalewski said he assumed the incursion was deliberate, coming three days after three Russian cruise missiles crashed in eastern Poland.
Reporting from Kyiv, Al Jazeera’s Abdelaziz Mujahid said the incursion “may also signal that the conflict and these confrontations are widening”.
It follows Ukraine’s attack on the Russian corvette Merkury in the Libyan port of Benghazi on Sunday. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said seven Ukrainian-built naval drones were used in the “completely legitimate operation against enemy ships”.
“The strike in Benghazi has left Russia without one of its newest combat ships,” said Al Jazeera’s Yulia Shapovalova, reporting from Moscow. “It was commissioned only three years ago.”
Russia’s UN envoy, Vassily Nebenzia, accused Western countries of backing Ukraine’s recent attacks and said Moscow would keep using military means to ensure its security.
On Monday, debris from Russian drones fell in central Kyiv, close to the president’s office and set a five-storey building on fire. Mayor Vitali Klitschko said five people were injured, including a foreign national.
“All of this is a bit too close for comfort for Ukrainians, especially considering that the presidential palace is just a few hundred metres up the road,” reported Al Jazeera’s Audrey McAlpine from the scene.
Zelenskyy said on Monday evening that Ukrainian intelligence warned that Russia was preparing a new series of strikes and urged residents to heed air raid alerts.

items.title: DR Congo says aircraft missing as rebels claim to shoot down plane
items.summary:
The Democratic Republic of Congo says it is searching for one of its aircraft, after rebels said they had shot down a warplane in the east.
The military said it had lost contact with a small Cessna 208 cargo plane on Sunday following “poor weather conditions”. The fate of the plane and its crew rema
items.text:
The Democratic Republic of Congo says it is searching for one of its aircraft, after rebels said they had shot down a warplane in the east.
The military said it had lost contact with a small Cessna 208 cargo plane on Sunday following “poor weather conditions”. The fate of the plane and its crew remained uncertain, it added.
On the same day, the rebel Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN) said it had shot down a warplane that was on a mission to bomb Minembwe in South Kivu province.
Four people were reportedly on board, including a Ugandan and a South African pilot, who is said to have been captured alive.
The BBC has not independently verified the rebels’ claim.
It is also unclear whether the aircraft reported missing by the DR Congo military is the same one rebels say they shot down.
Uganda’s military on Monday denied any involvement.
A statement attributed to army chief Muhoozi Kainerugaba posted on X said: “UPDF had nothing to do with the aircraft that was shot down in Minembwe. We have penalized that company.”
The statement did not identify the company or explain what penalty had been imposed.
Gen Kainerugaba later posted that “no Ugandan is allowed to work for mercenary companies in [DR Congo]”.
Uganda’s denial followed the circulation of a video apparently showing a man being questioned beside the plane’s wreckage.
In the footage, the man identifies himself as Ugandan and claims he had been sent by the government. The BBC has not independently verified the video or established the man’s identity.
He and the alleged South African pilot are said to be the only other survivors.
South African media outlet Mail & Guardian quoted an FRN spokesperson identifying the pilot as a South African and a “mercenary [who] has no link to the place that he was hired to destroy”.
“Unfortunately, we have a multi-country conflict in the eastern DRC,” deputy FRN spokesperson Oscar Balinda told the outlet.
The Congolese government has in the past used foreign mercenaries to fight the rebels.
In recent days, fighting between the FRN and the government has intensified with the rebel group accusing the government of targeting heavily populated areas.
The rebels control large areas of eastern DR Congo, including the major city of Goma, after major territorial advances last year.
Aid agencies say the violence is increasingly disrupting healthcare services.
Over the weekend, medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières said fighting in North Kivu had forced some of its teams to temporarily suspend outreach activities.
The fighting has also affected the response to the Ebola outbreak, with many health workers trapped, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
The epicentre of the outbreak is in eastern DR Congo, which has been wracked by conflict for many decades, with some affected areas under rebel control.

Fiona, a social media star since her premature birth at the zoo in 201
items.text:
Dead hippo to be honoured on football club tifo
- Published
Major League Soccer side FC Cincinnati will honour Fiona, a hippo that recently died at the city's zoo, with a tifo display at their match with Nashville SC on Saturday.
Fiona, a social media star since her premature birth at the zoo in 2017, died on Thursday after swallowing a woollen hat that had slipped into her enclosure.
The Ohio side will now raise a banner depicting the nine-year-old semi-aquatic mammal in their post-season MLS Cup encounter with Nashville, who won the Supporters' Shield for being the highest-placed team in the league campaign.
Cincinnati said Fiona was a "beloved hippo who became a symbol of Cincinnati and captured hearts around the world".
The tifo will be produced by fan group The Forge Cincy, who painted the display on Sunday in a garage next to Cincinnati's TQL Stadium.
The club will also make a donation in Fiona's memory for every fan in attendance to the Cincinnati Zoo and Botanical Garden.
- Removal of hat inside Fiona the hippo was 'impossible', Cincinnati Zoo says 
  - Published3 days ago
- Fiona the hippo dies after swallowing a hat at Cincinnati Zoo 
  - Published4 days ago
Cincinnati's Nick Hagglund, who hails from the city and is in his eighth season with the team, previously paid tribute to Fiona after scoring in his side's 3-1 victory over Orlando on the day of her death.
The defender yelled "that's for Fiona", mimicking the ears on top of her head, in a celebration video, external on the club's Instagram.
Later, on his Instagram account, external, Hagglund posted, "This one was for her @fionahippo @cincinnatizoo.
"Cincinnati needed a win on the day after the passing of our beloved hippo, a symbol of hope and resilience for our city, and the lads answered the call."
Cincinnati's tifo is one of a number of tributes paid to the hippo, with Cincinnati Bengals wide receiver Tee Higgins wearing a Fiona sweater, external prior to his American football franchise's defeat by the Washington Commanders on Monday.
Meanwhile handlers of the blue hippo balloon at New York's annual Macy's Thanksgiving Parade will wear a purple patch in her honour.
At birth Fiona weighed 13kg (29lb), which the zoo said was about half the previous lowest recorded birth weight for her species, and previously inspired an ice cream flavour and a character in Cincinnati's ballet.
Fiona swallowed the woollen hat around 10 days prior to her death, with the item getting into her enclosure by accident after a visitor tossed it in the air and it caught on a ceiling fan that flung it through a small opening.
"We probably couldn't make [it] happen again if we tried," said zoo spokesperson Michelle Curley.
Hippos normally live up to 50 years in human care, according to the zoo.
Nashville finished top of the MLS Eastern Conference, 31 points ahead of ninth-placed Cincinnati.
However, having beaten Orlando in a one-off wildcard round, Cincinnati defeated Nashville 1-0 in the opening match of their best-of-three round one series.
Should Cincinnati win on Saturday they will progress to a one-off conference semi-final with either Chicago Fire or Charlotte FC, with a conference final prior to the season-ending MLS Cup final.

items.title: How two directors fought back when their film was stolen — and won an International Emmy Award
items.summary:
German directors' doc on stolen film wins International Emmy Award
November 24, 2026
It sounds like the plot of a screenplay, but it happened to two Berlin film students in real life. The documentary they made out of their unusual story, "The Talented Mr. F," has now won an International Emmy Award.
items.text:
German directors' doc on stolen film wins International Emmy Award
November 24, 2026
It sounds like the plot of a screenplay, but it happened to two Berlin film students in real life. The documentary they made out of their unusual story, "The Talented Mr. F," has now won an International Emmy Award.
Moritz Henneberg and Julius Drost had created an animated short film for their final project at university.
"Butty" tells the tale of a household robot that gets kicked out when it can't do its job properly.
When the two filmmakers posted the work on YouTube, this touching tale quickly went viral. After generating a huge amount of hits, the duo decided to submit their work to festivals — but they were in for a shock: Organizers told them the film had already been submitted under a different name.
How could that have happened?
US student Samuel Felinton had downloaded the film, made minimal edits, given it a new title, "T-130," and got rid of the original credits. As the alleged author, he went on to win numerous prizes and made a name for himself in the United States.
A story turned into a documentary, 'The Talented Mr. F'
Shocked by the blatant theft of their work, Henneberg and Drost sought legal advice. They were told that if they opted to sue, the process would be arduous and costly. So, the filmmakers took matters into their own hands and went to the US to confront Felinton — filming their journey along the way.
"We'd already made documentary films," Henneberg told DW. "And the idea just popped into our heads: This is a brilliant story — let's make a documentary about it."
The two directors had in fact developed a kind of fascination for the man who'd stolen their film.
"We looked at his vlogs and sort of took a deep dive into his world," said Drost. "We almost saw him as a kind of celebrity. We discovered a lot about him and really wanted to meet him in person."
Fascination instead of anger
While family and friends reacted with anger, the two young filmmakers remained surprisingly calm. They were more perplexed than anything: "Our families and friends hated Samuel. But we just wanted to understand what had happened," they said.
The pair put together a film crew and traveled to Morgantown, West Virginia — the university town where Felinton lives. With the help of a New York filmmaker pretending to be making a documentary about young animators, they won Felinton's trust — and then Henneberg, Drost and Felinton were finally in a room together.
The two German filmmakers had prepared for all manner of scenarios ahead of the meeting: "We expected an emotional reaction — that he'd run away, cry, be ashamed or get aggressive. But he remained completely calm. That was the only thing we hadn't bargained for. We thought his world would implode. But he showed barely any emotion at all," they recalled.
Felinton explained how he'd shortened and "improved" the film and that this was how it came to be such a success. He agreed to transfer any prize money. His manner was cool and matter-of-fact, which Drost and Henneberg found both unsettling and fascinating. After their chat, the three barbecued together and played a round of basketball.
Sue or stay creative?
Later, many viewers accused the two German filmmakers of being too soft on the plagiarist. Others praised their approach.
"The reactions were very divided," said Drost. "Some said we should've sued him or punched him in the face. Others said we'd shown new ways to resolve conflicts."
"And in the end, it wasn't personal," added Henneberg. "He wanted to make something of himself — he could've taken another film. But if a big studio like Pixar had stolen our film, that'd be quite a different story."
And so, Henneberg and Drost made the conscious decision keep things respectful.
They didn't want to "publicly embarrass him or punish him any more than necessary," they said, adding that their documentary was sufficient "revenge."
The title of the documentary, "Der talentierte Mister F." ("The Talented Mister F."), is no coincidence. It's a play on the movie title "The Talented Mr. Ripley," the story of a young man who assumes the identity of a wealthy heir and ends up mired in a web of lies, fraud and, finally, murder. And just like Mr. Ripley, Felinton had also assumed a false identity.
Award-winning works
Felinton did actually end up sending them the trophies he had won, as well as a sum of money.
For their part, however, the festivals preferred to keep their distance from the saga. As one organizer said: The prize has been awarded, and there's nothing we can do about it — it's up to these guys to work things out between themselves.
For the original filmmakers themselves, the scandal has also had a positive impact: Since the documentary was released in Germany in October 2025, their animation film has garnered even more attention on YouTube. Henneberg and Drost uploaded it again, and in the credits, special thanks also go out to Samuel Felinton.
And now, the documentary is winning its own awards: Before being honored with the International Emmy Award, it also won a Grimme Prize, one of Germany's most prestigious television awards.
'Don't be afraid to show yourselves'
Felinton was able to steal the film in the first place in part because when it first appeared online in 2023, it could just be downloaded from YouTube.
Drost and Henneberg say uploading "Butty" back then wasn't a mistake, however, saying that was the risk of putting something online.
The alternative would have been not to show the film at all, they said, then no one would have seen it.
They have a clear message for young creatives.
"Don't be discouraged. Be aware that something like this can happen — but stay creative in how you deal with it. Suing is expensive and often doesn't do much good. Instead, show the world that you're the authors."
What started out as film plagiarism ended up becoming material for another project. And that's perhaps the most unusual twist in this very quirky stor

items.title: Indonesia expo targets new trade and investment partnerships with Kenya
items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 24– Indonesia is seeking to deepen its economic ties with Kenya through a Nairobi business expo showcasing investment and trade opportunities in education, aviation, pharmaceuticals, agriculture and consumer goods.
The two-day Indonesia-Nairobi Expo (IndoNEX) 2026, scheduled for
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 24– Indonesia is seeking to deepen its economic ties with Kenya through a Nairobi business expo showcasing investment and trade opportunities in education, aviation, pharmaceuticals, agriculture and consumer goods.
The two-day Indonesia-Nairobi Expo (IndoNEX) 2026, scheduled for November 26–27 at the Trademark Hotel and Village Market, will bring together businesses and stakeholders from the two countries to explore partnerships, expand market access and strengthen commercial relations.
The expo will feature business and investment opportunities, trade and product exhibitions, business-to-business networking and education opportunities, with Indonesian companies expected to showcase products and services across various sectors.
Among the sectors targeted are agriculture, fast-moving consumer goods, tourism, jewellery, food and beverages, education, aviation and pharmaceuticals, reflecting Indonesia’s ambition to broaden economic cooperation with Kenya beyond traditional trade engagements.
The first day, on November 26, will feature the IndoNEX Business Seminar and Expo at Trademark Hotel, Village Market, providing a platform for business discussions, investment engagements and networking between Kenyan and Indonesian stakeholders.
The second day will shift focus to cultural exchange and consumer engagement, with the Indonesian Festival scheduled for November 27 from 2pm at the Village Market Food Court.
The festival will feature Indonesian cultural performances, a batik fashion show, a traditional batik-making workshop and exhibitions of Indonesian food and products. Entry will be free.
The Embassy of Indonesia in Nairobi said the festival was part of efforts to bring the two countries closer through new connections, partnerships and opportunities.
The event is being organised under the theme, Grow Your Business with Indonesia: Building Strategic Partnerships for Shared Prosperity, with the broader message that Indonesia and Kenya are stronger together.
The expo comes amid growing efforts by both countries to strengthen economic and diplomatic relations, with trade, investment and people-to-people exchanges offering opportunities for deeper cooperation.

A large-scale search operation for a suspected lion sighted in woodland north of Istanbul has ended, with the animal in question found to be neither a lion nor any other type of big c
items.text:
Istanbul 'lion hunt' ends after no big cat found after all
Published November 23, 2026last updated November 24, 2026
A large-scale search operation for a suspected lion sighted in woodland north of Istanbul has ended, with the animal in question found to be neither a lion nor any other type of big cat, according to the Istanbul governor's office.
The governor's office first issued a statement on Sunday evening saying that security cameras had captured footage of a lion on the loose in Sariyer, north of Istanbul's European side. It said "the lion has been located and the efforts to capture it were underway."
The parks authority also said in an online statement that police officers in the area had spotted "an animal resembling a lion" on surveillance cameras.
Turkish media published grainy images purportedly showing a lioness walking through a grassy area. Some media reports suggested it had escaped from a nearby home.
The Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor's Office also issued a statement saying it had launched an investigation focused on identifying the lion's owner.
After a day of searching, however, the Istanbul governor's office said "no concrete evidence indicating ‌the presence of a lion was found."
It said based on new footage, "it has been determined that the animal in the footage is neither a lion nor any other species of big cat."
The governor's office did not provide further information about what the animal seen in the footage was.
Outcry among activists
The earlier reports about a lion on the loose had sparked an outrage among activists.
Northern Forests Defense, an independent ecology advocacy movement, called for "the individuals who illegally held this lion captive to be identified and brought to justice."
"Removing wild animals from their natural habitats and keeping them in captivity in villas is a crime," the organization said on X.
Wildlife conservationist Gokce Coskun said on X that "there are thousands of people keeping lions illegally in Turkey" and "licensed 'lion parks' have sprung up everywhere."
Last year, a lion that escaped from a "theme park" near the southern city of Antalya was shot dead after attacking a man.
Doganay Tolunay, an ecology professor at Istanbul University, said questions must be asked about how a globally threatened species was brought into Turkey, how it passed through customs and why those keeping it have not been identified.
Although keeping wild animals as pets is forbidden in Turkey, the country has become a hub for the illegal wild animal trade as traffickers exploit its air links to Africa and Asia.
In December 2024, a young gorilla was rescued after being discovered in a crate at Istanbul Airport.

items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 24 – Court of Appeal Judge Fatuma Sichale has warned that Kenya’s fight against corruption will remain unsuccessful unless citizens take personal responsibility for confronting graft, saying the burden cannot be left to investigative agencies and the Judiciary.
Sichale said insti
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 24 – Court of Appeal Judge Fatuma Sichale has warned that Kenya’s fight against corruption will remain unsuccessful unless citizens take personal responsibility for confronting graft, saying the burden cannot be left to investigative agencies and the Judiciary.
Sichale said institutional efforts by the Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission (EACC), the courts and the media had helped advance accountability, but lasting change would depend on Kenyans rejecting corruption in their everyday dealings.
Speaking on Tuesday during the second day of an EACC workshop for media practitioners on integrity in leadership and elections in Mombasa, the judge said corruption had become deeply entrenched across public institutions and society, undermining efforts to build a culture of accountability.
Drawing from her experience as a former EACC commissioner and her involvement in the establishment of the country’s anti-graft institutions, Sichale said she had initially believed that the commission could lead the country towards defeating corruption.
However, she said her five-year experience at the commission left her with the realisation that no single institution could win the fight without broader public commitment.
“At the end of the five years, as I walked outside, as I left the Integrity Centre, I think I came to one conclusion: that the fight against corruption cannot be fought by one institution,” she said.
“The Anti-Corruption Commission will lead the fight against corruption, but it is upon all of us to fight corruption. Unless and until the Kenyan people are ready to fight corruption, you as an institution fighting corruption cannot succeed.”
Accountability
Sichale challenged Kenyans to examine their individual contribution to the fight against graft, regardless of their positions in society, arguing that personal accountability must begin within the spaces people occupy.
She invoked the late musician Michael Jackson’s message that change begins with the person in the mirror, saying the principle applied to the country’s struggle against corruption.
The judge also warned that dishonesty had spread beyond senior public officials, citing a case involving a magistrate who allegedly colluded with an applicant to fraudulently obtain letters of administration to access Sh15 million belonging to a person who was still alive.
She described how the scheme allegedly involved several actors, including a local chief, guarantors, officials responsible for civil registration and a doctor whose medical report was used to justify the applicant’s absence from court.
The case, she said, illustrated how corruption could thrive when different actors across institutions participated in or facilitated fraudulent transactions.
“We live in such a rotten society. It is the chief, it is the applicant, it is the guarantors, it is the registrar of births and deaths. It is the doctor. Who will save us?” she posed.
Sichale said the example demonstrated why the fight against corruption must go beyond targeting high-profile individuals to confronting dishonesty at every level of society.
On the role of the Judiciary, Sichale said courts had progressively given effect to Chapter Six of the Constitution on leadership and integrity, reinforcing the principle that public office is a public trust rather than a privilege.
She cited several landmark decisions that have shaped the interpretation of integrity requirements for individuals seeking or holding public office.
Among them was the Supreme Court’s decision in the impeachment case involving former Nairobi Governor Mike Sonko, which reaffirmed that constitutional provisions on leadership and integrity were not intended to be cosmetic.
The court emphasised that state officers exercise authority on behalf of the public and must demonstrate transparency, accountability and commitment to good governance.
Quoting the Supreme Court, Sichale said public authority carried the responsibility to serve citizens rather than the power to rule over them.
She also cited the case involving former Samburu Governor Moses Lenolkulal, in which the court upheld restrictions requiring him to obtain authorisation from the EACC before accessing county government offices while facing corruption charges.
The ruling, she explained, recognised the risk of interference with witnesses and public resources where an official facing corruption allegations continued exercising control over the institution under investigation.
Sichale said the decision reinforced the principle that constitutional provisions governing the removal of governors should not be used to undermine accountability during criminal proceedings.
She further highlighted the Court of Appeal’s decision in the case involving former Nairobi Governor Mike Sonko and the rulings on unexplained wealth, which affirmed the EACC’s authority to investigate assets disproportionate to a public officer’s known legitimate sources of income.
Citing the case involving former public official Jimmy Kiamba, she said courts had upheld the constitutionality of investigations into unexplained assets and the requirement for individuals to account for wealth once investigators establish that it is disproportionate to their known legitimate income.
She stressed that the constitutional right to privacy and protection of property did not provide blanket immunity for assets suspected to have been acquired unlawfully.
“The right protects the estate of the owner. It does not protect property acquired through embezzlement, money laundering or proceeds of crime,” she said, citing jurisprudence on unexplained wealth.

The China Manned Space Agency (CMSA) sa
items.text:
Pakistani astronaut to join Chinese space mission
November 24, 2026
China on Tuesday unveiled the crew for this week's Shenzhou-24 space mission, with a Pakistani payload specialist set to become the first foreign astronaut to board its Tiangong space station.
The China Manned Space Agency (CMSA) said that Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, a 40-year-old former Pakistani air force pilot, would join two Chinese colleagues when the mission launches from the Jiuquan launch center in China's northwestern Gobi Desert at 8:18 a.m. local time (0018 GMT) on Wednesday.
"I carry the name of Pakistan on my shoulder, the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis," Ali told a news conference on Tuesday, switching between Urdu, Mandarin and English.
"To every child who is watching while I'm in orbit, just look up at the sky and remember that I am up there with your dreams," he said.
Pakistan: 'Source of joy and pride'
Pakistani officials welcomed Ali's selection as a significant milestone in relations between Islamabad and Beijing who are this year marking 75 years of cooperation in space.
Information Minister Attaullah Tarar described the mission as a "source of joy and pride for the entire nation" and Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal said the mission underscored the "iron brotherhood" between the two countries.
"This mission is not a finish line; I hope the next chapter of China-Pakistan space cooperation will grow from one astronaut and one flight to multiple joint flights, to the Moon, to Mars, and beyond," said Ali.
"Together with my Chinese crew mates, I will show that this friendship is real, not only on paper, but also in orbit."
What will Pakistani astronaut Ali do in space?
Ali will not be the first Pakistani in space, with Monaco-based polar explorer Namira Salim having flown on Virgin Galactic's Galactic 04 mission in October 2023. But he will be the first foreign astronaut to join a Chinese mission.
During a short orbital flight expected to last around five days, Ali will carry out a series of experiments in the fields of biotechnology and photosynthetic microorganisms before returning to Earth aboard the Shenzhou-23 spacecraft, which docked at the Tiangong in May.
China has poured billions of dollars into its space program. Its prized Tiangong space station is stewarded by teams of three astronauts that are typically rotated every six months.
Beijing is aiming to land Chinese astronauts on the moon for the first time by 2030 and is seen as the main space rival to the United States, which is hoping to return to the lunar surface in 2028.

items.title: High Court Declares 2pc HIMS Fee Deducted from SHA Unconstitutional
items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 24 – The High Court has declared the 2 per cent fee deducted from the Social Health Authority (SHA) through the Health Information Management System (HIMS) unconstitutional, giving the government 120 days to address legal shortcomings surrounding the charge.
In a judgment deliver
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 24 – The High Court has declared the 2 per cent fee deducted from the Social Health Authority (SHA) through the Health Information Management System (HIMS) unconstitutional, giving the government 120 days to address legal shortcomings surrounding the charge.
In a judgment delivered by Justice Reuben Nyakundi, the court ruled that the fee was introduced without adequate public participation, contrary to Articles 10(2)(a) and 201(a) of the Constitution and Section 5 of the Statutory Instruments Act.
The petition was filed by Nakuru-based surgeon Dr Benjamin Gikenyi, who challenged the legality of the charge imposed under the Third Schedule of the Digital Health (Data Exchange Component) Regulations, 2025.
However, the judge suspended the declaration of invalidity for 120 days to allow the government to regularise the fee through the constitutionally required process.
Justice Nyakundi observed that an immediate invalidation could disrupt a funding stream supporting the HIMS platform, which processes approximately 26,000 claims daily, potentially affecting healthcare facilities and patients.
The court directed the regulation-making authority to undertake public participation involving relevant sector stakeholders within the 120-day period.
It further ordered that any proposed fee must be accompanied by a Regulatory Impact Statement explaining the basis for calculating the charge.
The judge questioned how the 2 per cent deduction, capped at Sh5,000, had been determined and whether it was intended to be permanent or subject to periodic review.
The court warned that failure to introduce a lawful fee provision within the stipulated period would result in the existing entry in the regulations lapsing.
Despite declaring the fee unconstitutional, the court declined to order refunds of money already collected through the HIMS system.
Justice Nyakundi noted that the charges had been imposed under a published legal instrument that was presumed valid at the time the collections were made.
The court further observed that the payments had been collected in exchange for services already rendered and that refunding amounts deducted across hundreds of thousands of claims would be disproportionate to the procedural violation.
On accountability, the judge pointed to the Auditor General’s constitutional mandate to audit the Department of Health’s accounts, including revenue collected through the HIMS fee.
The court also noted that personal liability under Article 226(5) of the Constitution would require proof of loss arising from the unlawful use of public funds, which had not been established in the petition.
The High Court also questioned whether the 2 per cent charge had received the necessary Senate concurrence, given that health services are devolved functions under the Fourth Schedule of the Constitution.
It directed relevant State organs to take steps towards fulfilling their constitutional obligations and submit monthly implementation progress reports to the Deputy Registrar of the High Court under the advisory of the Attorney General.
The court declined to issue broader guidelines on government institutions doing business with citizens, saying such policy matters fell outside its judicial mandate.
Separately, Justice Nyakundi ruled that the appointment of private advocates by State institutions and county governments was not purely a private contractual matter, as such engagements carry public-interest implications.
The judge said the process must comply with constitutional principles of fairness, transparency, non-arbitrariness and equal opportunity.
The ruling gives the government 120 days to address the legal and procedural shortcomings surrounding the HIMS fee, failing which the existing provision will lapse.

items.summary:
China to launch first space mission with a foreign astronaut
Pakistan's Muhammad Zeeshan Ali will become the first foreign astronaut to board China's Tiangong space station when the latest crew blasts off Wednesday. Ali said he would be carrying "the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis" with him.
The fi
items.text:
China to launch first space mission with a foreign astronaut
Pakistan's Muhammad Zeeshan Ali will become the first foreign astronaut to board China's Tiangong space station when the latest crew blasts off Wednesday. Ali said he would be carrying "the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis" with him.
The first foreign astronaut on a Chinese space mission said on Tuesday that he will be carrying "the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis" when the latest crew blasts off on Wednesday.
Beijing has poured billions into the Chinese space programme, whose prized Tiangong space station is stewarded by teams of three astronauts that are typically rotated every six months.
The Shenzhou-24 mission is set to lift off at 8:18am (0018 GMT) on Wednesday from the Jiuquan launch centre in China's northwestern Gobi Desert, China Manned Space Agency (CMSA) spokesman Zhang Jingbo told a news conference on Tuesday.
Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, a Pakistani payload specialist, will become the first foreign astronaut to board China's Tiangong space station.
"I carry the name of Pakistan on my shoulder, the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis," Ali told a separate news conference held later to introduce the crew.
"To every child who is watching while I'm in orbit, just look up at the sky and remember that I am up there with your dreams," he said in English, following other remarks in fluent Mandarin and Urdu.
Ali will join a short orbital flight expected to last around five days before returning with the Shenzhou-23 spaceship, which docked at the Tiangong in May.
Pakistani officials welcomed Ali's selection as a significant step in relations between Islamabad and Beijing.
Information Minister Attaullah Tarar described the mission as a "source of joy and pride for the entire nation".
Rivalling the US
Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal said the mission underscored the trust and "iron brotherhood" between the two countries.
Ali is not the first Pakistani in space, with Monaco-based polar explorer Namira Salim having flown on Virgin Galactic's Galactic 04 mission in October 2023.
Beijing has invested heavily in its space programme in recent years, seeking to catch up with its principal rival, the United States.
Pakistan, which maintains close diplomatic and trade ties with Beijing, is a natural partner in the endeavour.
The crew currently aboard the Tiangong space station is headed by 40-year-old Zhu Yangzhu, Lai Ka-ying and Zhang Zhiyuan, also 40.
Lai is Hong Kong's first astronaut and the only woman currently aboard the space station.
Watch moreConquering the far side of the Moon: Breaking down China's historic lunar mission
After the new, all-male crew reaches the Tiangong, Pakistan's Ali will return to Earth alongside Lai and Zhang.
Zhu will remain on board to complete China's first full-year stay in space – a key test of endurance critical for future lunar and potentially deep-space ambitions.
Zhu will be accompanied for the next six-month Tiangong rotation by 51-year-old space veteran Tang Hongbo and Wu Yi, in his late thirties and making his first voyage to space.
Tang told reporters that learning to work together was more challenging in this mission, pointing to differences in language, culture and even psychology. But efforts from both sides have been paying off, Tang said.
“The labels and operating instructions aboard the spacecraft and space station are all in Chinese, and the Pakistani astronaut began training with virtually no foundation of the language," he said, adding that he and Wu also stepped up their English learning.
The Long March-2F rocket that will carry the crew into space will soon be filled with propellant, the CMSA's Zhang said.
The crew is in good condition and the space station is functioning normally, meeting all requirements for the mission, he said.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP and AP)

items.text:
Chinese official gets death sentence in spy case, report says
November 24, 2026
A Chinese court has sentenced a government official to death for spying for a foreign country, according to a report published Monday by a state-linked social media account.
The official was reportedly convicted of passing on secret information in exchange for payment.
What do we know?
The report was published on an online account run by Gold Wall Press, a publisher tied to the National Administration of State Secrets Protection.
The report named the man only as Ma. The AFP news agency called him a ministerial official, while Reuters described him as an administrative official in China's central apparatus.
According to the report, a foreign operative called "Kailin" recruited Ma while he worked overseas. Kailin first met him regularly on the pretext of learning Chinese. The talks then turned to politically sensitive topics.
A colleague of Kailin's later threatened to tell Chinese authorities about Ma's earlier disclosures unless he cooperated. Later, Ma signed an agreement committing him to confidentiality and loyalty. He received monthly payments and a laptop for sending and receiving intelligence, the report said.
What is the official accused of selling?
Upon returning to China, Ma kept passing on information, sending more than 100 intelligence reports, 35 of them later deemed "top secret," the report said. He was allegedly paid over one million yuan ($150,000, €138,000).
The sentence also includes confiscation of all his personal property.
The report did not say when or where Ma was sentenced, or whether he had already been executed.
Chinese courts rarely publish details of state security cases, but the secrecy regulator and the Ministry of State Security have increasingly publicized them as a warning to officials not to become spies.
"This shocking case serves as yet another wake-up call," the report said.
In recent years, the US CIA has published videos in Mandarin seeking informants in China's bureaucracy and military, which Beijing has called a "damning confession."

items.text:
Why Potts swapped West Ham for Club Brugge after 16 years
- Published
When Liverpool visit Club Brugge on Wednesday they are likely to come up against English midfielder Freddie Potts.
The 23-year-old ended a 16-year association with West Ham in the summer to join the Belgian champions for an undisclosed fee.
And he has started every game, bar one missed through suspension, in all competitions.
After losing to Aston Villa in the Champions League, they have defeated Inter Milan, Lens and PSV.
"It really is a dream because you hear the music and then you see your family in the stands and you remember all the times that you watched Champions League on TV," Potts told BBC Radio 5 Live's Euro Leagues Show.
"You think of all the memories that you make watching it and to be playing in it now is something that every kid dreams of."
Potts' whole life had been based around West Ham. He had been with the club since the age of six and his father Steve, who made 506 appearances for the Hammers, is a first-team coach.
Potts Jr played 28 times for West Ham, with 25 of them coming last season as they were relegated from the Premier League.
He also had loan spells with Wycombe in League One and Portsmouth in the Championship.
"In pre-season my minutes with West Ham were limited, they weren't as much as I wanted and then I spoke with my agent and said 'let's explore options because this season I'm 22, turning 23'," Potts said.
"It's a massive part of my career and I wanted to play. The opportunity of Club Brugge came along with Champions League football, the best club in Belgium and it was an opportunity I couldn't really turn down with how my minutes were going down with West Ham.
"I grew up in the area, going to the stadium watching the games. It was always going to be a tough decision but it was something that I had to do for my career.
"It was an emotional decision because it had to be made quite quickly. It's been the right decision for me and so far I'm enjoying it, I'm loving life here."
Club Brugge won the Belgian title last season and are second, just one point behind leaders Union Saint-Gilloise this campaign.
"It's a physical league," said Potts. "My running and physical stats have been higher than they've ever been. It's a demanding league in that way.
"Club Brugge demands a lot, from winning the ball back and going man for man in the press. And your responsibility off the ball is something that you have to take really seriously."
Potts says he has not started to learn French or Flemish and that team talks are done in English, with the side managed by Croat Ivan Leko.
And he revealed he has a lifelong history with the city.
"The whole move itself is funny because we used to visit Brugge when I was a kid," he said.
"We used to come around Christmas, so my family all know the city. And now I'm here they come out as much as they can.
"It's a great city with a lot of culture. It's brilliant. You won't find many places like it."
Next up for the side is the visit of Liverpool this week - with both clubs on nine points after four games.
The Reds are eighth and Club Brugge are ninth in the table.
"Everyone knows Liverpool as a club, the size and the Premier League teams," said Potts, who started for West Ham at home to the Reds last season.
"It's going to be a big game. We're level on points in the Champions League and we've put big performances in this competition and we're hoping that we're going to do the same."

items.text:
What happens if a nuclear weapon explodes in space?
November 24, 2026
A nuclear explosion in space would be unlikely to cause widespread injuries on Earth. But it could disable satellites that provide services we depend on every day, including some that save lives.
In the United States, satellite failures could make it harder for emergency crews to communicate in remote areas. If GPS were also disrupted, drivers and pilots could lose navigation guidance, and financial networks could lose a source of precise time.
We have some idea of what would happen because it's already been done.
What does history teach us?
On the evening of July 8, 1962, people in Hawaii held "watch-the-bomb parties" and followed the countdown on shortwave radio. Then the night sky lit up. The United States had detonated a nuclear weapon about 400 kilometers (250 miles) above the Pacific. The test was called Starfish Prime.
An electromagnetic pulse knocked out some streetlights in Hawaii, and some Pacific radio links briefly went down. The glow faded within minutes, but some satellites failed months later.
How does the physics change in space?
The air was too thin for a conventional fireball to form or for a destructive shock wave to reach the ground. Charged particles made denser air below glow, creating an artificial aurora. The atmosphere also absorbed much of the initial radiation.
Satellites are especially vulnerable because they orbit above most of the atmosphere that shields people on the ground from the initial radiation.
In orbit, the initial burst of X-rays can damage spacecraft right away. But Earth's magnetic field can also trap electrons released after the blast, as it did after Starfish Prime. Satellites receive another dose each time they cross the resulting radiation belt. Over time, that exposure can damage electronics and solar panels.
Which systems would be exposed?
That would depend on where the explosion happened and which satellites crossed the radiation belt. GPS satellites send signals that help phones, planes and ships work out where they are. They orbit about 20,200 kilometers above Earth and could keep working even if satellites closer to Earth failed.
But satellites do different jobs. A ship's emergency beacon can use GPS to work out its location, then send it to rescuers through a separate satellite network. If part of that network failed, the alert could take longer to get through.
Is it legal, and could it be detected?
The 1967 Outer Space Treaty bars its parties from placing nuclear weapons in orbit. The 1963 Limited Test Ban Treaty prohibits its parties from carrying out nuclear explosions in space.
The Outer Space Treaty has no dedicated system for checking what spacecraft carry. A detonation is easier to detect because US satellite sensors are designed to pick up the signals it gives off.
Can the US protect itself?
Shielding could help protect satellite electronics, and backups could keep some services running. During a GPS outage, pilots over the contiguous US can use ground-based navigation aids. Operators could launch replacements, but those satellites could still face lingering radiation or debris.
Radiation could leave many satellites intact but unable to steer. If two objects collided, fragments from the crash could hit other satellites, creating more debris and triggering further collisions. If enough debris built up for the chain reaction to keep going on its own, it could continue even if no new satellites were launched. This is known as Kessler syndrome.
Whether an explosion would trigger such a cascade is uncertain. If it did, the debris could endanger replacement satellites for years.
Could radioactive fallout reach the ground?
Some radioactive particles could enter the atmosphere and eventually settle on the ground. But a blast in space is too far away to sweep up the soil and water that carry fallout from a surface explosion.
As the particles disperse, their radioactivity decreases over time. The concentrated local fallout that can expose people near a ground-level blast to high doses would be unlikely.

items.summary:
US army says detonation of lead explosives in Iowa will proceed
Public outcry led to a legal battle when details surfaced of the plans to conduct two controlled detonations.
The United States military will proceed with its plan to blow up a deteriorating stockpile of toxic lead explosives in rural I
items.text:
US army says detonation of lead explosives in Iowa will proceed
Public outcry led to a legal battle when details surfaced of the plans to conduct two controlled detonations.
The United States military will proceed with its plan to blow up a deteriorating stockpile of toxic lead explosives in rural Iowa, according to the army’s top civilian official, after a federal appeals court gave clearance to the waste disposal operation.
In an announcement late Monday on X, Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle called the choice to move forward a “consensus decision” among all the federal agencies involved, as well as the courts and state officials.
“Every expert agency agrees, and both Iowa’s current and incoming governors say the call belongs to the experts,” Telle said.
“We are proceeding with the controlled removal in full coordination with all state, local and federal authorities.”
The Army prompted a public outcry last week when details surfaced of its plan to conduct two controlled detonations of 68 drums containing almost 4,500kg (10,000lb) of degraded lead azide, a chemical used in munitions, at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa.
Legal battle
Environmental groups immediately filed suit to block the plan, raising public safety concerns over the likelihood that the explosions would release a plume of toxic lead dust over homes, crops and livestock far beyond the detonation site, about 240km (150 miles) southeast of Des Moines.
The lawsuit challenged a special permit granted for the operation by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).
The EPA countered that a managed detonation would be far less risky than an uncontrolled, spontaneous explosion of the highly volatile material, a scenario the agency said was growing more likely as the weather turns colder in Iowa.
According to the EPA, any attempt to chemically neutralise or relocate the storage drums would also risk an uncontrolled blast.
A three-judge panel of the 8th US Circuit Court of Appeals last Thursday issued a temporary stay blocking the EPA’s permit while the court more thoroughly reviewed the case.
But Trump administration lawyers filed a legal notice two days later asserting that the Army intended to carry out the controlled detonation with or without court approval, citing an emergency exemption to federal environmental laws.
Then, in another twist on Monday, US President Donald Trump weighed in on the controversy, ordering the Army to hold off on its disposal plan until the appeals court had ruled in its favour.
Hours after Trump’s edict on Monday pausing the army’s demolition plan, the 8th Circuit sided with the EPA and lifted the court’s earlier stay, removing the final legal obstacle. But the status of the detonation plan remained unclear until Telle’s announcement on Monday night.
