items.text:
Malaysia set to return thousands of Rohingya refugees to Myanmar
The announcement comes five days after the ICJ ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority.
Malaysia will send more than 6,500 Rohingya refugees back to Myanmar in a new round of repatriations, said Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim.
The announcement on Tuesday comes five days after the International Court of Justice in The Hague ruled that Myanmar’s security forces committed genocide against the Rohingya minority.
Malaysia has historically offered safe haven to exiles from Myanmar but has grown increasingly frustrated by large numbers of refugees, saying that hosting them has become a financial burden and security risk.
In late September, around 1,500 migrants were sent back to war-torn Myanmar in an opaque scheme that concerns rights groups.
Addressing the Malaysian parliament, Anwar said 1,500 Myanmar nationals will be returned on three navy vessels from December 6 to 7. “For the month of December, 5,303 will be brought back by aircraft at the expense of the Myanmar government,” he said.
As of August, there were 225,740 refugees and asylum seekers registered with the UNHCR in Malaysia, around 90 percent of them from Myanmar, according to the agency’s data.
The UN’s highest court ruled last week that Myanmar authorities must “allow and facilitate the safe, voluntary and dignified return” of refugees displaced either within Myanmar or abroad.
Malaysia hosted Myanmar’s former junta chief-turned-President Min Aung Hlaing last month, despite criticisms from rights groups that the move risked legitimising Myanmar’s government and posed dangers for those being returned.
Anwar said his engagements with Myanmar’s former leader were part of efforts to safeguard Malaysia’s interests and in line with the ruling by the International Court of Justice, which was “to guarantee a safe and dignified return” for those fleeing persecution.
The PM acknowledged that many asylum seekers in Malaysia were “victims of atrocities carried out by the Myanmar regime”, but said Malaysia could no longer afford to ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌host refugees and that hoping for them to be resettled in third countries had not worked.
Late last month, Malaysia said it would seek clarification from Myanmar about reports that hundreds of migrants recently returned to the country were being held in military detention.
Anwar did not mention the request for clarification, but said Malaysia reiterated its stance over concerns about the Rohingya and other ethnic groups, which was also underscored by the ICJ’s ruling.
The mainly Muslim Rohingya – described as the ‘world’s most persecuted minority’ – make up two-thirds of the 190,000 Myanmar refugees and asylum seekers in Malaysia, according to the United Nations.

items.text:
Germany news: Volkswagen begins wage talks with IG Metall union
Published November 24, 2026last updated November 24, 2026
What you need to know
- IG Metall and Volkswagen to hold negotiations with strikes threatened
- VW seeks two-year wage freeze and to increase work week on same pay
- Germany automaking sector is grappling with high production costs and faces stiff competition from China
- German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier to open German-African business summit in Accra
Read below for a roundup of headlines from and about Germany on Tuesday, November 24:
Steinmeier to open German-African Business Summit in Accra
German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is in Ghana's capital, Accra, on Tuesday, on the second stop of his three-nation tour of African states.
Steinmeier is due to get the sixth German-African Business Summit started in Ghana along with President John Mahama.
Representatives of companies and business associations from Germany and Africa will be attending.
The previous summit took place in Kenya two years ago.
Steinmeier is hoping to encourage German companies to become more involved in African markets that could help patch up declining business in traditional markets such as the United States and China.
According to figures from Germany's Federal Statistical Office, German foreign trade with Africa grew by 10.5% in 2025, reaching a record value of €63.4 billion ($68.3 billion).
Steinmeier was in Ivory Coast on Monday, and after Ghana he is scheduled to travel to Kenya for the last leg of his trip.
Volkswagen and IG Metall hold talks amid threat to strike
Germany's largest labor union IG Metall and the country's largest automaker Volkswagen (VW) are embarking on a first round of talks in the northern city of Emden amid protests and threats to strike.
Volkswagen has said it wants to place German workers' ‌pay in 2027 and 2028 on ice, while also cutting a range of benefits. It is also looking to tinker with the union's 35-hour week, asking staff to work longer on the same pay when needed.
VW is facing increasing competition from China and has told its German workforce that domestic production costs have become too expensive.
"The VW board is stabbing its employees in the back. Volkswagen is facing a critical test, the extent of which the employers apparently still don't grasp," said chief negotiator Thorsten Gröger, IG Metall district manager for Lower Saxony, last week.
IG Metall has warned that strikes could begin from January 1, with the union saying that VW's restructuring push puts it in violation of a 2024 deal which included 35,000 layoffs in return for employment and investment guarantees.
Welcome to our coverage!
Guten Morgen from a chilly newsroom in Bonn.
We're looking at the first round of wage talks taking place between IG Metall and Volkswagen management.
Pressure from China has put Germany's largest automaker's production costs into sharp focus with the company seeking to freeze wages in Germany for two years while also looking to make changes to the 35-hour work week.
The company has plans to cut 100,000 jobs worldwide and could shut four production plants in Germany by the end of the decade.
We're also tracking German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier's visit to Africa, where he is opening the German-African Business Summit in Accra, Ghana.
We'll bring you the latest news and analysis on these stories and more throughout the day. Stay with us!

items.title: Nwaneri at risk of becoming Arsenal’s forgotten teenager on return with Dortmund
items.summary: Ethan Nwaneri has one record Max Dowman can never break. It is more than four years since he became the youngest player to appear in the Premier League, with Dowman, his fellow Hale End academy graduate, older by 54 days when he made his highly anticipated debut. But after a week when Arsenal publis
items.text:
Ethan Nwaneri has one record Max Dowman can never break. It is more than four years since he became the youngest player to appear in the Premier League, with Dowman, his fellow Hale End academy graduate, older by 54 days when he made his highly anticipated debut. But after a week when Arsenal published an article dedicated to Dowman’s growing collection of milestones, Nwaneri risks becoming the club’s forgotten teenager.
Nwaneri joined Borussia Dortmund on loan in the summer and returns to the Emirates Stadium in the Champions League on Tuesday, although the 19-year-old will probably be on the bench, having not started for the German club yet in the competition. Despite making a good impression with an assist on his Bundesliga debut, against Hoffenheim, he has not started in the league since 17 October and has yet to complete more than 65 minutes in a Bundesliga match.
He was a stoppage-time substitute in Saturday’s win against Borussia Mönchengladbach, with Dortmund’s manager, Niko Kovac, saying Nwaneri faces a fight to get back in a team who lead Bayern Munich by two points and deploy the exciting Greece teenager Kosta Karetsas as one of two No 10s.
“We have some very good players in those attacking positions,” Kovac said before the Gladbach game. “The competition is fierce. He [Nwaneri] has played a lot of games and, at just 19 years of age, he will certainly play many more games for us.”
Nwaneri established that Premier League record in September 2022, at 15 years and 181 days old, but his real breakthrough came in the 2024-25 campaign as a replacement for the injured Bukayo Saka on the right. He scored eight goals, matching records set by Wayne Rooney and Michael Owen, and was even compared with Barcelona’s Lamine Yamal, who was also born in 2007.
Nwaneri was rewarded with a new long-term contract despite strong interest from Chelsea and Dortmund, who have a record of signing emerging English talent. Heavy investment by Arsenal that summer, including Eberechi Eze and Noni Madueke, meant he barely featured in the first half of last season and was allowed to join Marseille in January.
Arsenal chose the French club from a long list of suitors because they wanted him to develop under Roberto De Zerbi. Nwaneri scored on debut, but De Zerbi left by mutual consent a few weeks later and the attacking midfielder barely featured towards the end of the season.
The emergence of Dowman, who, as a 14-year-old, in December 2024, broke Nwaneri’s record as the youngest player to appear for Arsenal Under-21s, means he has slipped further down the pecking order. Mikel Arteta is understood to be keen for Nwaneri to develop as a No 10 rather than a winger and loaned him again despite not signing attacking reinforcements in the summer after the departures of Gabriel Martinelli and Gabriel Jesus. Arsenal’s manager said on Monday he had been disappointed by Nwaneri’s fortunes in Germany.
“Because you go there and because you come from Arsenal, it doesn’t give you any advantage, so you need to earn it,” he said. “You can have patches, but to find that consistency and to play a big amount of minutes and have a huge impact in such big football clubs like Arsenal or Dortmund, it’s extremely difficult. That’s the reality.
“You can just shine in moments, but moments are not enough. Now you need to show the consistency. Ethan has the capacity and the mentality to do that and it takes some time.”
While Nwaneri’s Arsenal career has stalled, he has seen his childhood friend Myles Lewis-Skelly begin to establish himself in his preferred central midfield role for club and country. The England Under-21s manager, Lee Carsley, remains a big fan, though, and Nwaneri repaid that faith by setting up the first two goals in a 3-2 win against France last week, even if Dowman took the headlines again by breaking Jude Bellingham’s record as their youngest goalscorer with a late winner.
Nwaneri, whose brother Emerson plays for ArsenalUnder-18s, was one of four training players called up for England’s World Cup preparation camp in Florida, with Rio Ngumoha, Josh King and Alex Scott, and remains on Thomas Tuchel’s radar. But as Arteta, who was sent on loan from Barcelona to Paris Saint-Germain at the start of his career, acknowledged when asked whether Arsenal may consider a January recall that it is up to Nwaneri to rediscover his best form at Dortmund.
“He was in Marseille as well. Marseille had a completely different context for a lot of things that I saw and expected to happen. But that builds a player, that builds the character and the career of a player. I’m so convinced of that.”
For Arteta, there is only one meaningful way for Nwaneri to deal with the frustration of his role as a substitute. “Try to change it for the one that you want,” he said. “That’s football.”

items.title: De Bruyne’s Napoli return will remind Manchester City what they are missing
items.summary: As Manchester City come to terms with turbulence, one of their all-time greats has flown in to remind them of the best of times. Kevin De Bruyne will be back at the Etihad Stadium on Tuesday, evoking the greatest period of Pep Guardiola’s decade in charge when they won four straight Premier League t
items.text:
As Manchester City come to terms with turbulence, one of their all-time greats has flown in to remind them of the best of times. Kevin De Bruyne will be back at the Etihad Stadium on Tuesday, evoking the greatest period of Pep Guardiola’s decade in charge when they won four straight Premier League titles and the Champions League.
In Europe, things are comfortable for Enzo Maresca, with three wins from four, but they have collected a solitary point from 12 domestically recently. They are struggling to score and conceding too easily at the back, leading the Italian to experiment in his attempts to find solutions.
De Bruyne left for nothing in the summer of 2025, but had fully returned the £55m City paid for him 10 years previously. Six Premier League titles, two FA Cups, five League Cups, a Club World Cup and that night in Istanbul when City conquered Inter, successes he will for ever cherish. Admittedly, the Belgian departed early that night in Turkey through injury, something he battled with in his later years in England.
Maresca was Guardiola’s assistant for the 2023 treble season, working closely with De Bruyne. “In the last 10 years, all the trophies the club achieved, Kevin was here and an important player, a fantastic player, a top guy, polite, fantastic,” he said. “It was a pleasure to work with him.”
His return may be made slightly more appealing because his powers have waned in Serie A and his teammates are not faring any better, although his compatriot Jérémy Doku said: “It’s fun to play with him. The quality he has is unbelievable, but we are all competitive so we all have to be on our best.”
At his peak, De Bruyne was the driving force for Guardiola, a two‑footed mercurial talent who could change a game in an instant. He was someone clearly more talented than most of the elite, able to glide past opponents, find a pass no one else could or just shift the ball from one foot to the other and smash in a goal from distance.
“I play more based on the feeling I have and where the space is, where I can feel I’m the most dangerous,” De Bruyne said on Monday. A reminder City do not possess someone of the same mould; even if Rayan Cherki may think he can be the heir, he is yet to consistently prove it.
“You always have to have courage to play football, you cannot only go long and just play for duels,” De Bruyne says of a style that evolved under Guardiola.
City have enjoyed these glorious talents for years; Yaya Touré could control a midfield, David Silva was able to control entire games. Maresca does not have access to someone like that and instead is attempting to create a unified team that makes the most of its expensive parts, but is yet to strike the perfect balance. For all of Erling Haaland’s incredible qualities as a striker, he cannot do it all by himself; he is reliant on service, something he is not getting from midfield or out wide.
Maresca tried the teenager Ayyoub Bouaddi alongside Elliot Anderson against Fulham on Saturday, leaving out the £125m summer signing Enzo Fernández.
Anderson was given a more attacking role, provided the sort of thrust De Bruyne often did. He does not possess the same technical expertise as the Belgian, although his volley may have earned a round of applause from his predecessor.
“It is not complicated, it is just a matter of knowing each other,” Maresca said. “I need to understand who is the ideal one for this kind of game and different kind of games. I don’t think it is just midfielders, also we are trying with defensive players to find the right solution.
“It’s part of the process. It is like a restart after 10 years with the same manager, same faces, same words, same methods. It’s not easy to change all of a sudden.”
Cherki is capable of amazing things, while Phil Foden infrequently threatens to rediscover his best form. De Bruyne, however, was part of a team that dominated. Often alongside Rodri and Ilkay Gündogan, the trio were almost the perfect balance of defensive diligence and attacking expertise, leaving opponents facing an nigh-on impossible task.
It is likely Maresca will change things for Napoli’s visit, with the ambition of a fourth win from five games in the Champions League, as City seek to secure progression as early as possible. Whichever team is put out, it will not have a talent like De Bruyne, meaning Maresca will have to work even harder to return to City’s Belgian-inspired peak.

Tuesday 24 November 2026 08:11, UK
The World Series of Darts will return to Dubai in 2027, with the Dubai Darts Masters set to be played for the first time in 10 years.
Dubai was one of the tour's original destinations and had previously hosted a World Series event between 2013 and 2017.
The World Series will kick off its 2027 season in Bahrain on January 15, before heading to the United Arab Emirates for the Dubai Darts Masters.

The tournament will see eight of the world's top PDC players battle it out in a 16-player knockout event between January 22 and 23 at the Coca-Cola Arena.
Scotland's Gary Anderson successfully defended his Dubai Darts Masters title when it was last held in 2017, beating Michael van Gerwen 11-7 in the final.
PDC chief executive Matt Porter said: "We're delighted to be taking the World Series of Darts back to Dubai.
"The city has a great history with the series, and Coca-Cola Arena will provide a brilliant setting for two days of top-class darts.
"We're looking forward to welcoming the world's best players and fans from across the region."
Eight first-round matches will be played on the opening night, before the knockout stages and the final are played on day two.
World Series ranking points will be up for grabs, as players look to secure their spots at the season-ending Finals in Amsterdam.
Ross Smith is out to defend his title after he thrashed Gerwyn Price 11-5 to become the 2026 World Series of Darts Finals champion in September, winning his second PDC major.

items.summary:
Pakistan’s Zeeshan Ali set for historic flight to China’s space station
The Pakistan Air Force pilot will spend about a week on board the Tiangong, conducting experiments with China’s crew.
Islamabad, Pakistan – Pakistan is poised to send an astronaut into space for the first time on Wednesday, when
items.text:
Pakistan’s Zeeshan Ali set for historic flight to China’s space station
The Pakistan Air Force pilot will spend about a week on board the Tiangong, conducting experiments with China’s crew.
Islamabad, Pakistan – Pakistan is poised to send an astronaut into space for the first time on Wednesday, when an air force pilot joins China’s Shenzhou-24 mission to the country’s Tiangong space station.
Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, 40, will fly as a payload specialist alongside commander Tang Hongbo and flight engineer Wu Yi. The spacecraft is scheduled to launch from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China at 8:18am Beijing time (00:18 GMT), or 5:18am in Pakistan.
Speaking at a news conference in Jiuquan on Tuesday, China Manned Space Agency (CMSA) spokesperson Zhang Jingbo said the mission would mark the first joint flight by Chinese and foreign astronauts in the country’s crewed space programme.
After reaching orbit, the spacecraft will carry out a rapid, autonomous rendezvous lasting about three and a half hours before docking with the forward port of the station’s Tianhe core module, Zhang said.
Ali’s stay will be brief. He will return to Earth on board the Shenzhou-23 spacecraft after a short joint flight, while Zhu Yangzhu, a member of that crew, remains in orbit for a year, Zhang said.
Pakistan’s Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission (SUPARCO) has said Ali will spend about a week on the station.
“I want to assure you that I am not flying for myself. I carry the name of Pakistan on my shoulder, the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis,” Ali told reporters during the crew’s conversation with the media.
The two pilots
Ali and Khurram Daud, a second Pakistani selected for astronaut training, are Pakistan Air Force pilots.
They were selected through a three-stage process that began with screening in Pakistan and included medical, psychological and technical assessments.
CMSA named them reserve astronauts on April 22 earlier this year. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif met them in Islamabad the following day, and on April 24, China’s Space Day, they joined the Astronaut Center of China in Beijing for training.
Before leaving, Daud asked Pakistanis to pray for him in a video released by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.
“My message to you all is to pray for me, so that I can complete this training and this mission well, and make my nation and my country proud,” he said in Urdu.
Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal, who is in China for the launch, paid tribute to both men on X on Tuesday.
“They trained in centrifuges and simulators, in emergency drills and in a new language. Both performed exceptionally well in training. Though Zeeshan Ali will fly tomorrow both have already made Pakistan proud,” he wrote.
Thanking his instructors, SUPARCO and CMSA, at Tuesday’s news conference, Ali said: “No matter who flies, we have already made the history together.”
Daud was not named in the crew, and it is not yet clear whether he will fly on a later mission.
In written responses to Al Jazeera, SUPARCO said the backup astronauts would serve as experts to help carry the programme forward.
Scientific experiments
Zhang said Ali would take part in the crew’s daily work but would mainly oversee China-Pakistan experiments, install samples and equipment and conduct tests in orbit.
The mission will include four joint science projects in biotechnology and materials, Zhang said. Ali will also conduct an experiment involving cyanobacteria, photosynthetic microorganisms.
Pakistan’s Information Ministry said in April that the experiments would cover materials science, fluid physics, life sciences and biotechnology, with potential applications in climate resilience, food security and industrial innovation.
Qamarul Islam, a space scientist and former senior official in the state-affiliated Institute of Space Technology (IST) in Islamabad, said the experiments had been shortlisted after SUPARCO invited research institutes in Pakistan to submit proposals.
“Primarily these experiments are the experiments of the research institutes, universities and others, from Pakistan,” he told Al Jazeera.
SUPARCO said the station was a fully equipped laboratory. It added in its response that Ali’s week in orbit was meant to start and install the experiments, and to record data confirming that the equipment had survived launch loads and vibrations and was safely installed in microgravity.
“Completing the four experiments takes between six and 12 months,” it said.
Training for orbit
According to Zhang, preparations focused on professional skills, crew coordination and language.
“We focus on Chinese commands and technical terms to ensure accurate execution,” he said, in the English interpretation of his remarks.
In a promotional video by the Chinese space agency, Ali, who described himself as a fighter pilot, said centrifuge, rescue and survival, and emergency procedures training were part of his preparation.
“But the real challenge, honestly speaking, was mastering the Chinese language, because all the switches, all the software, all the programmes, all the voice announcements, everything is in Chinese. So we had to learn that and master that technical Chinese,” he said.
SUPARCO and CMSA signed their astronaut agreement in Islamabad in February 2025. Ali said the two countries had since moved quickly.
“The two great nations of China and Pakistan have turned a pilot into an astronaut in a remarkably short span of time,” he said.
A new milestone
This year marks 75 years of diplomatic ties between the two neighbours. Zhang described the flight as another milestone in their cooperation.
“Pakistan is China’s all-weather strategic cooperative partner,” Zhang said, according to the English interpretation of his remarks.
Pakistan’s Information Ministry said in April that the programme placed the country among a select group of nations involved in human spaceflight.

WFP Executive Director Luke Lindberg decries ‘political problem’ as grain is ‘not reaching the people who need it’.
The head of the World Food Programme (WFP) has warned that disruption to three critical trade routes is pushin
items.text:
Wars choke global food routes, threatening aid for 7.3 million, WFP warns
WFP Executive Director Luke Lindberg decries ‘political problem’ as grain is ‘not reaching the people who need it’.
The head of the World Food Programme (WFP) has warned that disruption to three critical trade routes is pushing up food and humanitarian costs, threatening assistance to millions of people.
Addressing the United Nations Security Council in New York on Monday, WFP Executive Director Luke Lindberg said a “triple chokepoint” in the Strait of Hormuz, the Bab al-Mandeb and the Black Sea had “dramatically tightened the supply of food exports and farming inputs”.
“Combined with a surge in conflicts and climate shocks like El Nino, the effect on food production and prices has been very real,” he said.
If current conditions persist, the agency expects $727m in additional costs by mid-2027, potentially putting assistance for 7.3 million people at risk.
“This is taking money straight out of WFP’s operations, directly translating into less food for fewer families,” Lindberg said.
The warning comes as 266 million people worldwide face acute hunger, with a risk of famine in parts of Sudan, South Sudan and Somalia.
About 30 percent of global fertiliser supplies pass through the Strait of Hormuz. The Black Sea is a key source of grain for countries including Somalia and Yemen, which imports 90 percent of its food.
By mid-October, 63 percent fewer wheat and maize vessels were moving through the Bosphorus than a year earlier, the WFP said. About 10 million tonnes of Russian and Ukrainian wheat could fail to reach global markets, enough to feed an estimated 44 million people.
“This is not a problem of production. It is a political problem,” Lindberg said. “Grain is available, but it is not reaching the people who need it.”
In Sudan, the cost of a basic diet has risen by 130 percent since February.
Lindberg urged member states to commit to three “red lines”: no more famines, no more weaponisation of food and no more attacks on humanitarians.

items.title: I wouldn’t be here: IEBC Chair Ethekon recalls 1992 election chaos
items.summary: NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 24 – The Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) Chair Erastus Ethekon has recalled how he narrowly escaped death during the 1992 election period, sharing a personal account of ethnic violence as he warned Kenyans against inflammatory political campaigns ahead of th
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 24 – The Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) Chair Erastus Ethekon has recalled how he narrowly escaped death during the 1992 election period, sharing a personal account of ethnic violence as he warned Kenyans against inflammatory political campaigns ahead of the 2027 General Election.
Ethekon said he was still in Form One when he was removed from a vehicle travelling between Kitale and Eldoret and confronted by a group of youths armed with machetes.
He said the youths questioned him about his tribe, with his minority community background possibly saving his life.
“1992 when I was in Form 1, I was almost being slaughtered between Kitale and Eldoret,” he said during a consulation meeting with political journalists.
The IEBC chair explained that the attackers were looking for people from particular communities, adding that he could have been killed had he belonged to one of the targeted groups.
“I was removed out of the vehicle and I was asked which tribe are you. It’s only my tribe that saved me because we are minorities,” he recalled.
Ethekon said the experience shaped his understanding of how political incitement and ethnic divisions can turn elections into dangerous periods for ordinary Kenyans.
He blamed inflammatory statements by politicians and media messaging that amplifies ethnic emotions for contributing to violence during election periods.
“Because of the incitement. What the politicians say and do and what the media supports them to advance. To whip emotions. To incite the public to violence,” he said.
His account comes as political activities intensify ahead of the August 10, 2027 General Election, with leaders increasingly positioning themselves for the contest.
Ethekon also recalled the 2007-2008 post-election violence, which claimed more than 1,000 lives and left thousands displaced.
He said Kenya must avoid returning to the dark period, warning that irresponsible political communication could undermine national cohesion.
The IEBC chair urged journalists to report responsibly and avoid amplifying unverified claims that could fuel ethnic tensions.
“We want as a Commission, we want to have peaceful elections and we want to continue promoting national cohesion even as we go through this electoral cycle, because elections come and go,” he said.
Ethekon said the commission would work with media houses to promote voter education and ensure Kenyans receive accurate information about the electoral process.

items.text:
Why has Yemen’s offensive against the Houthis in al-Bayda stalled?
Government forces made early gains in September, but Houthi defences and fighting on multiple fronts have slowed the offensive.
When Yemen’s internationally recognised government launched a counteroffensive against the Houthis in the strategically important al-Bayda province in September, it appeared to open a major new front against the group.
Al-Bayda, a province in central Yemen, has become one of the flashpoints since the Yemeni government launched its response to a series of Houthi advances on the coast and around Taiz in September.
Fighting continues in and around the central province, but government forces have failed to achieve a significant breakthrough since the September counteroffensive.
There have been hundreds of air raids on Houthi positions in al-Bayda since then, but initial advances on the ground have failed to develop into a broader push towards the provincial capital.
Houthi fortifications, minefields and difficult terrain reportedly slowed the offensive, while government forces faced pressure from simultaneous fighting elsewhere in Yemen.
On November 21, Houthi media reported eight air strikes on telecommunications towers in al-Bayda’s Mukayras district.
In mid-November, government-aligned forces withdrew from areas near the strategically important Bab al-Mandeb Strait to reinforce their defences around Aden, the government’s main base of operations.
Why is al-Bayda important?
Located southeast of Sanaa, al-Bayda occupies a strategic position connecting northern and southern Yemen and holds several important military fronts.
For the Houthis, the province provides a defensive buffer and access to supply routes linking their positions in neighbouring areas.
For government forces, retaking al-Bayda could disrupt Houthi supply lines, ease pressure on surrounding provinces and potentially open routes towards the capital Sanaa, held by the Iran-backed rebels since September 2014 and triggering an ongoing war with forces linked to the government.
But the province’s mountainous terrain, winding roads and valleys make it difficult for attacking forces to advance, secure territory and maintain supply lines.
Brigadier General Mohammed al-Kumaim, a Yemeni military analyst, previously told Al Jazeera that if the government took control of al-Bayda, it would cut Houthi supply routes and increase pressure on the group’s other strongholds.
Such gains, however, would depend on the government’s ability to hold this territory and sustain military operations.
Al-Bayda has seen repeated clashes since the Houthis expanded their control beyond Sanaa in 2014. Government forces and allied tribal fighters have periodically captured territory, only to lose it during subsequent Houthi counteroffensives.
In July 2021, government forces advanced into parts of the province before the Houthis recaptured the lost territory.
What has prevented a breakthrough?
Beyond the military challenges, divisions among forces opposed to the Houthis have complicated efforts to sustain the government offensive. There remain deep divisions between forces aligned to the Yemeni government and the Southern Transitional Council (STC), a coalition of separatist groups who want independence for south Yemen.
While officially dissolved earlier this year, armed groups once under the STC umbrella remain important actors in Adan and southern Yemen. Continued differences between the Yemeni government and southern separatists reportedly remain a problem in creating a united front against the Houthis.
Ali al-Dhahab, a Yemeni military and strategic analyst, told Al Jazeera that local resistance groups had repeatedly suffered from inconsistent government support, disrupted supply lines and political rivalries among anti-Houthi factions.
He said violence in neighbouring southern areas had also prevented fighters in al-Bayda from establishing reliable supply routes and securing the support needed for prolonged operations.
The latest fighting reflects the broader difficulties facing Yemen’s fragmented anti-Houthi forces, which are attempting to defend multiple fronts while challenging the group’s control of strategically important territory.
The government’s recent withdrawal from areas near Bab al-Mandeb has added to those pressures, as forces concentrate on defending Aden against further Houthi advances.
The central challenge for the government in al-Bayda remains unchanged: Converting the province’s strategic importance into lasting territorial gains.

items.summary:
Sheikh Hasina plans to return to Bangladesh from exile on December 16
Hasina urges Dhaka to arrange her return on the national airline, as government says she can only return through extradition.
Sheikh Hasina, the former prime minister of Bangladesh who was overthrown more than two years ago, plans
items.text:
Sheikh Hasina plans to return to Bangladesh from exile on December 16
Hasina urges Dhaka to arrange her return on the national airline, as government says she can only return through extradition.
Sheikh Hasina, the former prime minister of Bangladesh who was overthrown more than two years ago, plans to return home from exile in India on December 16, her spokesperson said, as the government said she can only return through extradition.
Hasina went into exile in August 2024 after a student-led mass uprising forced her to end her 15-year rule.
She was later sentenced to death by a Bangladesh court in her absence for ordering the deadly crackdown on the uprising in which hundreds of protesters were killed.
Hasina rejected the verdict and has said she is ready to fight the case once she is back.
Announcing her plan to return on the anniversary of the end of her country’s 1971 liberation war with Pakistan, she urged Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to arrange her flight on the national airline.
“Since Sheikh Hasina was flown to India on a Bangladesh aircraft on August 5, 2024, she now calls upon the government to arrange for her air transport from Delhi back to Dhaka,” spokesperson Syed Mozammel Ali said in a statement on Tuesday.
Government position ‘very clear’
Abu Abdullah M Saleh, Prime Minister Rahman’s press secretary, told the Associated Press news agency that the government would stick to its position on Hasina’s extradition as a convict.
“My government’s stand is very clear. She has been convicted in a tribunal. We have sought her extradition,” he said by phone.
Hasina is expected to be arrested upon her return and sent to jail.
Aminul Islam, chief prosecutor of Bangladesh’s International Crimes Tribunal, which sentenced Hasina to death, said it was unreasonable for a convicted fugitive to expect the government to arrange her return.
The judiciary had earlier said that Hasina would not be able to appeal her death sentence as she missed the required deadline and there would be no legal basis to stop her execution.
In Bangladesh, presidential clemency is allowed, but Hasina has never sought that in earlier statements and has rejected the verdict outright.
The United Nations has said as many as 1,400 people were killed during the unrest that forced Hasina from power.
Hasina’s father led the war against Pakistan and after independence was the first leader of the new People’s Republic of Bangladesh.
He was killed in a military coup in 1975, along with most of his family members. Hasina and her younger sister survived as they were out of the country.

That's despite the Bangladeshi government saying she
items.text:
Exiled leader Sheikh Hasina plans to return to Bangladesh on Dec. 16
November 24, 2026
Ousted Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina plans to return to her country on December 16 after two years of exile in India, according to her spokesperson.
That's despite the Bangladeshi government saying she can only return from the neighboring nation through extradition.
"Hasina is a convicted criminal; a fugitive terrorist," Humaiun Kobir, Bangladesh's minister of state for foreign affairs, told Reuters.
"She can only return home by extradition treaty; in handcuffs, and under strict surveillance."
Hasina, however, urged current Bangladeshi Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to arrange her return on the national airline.
"Since Sheikh Hasina was flown to India on a Bangladesh aircraft on August 5th, 2024, she now calls upon the Government to arrange for ‌her air transport from Delhi back to Dhaka," the spokesperson, Syed Mozammel Ali, said in a ‌statement.
"Having exiled her contrary to the Constitution under such circumstances, it is now the responsibility of the government to make possible her return to Bangladesh on Victory Day on December 16th."
December 16 is the anniversary of the end of Bangladesh's 1971 liberation war with Pakistan.
Hasina faces death penalty at home
Hasina, having been sentenced in absentia by a Bangladeshi court last year, faces the death penalty on returning home.
She was ousted by angry protesters in 2024 amid a deadly government crackdown that killed around 1,400 people, according to the UN.
Hasina rejected the verdict and has said she is ready to fight the case once she is back. She has also denied ordering the crackdown.
Earlier this year, Hasina had vowed to return to Bangladesh while speaking at a correspondents' event in New Delhi via live audio feed.
"I know that they may put me in jail, or they may kill me, or anything may happen, but still I have to go back," she said. "Fear cannot decide my duty to the people," she had said then.
This, however, is the first time she has set a date, setting the stage for potential legal disputes.
India did not immediately comment on the set return date.
In April, the Foreign Ministry said it was examining Bangladesh's request to extradite her and that it wanted ‌to "engage constructively with the new government and further strengthen bilateral ties."

items.title: Smith: I want to play on the PGA Tour
items.summary:
Cameron Smith plots pathway back to the PGA Tour after moving on from LIV Golf
Cameron Smith joined LIV Golf in 2022 after clinching his first major at The Open at St Andrews; the Australian will play select events on the DP World Tour in 2027; watch Smith in action at this week's BMW Australian PGA
items.text:
Cameron Smith plots pathway back to the PGA Tour after moving on from LIV Golf
Cameron Smith joined LIV Golf in 2022 after clinching his first major at The Open at St Andrews; the Australian will play select events on the DP World Tour in 2027; watch Smith in action at this week's BMW Australian PGA Championship live on Sky Sports
Tuesday 24 November 2026 07:49, UK
Cameron Smith has moved on from LIV Golf, is preparing for his invitation-only appearances on the DP World Tour and is already thinking about a return to the PGA Tour.
As the 2022 British Open champion prepared for the BMW Australian PGA Championship starting Thursday at The Lakes in Sydney, attention inevitably turned to his career goals and his steps toward a possible return to the PGA Tour.
"I guess that's the path. That's where I want to be now for sure," Smith told the Australian Associated Press.
"DP's given us a chance to kind of fulfil that. We'll see how that goes. There's plenty of good players out there and plenty of other guys that want to do the same thing, so it's going to be difficult.
"But for sure that's where I want to play."
How can Smith return to the PGA Tour?
Smith will not return as a full-time member on the DP World Tour, but is one of a number of former LIV players, including Dustin Johnson and Bubba Watson, to sign an agreement with the tour to receive invites to a specific number of tournaments during the 2027 season, excluding Rolex Series events.
He receives an exemption to play this week, having won the BMW Australian PGA Championship three times in 2017, 2018 and 2022.
Under the DP World Tour and PGA Tour's current agreement, the top 10 players on the Race to Dubai Rankings qualify for the PGA Tour.
The number of PGA Tour cards available to players finishing at the top of the Race to Dubai Rankings for the 2028 season is yet to be determined, with the PGA Tour set to launch its new two-tier championship structure the year after next.
However, to even have a chance at winning one of those coveted cards, Smith will need to play more tournaments on the DP World Tour's 2027 schedule.
He could do that by winning the co-sanctioned BMW Australian PGA Championship or the Australian Open at Kingston Heath, which begins on December 3 and also features Rory McIlroy.
"I think given what they've told me, I pretty much need to win this year to get membership," Smith said.
"It's all still very blurry to me at the moment. There are a lot of rules, but we'll have a few opportunities, and like I said, I've always managed to play pretty good down here, so why not start it off with a good one?"
The PGA Tour board last week said it had "thoughtful discussions" about the future of players at LIV Golf but otherwise seemed to be in no hurry to decide if there is room for them next season.
CEO Brian Rolapp said the Returning Member Program, which allowed Brooks Koepka to return to the PGA Tour at the beginning of 2026 with financial penalties, was not on the table.
Smith didn't take up that one-time offer in January, which applied only to players who'd won majors or The Players Championship from 2022 through 2025, which included himself, Koepka, Jon Rahm and Bryson DeChambeau.
'It was a big move to go to LIV'
Smith is in a kind of limbo. LIV Golf, which lost the financial support of Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) and filed for bankruptcy on September 8, told a bankruptcy court earlier this month it had abandoned plans for a new version of the league and had begun winding down its business.
"There was a lot of uncertainty and then in a way it was good to just like get the noise over and done with," Smith, who joined LIV after winning The Open at St Andrews in 2022, said.
"It was a big move to go LIV at the start for sure, and I think everyone that was close to me and all my friends saw why I was doing it and why I made the decision."
Adam Scott said he had no doubts about Smith fitting back in.
"Cam's incredibly talented and he'll adjust to his new environment," Scott said. "He'll be just fine."

items.title: IEBC warns rigging claims could trigger voter apathy
items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 24 – The Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) Chair Erastus Ethekon has warned that unsubstantiated claims of election rigging could discourage Kenyans from registering as voters and participating in the 2027 General Election.
Ethekon said repeated allegations th
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 24 – The Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) Chair Erastus Ethekon has warned that unsubstantiated claims of election rigging could discourage Kenyans from registering as voters and participating in the 2027 General Election.
Ethekon said repeated allegations that the electoral system was compromised could weaken public confidence in the commission and undermine voter participation.
Speaking during a consultative meeting with political journalists, he said some Kenyans could be discouraged from voting if they were made to believe that election results were predetermined or that certain candidates had already manipulated the system.
He challenged journalists to investigate such claims and establish the facts before publishing or broadcasting them.
Ethekon said misinformation and propaganda could create unnecessary suspicion around the electoral process.
“And what will happen? Some of them might not show up to register or to participate in the elections because they believe either the system is rigged or so-and-so has been bought,” he said.
The IEBC chair said the commission needed media support to correct misleading information and ensure Kenyans understand how elections are conducted.
He added that IEBC would continue engaging journalists and sharing information about its preparations, including voter registration, technology and results management.
Ethekon said the media had a responsibility to ensure that political allegations were properly examined rather than repeated without verification.
The commission is preparing for the General Election, with enhanced voter registration expected to begin around January 2027.

items.text:
What China's Xi could take away from Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia
- Published
Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO has riveted the world - including China, where it has become the top trending post on Weibo, the country's biggest social media platform.
Most users are pleased to see the return of the influential billionaire, who declared that he loved China, before videos appeared online of him eating noodles and drinking milk tea during a visit in May. Some wondered why - in the video of him returning to Nvidia's headquarters - he is not wearing one of his leather jackets.
But to many, Huang's return, which is being dubbed one of the greatest U-turns of all time, seems like a vindication for China.
That's probably how Xi Jinping sees it too.
Beijing has dismissed claims that one of the women who had an affair with Jensen Huang had been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security, its version of the CIA, as a spy. Chinese state media has also framed the spy saga as a smear campaign orchestrated by China hawks in Washington. The Global Times, a Communist Party mouthpiece, described it as a "witch hunt".
Now the White House, and President Donald Trump himself, have said Huang poses no national security threat, although investigations into the spy allegations are still ongoing.
Xi will have learned many lessons from this scandal, especially about Trump's pressure points.
For one, the fact that Huang's reappointment came so soon after Xi's meetings last week with Trump in Shenzhen could be read as a sign that direct engagement is an effective way to influence Washington.
Trump has said the two men discussed Huang, but did not elaborate further. Beijing has not commented.
The episode has also reinforced the view among Chinese officials that there are two camps in Washington: those in favour of restricting Chinese access to cutting edge tech to protect US national security, and those, like Huang, who believe that such restrictions will not limit Beijing's ambitions.
Huang has repeatedly argued that US export controls will force Chinese firms like Huawei to build independent alternatives - all the while shutting American companies out of the world's second-largest economy.
But him being back at the helm of Nvidia is no guarantee of relief for Beijing.
Rather, the sale of advanced chips will remain a key point of contention between the US and China, especially as the two sides try to reach a trade deal before another Trump-Xi meeting, which is expected in December.
Already new rules are being put in place that will worry Beijing.
The US Bureau of Industry and Security is tightening restrictions by targeting not only the direct export of advanced chips to China, but also Chinese firms' ability to use computing power in data centres overseas.
The measures are designed to close potential loopholes that allow Chinese companies to access advanced Nvidia and AMD chips through cloud providers operating in third countries, including Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand.
China has yet to react with measures of its own. But investors will be watching closely for any escalation which could weigh on US equity markets.
And having seen how eager Trump is to keep things stable, Xi may see this as leverage.
He now knows Trump is so worried about the stock market that he is prepared to intervene in the HR decisions of the world's biggest company. The president has also personally invested in Nvidia, although the White House has emphasised that Trump has placed his businesses in a trust managed by his sons.
China has already used its considerable chokehold over the world's rare earth metals to bring the US to the negotiating table over trade.
If Washington restricts chip exports and Beijing retaliates, that could be the start of a cycle that has a profound effect on the stock market because American companies, from car makers to defence firms to chip manufacturers, all rely on rare earths.
What China has realised is that more trouble lies ahead as it tries to build what it describes as a "constructive strategic relationship" with the US.
Trump's tariffs are no longer at the heart of that tussle. Now it's about control of critical technology and minerals which could, in turn, affect each side's military influence and economic power.
What happens next will depend on how the Jensen Huang saga unfolds because it is far from over.
Huang is set to testify before Congress next month, and come January, a Democrat-controlled Congress will raise the pressure. Even some Republican lawmakers have made clear they want answers.
Arkansas senator Tom Cotton wrote on X that the Nvidia controversy "is just the tip of the iceberg and it's not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back".

items.title: IEBC insists polling station results remain final
items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 24 – The Independent Electoral and Boundaries Comission (IEBC) Chair Erastus Ethekon insists that results announced at polling stations will remain final as the commission prepares for the 2027 General Election.
Ethekon said the National Tallying Centre will handle the final stage
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 24 – The Independent Electoral and Boundaries Comission (IEBC) Chair Erastus Ethekon insists that results announced at polling stations will remain final as the commission prepares for the 2027 General Election.
Ethekon said the National Tallying Centre will handle the final stages of verification, collation and announcement, dismissing concerns over its role in determining the presidential winner.
Speaking during a consultative meeting with political journalists, the IEBC chair said the commission would allow journalists, political party agents, election observers and international representatives to witness the process.
“The National Tallying Centre, we need to demystify this thing. You will have your cameras there. We do the final stages of verification and announcing the results,” he said.
Ethekon maintained that the commission was not planning to introduce a different results management system, adding that the Supreme Court had already addressed questions surrounding the management of election results.
“Results at the polling stations are final,” he stated.
He explained that IEBC would still be responsible for collating, tallying and verifying results to establish whether a presidential candidate had met the constitutional requirements for election.
Under the Constitution, a presidential candidate must receive more than half of all votes cast and at least 25 per cent of votes in more than half of the 47 counties to win in the first round.
Ethekon said journalists and other stakeholders would be present during the verification process to strengthen transparency and public confidence.
“All this, the journalists will be there, the party agents will be there, the international community will be there, international media will be there, electoral observers will be there. What more accountability are we asking for?” he posed.
The remarks come as the management and transmission of election results continue to attract political attention ahead of the polls.
Ethekon said IEBC would maintain open communication with the media and provide timely information as preparations for the polls gather pace.

Jensen Huang’s return has calmed markets but fears of an AI bubble still run deep
Nvidia's decision to bring back Jensen Huang as CEO pushed the AI computing company's stocks up more than 30 percent Monday. But the model of circular financing increasingly underwriting the AI boom still has some analysts worried that the party can't last forever.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
The next few weeks could determine whether Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO was the prudent one that cheering employees, shareholders and US President Donald Trump made it out to be – or a big mistake.
Huang’s supporters argued that he was indispensable, not only to the company but to the entire AI industry, at the moment a major engine of the economy.
But he carries some baggage Nvidia still has to deal with.
Huang likely violated the company's code of conduct. He acknowledged having an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. And national security issues aside, Huang’s unusual management style, which included striking deals with a mere handshake, would have doomed many other CEOs.
It’s not a given that Huang's second go-round will survive congressional investigations, lawsuits and a probe by a law firm hired by his own board. But investors pushed Nvidia shares up 31.5 percent on Monday and Nvidia employees chanted Huang’s name as he returned to headquarters.
Here is how Huang came back despite the odds, why he's widely seen as irreplaceable, and the challenges he still faces.
'Serious mistakes'
Soon after Huang resigned on November 12, the campaign for his return began. A petition started making the rounds in Silicon Valley with employees and celebrity leaders, including SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, arguing for a comeback.
“I would be honoured to answer these calls and return as CEO,” Huang wrote on social media early last week, while acknowledging he had made “serious mistakes”.
The company refused the offer.
Then came help from a US president who measures his success in no small part by investor returns and didn't like what he was seeing.
Nvidia stock was collapsing, down a third since November 9, and suddenly fears mounted that an AI bubble was popping. By Friday, the broader S&P 500 had fallen more than 10 percent from its recent high, the definition of a market correction.
“The board decided to do what we wanted them to do,” Trump said on CNBC on Monday of his lobbying efforts over the weekend. "I believe my intervention was very important.”
Watch moreWhy the Nvidia scandal is bad news for Europe’s AI ambitions
On Monday, the S&P 500 jumped 4.7 percent, enough to recover over half its loss from last week, which was one of the worst since the 2008 financial crisis. When asked if the falling market influenced his thinking in bringing Huang back, Trump told CNBC, “probably so”.
"You've basically had ‌this perfect storm of uncertainty that has created a crisis of confidence," said King Lip, chief strategist at BakerAvenue Wealth Management in San Francisco.
"This Nvidia fallout was one of those pieces of ... uncertainty. So this removes a pretty significant one with Jensen coming back."
One reason Silicon Valley luminaries pushed for Huang's return was he was considered an extraordinary deal-maker.
“Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia, but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract,” Musk wrote on X. “Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost.”
'Nobody had the big picture perspective'
Huang ran the company like a small business, including having an astounding 60 people report directly to him and employing three family members. And he himself boasted of his personal, idiosyncratic style, saying of TSMC, the giant Taiwanese company making Nvidia chips, “We don't have a contract, and that's pretty great.”
Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, the leadership expert at the Yale School of Management, has a different opinion.
“His lack of contracts for hundreds of millions of dollars of business is unparalleled in history – and there's no reason for it,” said Sonnenfeld, adding that the dozens of direct reports was “absurd” too.
“It made sure that nobody had the big picture perspective.”
Another aspect of Huang's tenure also explains why so many wanted to see him return: he became essential to the AI economy by propping up customers and suppliers.
Many AI companies buying Nvidia chips, including the newly public Anthropic, don't make a profit and have been burning through cash quickly in operating their businesses. Enter Nvidia and its vast resources. It helped them buy its chips by striking deals to buy computing capacity and other services from them in turn.
Such arrangements are called circular financing, and they pose big dangers for investors – a fact admitted by Nvidia itself in a recent report in which it warned it may have no use for “all the capacity we are committed to purchase”.
Read moreThe Nvidia affair: Are markets about to fall out of love with AI?
Nvidia has been tied to an array of companies involved in the sprawling AI buildout. It bought shares in data centre operator CoreWeave, South Korean internet and cloud service provider Naver and more besides.
Those stocks rose on news of Huang's return, but not enough to recover losses logged since his resignation, suggesting investors are still nervous about the outlook for Nvidia's financing of customers and the broader AI trade.
XTB analyst Kathleen Brooks says Huang is considered key to keeping this financial ecosystem running.
“His return suggests more of the same when it comes to circular financing and the rapid AI infrastructure build out,” wrote Brooks in a report, adding, “The market loves it.”

items.title: Member states must not betray the ICC
items.summary:
Member states must not betray the ICC
Succumbing to US pressure to change the Rome Statute would be devastating for international justice.
The International Criminal Court (ICC) is in danger of being hollowed out. There are growing signs that its member states are preparing to change the Rome Statut
items.text:
Member states must not betray the ICC
Succumbing to US pressure to change the Rome Statute would be devastating for international justice.
The International Criminal Court (ICC) is in danger of being hollowed out. There are growing signs that its member states are preparing to change the Rome Statute, which governs the court, to meet the demands of US President Donald Trump.
Amnesty International Secretary General Agnes Callamard recently warned that ICC member states are undertaking “a dangerous step towards ‘constructive dialogue’ with the Trump administration”. Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen has acknowledged that the Netherlands, which hosts the ICC, is engaged in negotiations with the US, but has refused to provide details.
The Trump administration has given a six-month “grace period” before implementing crippling sanctions on the ICC, framing it as a chance for member states “to demonstrate meaningful progress on diplomatic and legal resolutions”.
What the US wants is for the Rome Statute to be amended to ensure that no citizen of a state that has not joined the court can ever be subjected to its jurisdiction, regardless of where their crimes are committed. This flies against the principle that the ICC can investigate anyone if they commit war crimes, crimes against humanity, or genocide on a territory the court has jurisdiction over.
Members of the Trump administration have periodically claimed that US attacks on the ICC are intended to protect Americans from falling under the court’s scrutiny. But that hasn’t happened and isn’t the case now. ICC judges recently decided to end an investigation into alleged US crimes committed in Afghanistan, yet another signal that US citizens are not at risk of investigation by the ICC – even if there are grounds to believe they should be.
According to Callamard, the US also demands that heads of state are granted immunity from prosecution by the court and that the investigation into the situation in Palestine is dropped. Currently, the court is investigating not just possible war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in Gaza, but also atrocities committed in the occupied West Bank.
It would take more than a few states to change the ICC’s jurisdiction, but it is notable that none of the 125 member states has come out and explicitly stated that the Rome Statute is not up for negotiation – especially when the court and its supporters are being held over a barrel by the Trump administration.
Accepting American terms would be as damaging to the international justice system as any ICC sanctions Washington could muster. If US efforts to destroy the court – via sanctions or neutered jurisdiction – succeed, those who would benefit the most would be perpetrators of some of the worst crimes we have seen in the past few decades.
Those include first and foremost, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. It is for “Bibi”, more than anyone, that the US has gone all-out in its ambitions to crater the ICC. Trump has made that much clear, openly stating that the sanctions against the court weren’t about protecting American citizens, but Netanyahu.
If Trump is successful, the Israeli prime minister – who faces charges of war crimes and crimes against humanity over his prosecution of the war in Gaza – will enjoy impunity. Israel is not a member state, but Palestine is, which is what allowed the Court to take action against the Israeli prime minister.
The ICC’s investigations into Palestine are something of a litmus test for the institution’s independence and impartiality, and its ability to speak truth to power. If it is forced to drop the warrants it has already issued for atrocity crimes committed in Gaza, many will conclude that the court is operated in line with the narrow interests of the powerful and not the law or the needs of victims and survivors.
Another immediate beneficiary of the gutting-out of the ICC would be Russian President Vladimir Putin. The Trump administration has long been interested in currying favour with the Kremlin, despite the fact that its leader faces an ICC arrest warrant for abducting Ukrainian children and giving them to Russian families. Indeed, at the recent ASEAN conference, Trump openly offered to work with Putin to attack the ICC.
That warrant was made possible because Ukraine accepted the jurisdiction of the ICC. But if the US campaign against the court succeeds, Putin’s warrant will evaporate, since Russia is not a member state.
Then there are Myanmar’s junta leaders. It is well established that Myanmar’s military committed a litany of atrocities against the Rohingya minority in what many states – including the United States – officially consider genocide. Last week, the International Court of Justice also found that Myanmar carried out a genocide against the Rohingya, concluding that this was the “only reasonable inference” that could explain Myanmar’s actions towards the Muslim minority.
In 2024, the ICC Prosecutor applied for a warrant for Myanmar’s Senior General and Acting President Min Aung Hlaing, alleging he committed the crimes against humanity of forced deportation and persecution against the Rohingya.
Myanmar is not a member-state of the ICC. But Bangladesh, where many Rohingya were forcibly displaced to, is what gave the court jurisdiction. If Trump achieves his goal of castrating the court, Min Aung Hlaing and other suspected genocidaires in Myanmar won’t ever have to worry about facing justice in The Hague.
This is all bad enough. But it is not just that those who have already committed atrocities that will be let off the hook if the US campaign against the ICC succeeds. New perpetrators will also be emboldened. While the court has not been able ensure that the warrants against Netanyahu, Putin or Min Aung Hlaing are enforced, what would the likes of these atrocity perpetrators do if they knew that no court would ever hold them to account for their crimes?

items.text:
Wolves hit their stride, Stoke continue to dream but can they last the course and are QPR dark horses of Championship?
Wolves are improving defensively, Stoke look strong and QPR look resolute; Andy Hinchcliffe picks out the key stories in The Championship catch-up; a Sky Sports column focusing on the second tier.
Monday 23 November 2026 13:31, UK
Welcome to The Championship Catch-up, a new Sky Sports column in which Andy Hinchcliffe rounds up some of the key stories from the second tier. This week:
- Wolves are coming together under Peixoto
- Stoke look like they can last the course
- QPR's defensive improvements prove key
Wolves have added solidity at the back to attacking prowess
With the players Wolves have got and the way they play, they were always going to score goals. They've averaged around 1.7 goals per game across those periods, so they're still good for a goal under Cesar Peixoto.
But in the last seven games they've conceded only five, compared to the 14 goals they shipped in their first nine. They're not playing defensively, they're just defending well. They're keeping the ball and keeping teams away from their penalty area.
At the start of the season they were too open. They were great to watch and scoring goals, but conceding too many. They needed to find a balance. They didn't have to become ultra-defensive, but they did need some defensive strength.
- Transfer Centre LIVE! | Latest EFL news and rumours
- Championship table | Championship fixtures & results
They've got plenty of attacking threats. Raul Jimenez is still missing, but Adam Armstrong is doing really well and is a proven goalscorer at this level. They've got width, dynamism and options, while Andre plays a really important role sitting deep in midfield.
All I was looking for was more balanced performances. They didn't need to let the goals dry up just to keep clean sheets. They've managed to find that balance and do both. They're dominating games, keeping teams out and still scoring goals.
Even when they change the right-back, centre-half or left-back, they can maintain that defensive strength. They're clearly moving in the right direction and are now a much more balanced, complete team.
Kieran Trippier's experience has been invaluable. He cares about the club getting promoted back to the Premier League. Individually, he wants to do well, but he also wants the team to succeed.
He's perhaps not the player he was five years ago, but he can still have a huge effect. He'll have to get used to the fact that he might not play every game, but Wolves have the depth to manage that.
With Trippier, it's not just about his ability but also his leadership and experience. He can reinforce the standards they should be setting and what they're looking to achieve this season.

Can Stoke City last the course under Mark Robins?
Stoke City have won 10 of 16 games, more than any other Championship team. Would you have expected them to have won more games than Wolves, West Ham, Middlesbrough or Southampton after 16 matches? Probably not.
They're still overachieving in terms of the data, but Mark Robins spoke during the international break about the need to improve their performances. The league position doesn't really tell you how good you are. You have to monitor performances and look at how to develop and improve.
There's still work to do at both ends of the pitch, but they're getting goals from different players. George Hirst came in for big money and had been struggling for goals and not starting games. He won them the game against Birmingham, which is a lift for him and the team.
Against Birmingham, they were down to 10 men for a long time and showed the resilience to hold on to a 1-0 lead. When you look at everything, the foundations are there for them to get better.
How many experienced, very good coaches have gone to Stoke and not been able to make it work? We all hoped Mark Robins would succeed because of the work he did at Coventry, but there was always the question of whether he would become another coach who fell foul of a club where nobody seemed able to get things going.
I just think it's wonderful that it's him because he's such a brilliant coach. He's very understated and humble. I saw him after a game recently and asked him a couple of tactical questions. He was saying he was glad I'd noticed certain things he'd done. He's very engaging, but it's not all about him. It's about the job he's there to do.
Player for player, this Stoke side is better than last season's team. That's what I'm saying about their recruitment and the shape Mark is playing. They're better, and the fact they can improve further makes things look really positive.
But we're only 16 games into a long season. Mark will know winter is really tough for every team, particularly when you're up near the top and everyone is looking to knock you off your position. They'll be looking at their performances and adjusting their training because that's all you can do.
Could Stoke possibly be in the mix for a top-two finish? With the way they're playing and the players they've got, who could improve further, very possibly.
QPR have shown defensive improvements this season
Defensively for QPR there's been the big shift this season. They were 23rd last season for goals conceded and are now in the top four. That's the foundation. If you don't concede too many goals in the Championship, you've got a chance.

items.text:
Why has De Bruyne struggled at Napoli as he returns to Man City?
- Published
Kevin de Bruyne's move to Napoli in 2025 was supposed to mark a continuation of his glittering decade at Manchester City as he approaches the twilight years of his career.
Instead, the midfielder, who is widely regarded as one of the stand-out players of his generation, has seen his time in Naples threaten to turn sour amid an early injury, friction with his team-mates and rumours of a January exit.
Napoli were Serie A champions in 2024-25 - the year before De Bruyne's arrival - but are currently languishing in eighth, while they sit 27th in the Champions League after a heavy 4-1 defeat at Porto earlier this month.
Belgium international De Bruyne lifted 16 trophies in his 10 years at City and is guaranteed a generous ovation when he returns to the Etihad Stadium on Tuesday but the highs of his time in England are in contrast to the struggles he is seemingly enduring in Italy.
"Not a lot I can say for the moment," said De Bruyne when asked about his future. "I have played at 100% until now and obviously I am not 20 years old, I am turning 36.
"There is a lot of things going in my mind but there is not a lot to say. I am playing good football, trying to help the team to do well and it has been a bit of a challenging season with a lot of things happening."
- De Bruyne's feelings for Man City will 'never change' 
  - Published10 hours ago
- Did Man City let De Bruyne leave too soon? 
  - Published14 October 2025
- Statue, Pep's tears & a missed sitter - De Bruyne's emotional farewell 
  - Published20 May 2025
'A bad show' in quarrel with team-mate
City decided not to renew De Bruyne's contract during the 2024-25 season and the player had the choice of heading to the US with Chicago Fire or staying in one of the top-five leagues in Europe.
The 35-year-old felt he could still cut it at the highest level but his first season at Napoli was heavily disrupted by a hamstring injury which kept him out for more than four months, restricting him to 21 appearances.
Napoli finished runners up to Inter Milan to lose their Serie A title and De Bruyne reportedly said, external he was "happy" manager Antonio Conte had departed in the summer as promises were not kept regarding the style of play.
But despite making his name as a technically gifted number 10, De Bruyne's role has been remodelled into a deeper holding one under Massimiliano Allegri in an ageing squad that has struggled this season.
In Porto, the fractures were clear to see, with De Bruyne having a heated on-field confrontation, external with striker Lorenzo Lucca and his team-mates were forced to step in to diffuse the situation.
The passionate side of De Bruyne's game was shown in Manchester too.
The midfielder shouted "shut up" at manager Pep Guardiola during a Champions League game against Real Madrid in 2023, and said "let me talk" when David Silva and Fernandinho were ushering him off the pitch at half-time shortly after he was booked against Napoli in 2017.
"Speaking about the pitch, De Bruyne is the best player this year at Napoli," Naples-based journalist Vincenzo Credendino tells BBC Sport. "The point is that the whole team is having difficulties.
"We saw that there is a problem, at least between De Bruyne and Lorenzo Lucca. Their acting was very, very clear and I think that in that time, the two of them were wrong.
"On one hand you cannot swear at another team-mate but on the other hand, De Bruyne reproached Lucca without encouraging him, so it was a bad show."
De Bruyne 'annoyed' by wife's misinterpreted quotes
De Bruyne has played 16 times for Napoli this season - contributing four goals and two assists - but his long-term future at the club remains unclear.
In September, De Bruyne's wife reportedly, external told a Belgian publication about their desire to move back home, saying "the sooner we get there, the better" as the player leads a "very restricted life" in Naples.
Asked if the quotes had been misinterpreted, De Bruyne said: "To be honest, I am pretty annoyed because if you read the article, that none of you have read, to understand what she said.
"I was away in Belgium and a lot of noise came and a lot of bad reactions to my wife and family. I saw pictures of my house, I don't think it is OK but it is what it is and some press created this in Italy. I don't know why.
"Nobody knows my life, you will never know. People who work with me are not allowed to say anything but obviously it is something that I take away and think about. It has not been nice for my wife or for my family."
It has led to interest from the Netherlands with PSV Eindhoven making a £1.67m offer to sign him in January, but the two clubs are apart in their valuations as Napoli want up to £6.7m, according to Credendino.
"Napoli fans were not happy [with the interview]," he says. "There are many fans that say, 'OK, you can leave if you want, we are not putting chains on anybody'."
Napoli boss Allegri left the door open for a January exit by saying in his pre-match news conference the pair had "not spoken" about his future and it is "down to the players and who wants to leave" when the transfer window opens.
Maresca has fond memories of 'top guy' De Bruyne
City manager Enzo Maresca was assistant to Pep Guardiola during the 2022-23 campaign in which De Bruyne helped the club to a Treble of trophies and the Italian has fond memories of the "fantastic season" they spent together.
"No doubt, [he is] one of the best," Maresca said of De Bruyne in his pre-match news conference. "Not only personally but also for the history of this club. In the last 10 years all the trophies the club achieved Kevin was here.
"He was an important player, a top guy, polite and for me it was a pleasure to work with him."
This is not the first time De Bruyne will be facing his former club with a reunion with City in the Champions League last season.
