items.text:
Two goals in 15 games - what's going on with Gyokeres?
- Published
A Premier League trophy and 21 goals in his debut season and a - on paper things have worked out perfectly for Viktor Gyokeres since his £64m transfer to Arsenal.
But, even with those achievements, it has been a tough start to the current campaign for the 28-year-old striker.
The Swede has started just one Premier League game this season and is yet to score in his eight league appearances.
He has started three games in the Champions League, two in the Carabao Cup, and has scored just twice in 15 games in all competitions. Not the numbers he would have hoped for after last season's glory.
It is not just this season that has seen Gyokeres suitability questioned for Arsenal though.
Even though he scored more than 20 goals in his first season in all competitions as Arsenal ended their 22-year wait for a title, his all-round game had its critics.
It has been near enough a straight battle for the number nine role between Kai Havertz and Gyokeres since the Swedish international signed.
And Gyokeres was thrust into leading the line for Arsenal quicker and more frequently than planned after injury kept Havertz out for long periods last season.
Although the Swede may be the more natural finisher, Havertz's all-round play is considered superior with the German also one of Arteta's most trusted players for big games.
Gyokeres, a "win-now signing", was bought for his ability to find the net but also for how he could open up spaces for his team-mates, something they have praised him for.
But playing with his back to goal and linking up play is not natural to Gyokeres and his failure to hold up the ball or win duels with centre-backs has led to fan frustration.
Arteta has spoken about how the striker has been working on improving his hold-up play and connections, and there were hints of it in the Champions League win over Slavia Prague where Gyokeres assisted the opener and scored the winner in arguably his best game of the season.
- Raya to miss Dortmund game but injury 'not serious' 
  - Published15 hours ago
Why is Gyokeres not playing?
A big reason that Gyokeres is not starting games is that Havertz is fit.
Last season, Havertz suffered with knee and hamstring issues which meant Gyokeres was the only option Arteta had.
Had Havertz been fit, he would have played a lot more and the fact that he started the Champions League final and the key match away at Manchester City in last season's title race back this up.
This season Gyokeres has just six starts and Arteta says that his gametime and situation is similar to other members in the squad.
"We have rotated the team a lot and used the competitions as well to give minutes to players and exposure because they are all starters in my opinion," Arteta said.
"Viktor's case is one of many that they have been in the same situation where they play more in the Premier League or more in the Champions League which is not bad, eh?"
Arteta is open with his players about their standing in the squad and said that Gyokeres has not approached him directly about a lack of minutes.
"We have conversations with every player to make sure that they understand what we are doing and to gather information about the way we are feeling and so far it has been very positive with Viktor and the rest of the team," he said.
The signing of Gyokeres is an interesting one in its own right.
The Arsenal recruitment team had done a lot of due diligence on signing, now Manchester United forward, Benjamin Sesko.
It is understood work on that deal had been done but a change of direction to sign Gyokeres happened after Andrea Berta became Arsenal sporting director.
Some around Arsenal have always thought that Gyokeres is not the usual forward that the Gunners would go for and his predicament of a lack of game time was always likely to happen, even if he did play a big part in them ending their trophy drought.
What do the stats show?
Gyokeres ended last season with 14 league goals but those strikes actually only won Arsenal two points on their way to winning the league.
That is because, although his penalty in the 1-0 win at Everton was the only goal of the game, Arsenal would have come away with a draw, so that strike factually only accounted for two points and not three.
But Gyokeres did put the Gunners ahead five times last season in the league which shows that, among the frustrating performances, he had plenty of impact.
Max Dowman stole the show with his goal in the 2-0 home win over Everton, when he became the youngest scorer in Premier League history, but it was Gyokeres' goal in the 89th-minute which put Arsenal ahead and although it did not lead to a point score on its own, it set them on the way.
Gyokeres also scored in the 4-1 north London derby win, putting Arsenal ahead when Kolo Muani had equalised after Eberechi Eze's opener.
It is unlikely that Gyokeres will be sold in January as he continues to get games in the Champions League and is a senior player who can score goals in big moments.
But if his lack of minutes in the league continue, Gyokeres, who is a driven and ambitious individual, will not want to be the player who is left out of the starting XI in the long term.
Additional reporting Chris Collinson, BBC Sport Football data analyst and Sami Mokbel senior football correspondent.

items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 24 – The Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS) has announced new requirements for importers of used motor vehicles, restricting entry into the country from January 1, 2027, to vehicles first registered on or after January 1, 2020.
In a public notice, the Bureau said only right-hand-drive (RHD) vehicles meeting the eight-year age limit requirement would be allowed into Kenya under the revised importation guidelines.
The directive applies to all importers, including returning residents, diplomatic staff and members of the general public.
KEBS said the requirements are anchored in Clause 2.5 of KS 1515:2000, the Kenya Standard Code of Practice for Inspection of Road Vehicles, and Legal Notice No. 78 of April 28, 2020.
The standards body said the changes are intended to ensure imported vehicles comply with Kenya’s quality and safety requirements.
Additionally, vehicles imported from Japan, the United Arab Emirates, the United Kingdom, Thailand and South Africa will be required to have a Certificate of Roadworthiness (CoR).
The certificates must be issued by Quality Inspection Services Inc. Japan (QISJ) on behalf of KEBS.
KEBS has also issued a separate clarification concerning vehicles first registered in 2019, warning that they will not be allowed into the country after December 31, 2026.
The bureau said Certificates of Roadworthiness issued for such vehicles will expire on the same date and will no longer be valid for vehicle registration.
The latest notice reinforces Kenya’s eight-year age restriction on imported used vehicles, with prospective buyers and importers expected to ensure their vehicles meet the updated requirements before shipment.
KEBS urged importers to observe the requirements to avoid complications during inspection, clearance and registration.

items.summary:

items.text:
tl;dr trynix.dev boots GUI programs now. Try solitaire, GL gears, xeyes, a voice, the weather over curl, or Firefox.
I remember watching the talk The Birth & Death of JavaScript by Gary Bernhardt and falling in love with the whimsical yet dreadfully serious unfolding of the story of how JavaScript will come to dominate all software.
Others have noted the inevitability of JavaScript’s dominance, so perhaps it was not surprising that Atwood’s Law holds true.
  Atwood’s LawAny application that can be written in JavaScript, will eventually be written in JavaScript. — Jeff Atwood, 2009
I highly recommend watching the talk if you have not already seen it, but the short and skinny is a lookback from 2035 and how JavaScript came to be the defacto language for all software.
In Bernhardt’s retelling of events, the date is worked back from 2035, however unsurprisingly, large language models have rapidly sped up the timeline. What was once perceived to be the end-state at 2035 has arrived years earlier and you can witness it unfolding at trynix.dev.
One of the most impressive creations I’ve managed to build leveraging nixpkgs-multiverse is https://trynix.dev.
It still baffles my mind that I can run any Nix package, over 300,000 distinct package versions, straight from my browser. Truly insane capability. I was however a little dismayed at the speed of the QEMU emulation in the browser. It was slow enough that the creation tipped more towards novelty than practicality.
I woke on November 20th and saw Domen Kožar sharing a single message in our TacoSprint Discord channel: unkernel.dev
It was the fast browser Linux experience I had sought to achieve, but with Nix.
  Aside What is unkernel? It is Linux compiled to WebAssembly, allowing the kernel and system components to run at wasm speed while only user programs are emulated. It was published by Pooya Parsa on November 19th, 2026.
In an AI induced manic frenzy, I adopted the new engine along with a slough of long-wished features almost immediately.
The proof is in the pudding: unkernel delivers remarkable speed improvements over qemu-wasm,11With a very healthy set of patches applied to make it even faster. especially on first runs where kernel work dominates. The new engine is able to deliver 2x to 32x faster performance depending on the workload.22The benchmark page tracks both engines over time, measured through the real page and shell.
JavaScript & WebAssembly nirvana.
Amazingly not only does the kernel boot quickly, it also enables networking, full-fledged graphical and audio experiences directly in the browser.
Windows. A program’s Wayland surfaces are composited in the page by wland, and they float over the terminal you started them from.
GL. The VM includes a minimal Mesa build with only the virgl driver, compiled to WebAssembly, rendering through your browser’s WebGL2.
Sound. The VM has an ALSA sound card, and can play audio through your browser.
Network. curl, git clone and pip install work. Each TCP connection goes over one WebSocket to a Wisp relay.33Thank you to @_pi0_ for adding trynix.dev to his Wisp relay allow-list. 
The best joke in Bernhardt’s talk is a browser running inside another browser: the Windows GIMP under Wine, in Chrome, in Firefox. Of course, I had to try it with trynix. 😈
Here is Firefox in trynix, and it loading trynix.dev, and then loading Firefox again inside itself.44Do not be too overjoyed. It took more than an hour for this to render.
Sit and bask in that insanity. That is Firefox, on Linux compiled to WebAssembly, in a Firefox tab, loading the site and then loading Firefox again inside itself. 🤯
2035 came early.

items.title: High Court Rejects Petition to Declare Life Imprisonment Unconstitutional
items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 24 – The High Court has dismissed a petition challenging the constitutionality of life imprisonment, handing the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) a legal victory in a case seeking the release or resentencing of a convicted murderer.

items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 24 – The High Court has dismissed a petition challenging the constitutionality of life imprisonment, handing the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) a legal victory in a case seeking the release or resentencing of a convicted murderer.
Lady Justice Roselyne Aburili ruled that courts lack the authority to convert life imprisonment into a fixed prison term or determine parole eligibility periods without an enabling legislative framework.
The petition was filed by Peter Kinyua Mwangi, an inmate at Kamiti Main Prison serving a life sentence after President William Ruto’s predecessor commuted his death sentence under Article 133 of the Constitution.
Mwangi had asked the Milimani High Court to declare life imprisonment unconstitutional or, alternatively, interpret it in line with constitutional principles by replacing it with a definite prison term.
He also sought consideration of the period already spent in custody, his rehabilitation and the interests of justice, urging the court to either impose a determinate sentence or order his immediate release.
However, the DPP opposed the application, arguing that matters relating to Mwangi’s conviction and sentence had already been conclusively determined through the trial and appellate processes and could not be reopened through a constitutional petition.
The prosecution further submitted that granting the application would effectively require the High Court to review decisions made by courts of concurrent or superior jurisdiction, contrary to Article 165(6) of the Constitution.
In dismissing the petition, Justice Aburili relied on the Supreme Court decision in Republic v Ayako, which clarified the limits of judicial authority in determining the nature and duration of life sentences.
“The relief sought by the petitioner would require this court to sit in review of decisions already rendered by courts of concurrent or superior jurisdiction contrary to Article 165(6) of the Constitution, which bars the High Court from exercising supervisory jurisdiction over superior courts,” Justice Aburili ruled.
The court acknowledged that Mwangi had demonstrated significant rehabilitation, educational achievements, remorse and personal reform during his incarceration.
However, the judge held that these achievements alone could not empower the court to replace his life sentence with a definite prison term or order his release without an enabling legal framework.
Justice Aburili further found that the request for resentencing, conversion of the life sentence into a determinate term or immediate release was barred by the doctrines of functus officio and finality of judicial proceedings.
The court noted that Mwangi’s sentence had already been subjected to appellate review and could not be reopened through the fresh petition.
Mwangi was arrested on April 22, 2009, and charged with murder before being convicted on February 26, 2015, when he was sentenced to death.
The Court of Appeal subsequently upheld his conviction, while later applications seeking sentencing review before the High Court were dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.
His death sentence was later commuted to life imprisonment by the President under Article 133 of the Constitution.
The case was prosecuted by Kerungo Maatwa, representing the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions.

items.text:
115 days, 39 private-jet flights, one election - Infantino's globetrotting
- Published
Fifa president Gianni Infantino's globetrotting by private jet since his plan to sell off a stake in the World Cup can be revealed.
BBC Sport found Infantino has taken 39 private flights - the equivalent of one every three days - and visited 32 different countries since the news emerged on 28 July.
Our research found he travelled more than 102,800 air miles and spent just under nine days in the air in the space of 115 days.
Critics have accused of Infantino of using tools only at his disposal as president to aid his campaign for re-election next March.
They questioned whether his re-election campaign may have partly motivated any promises made or support offered during those visits.
Fifa said Infantino had a "statutory duty to maintain and develop good relations between and among Fifa, the confederations, 211 member associations, political bodies, and international organisations".
However, he visited nearly double the 18 countries he did in the same period in 2025.
The initial Times story that revealed Infantino's World Cup plan led to a wave of criticism around the world.
But, as BBC Sport revealed, many observers feel Infantino is now the favourite to be re-elected in the spring after his rivals struggled to find a candidate to run against him until the last moment.
And it appears Infantino has managed to shore up support around the world, with critics suggesting his globetrotting was a key part of that strategy.
There has also been concern about the environmental impact of his extensive travels.
Miguel Maduro - a former head of Fifa's governance committee - said Infantino's travelling was "part of his campaign".
He told BBC Sport: "The issue here is that Fifa does not have rules on campaign funding, so the president can claim that he's going there on official business when indirectly he's using that to campaign.
"And anyone else running against him very likely will not have the financial means to compete with that."
Infantino's position seemed vulnerable after it emerged he had been devising a plan to sell stakes in the World Cup and other competitions to private investors, in a proposal called Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE).
Before FFE was abandoned, Infantino wrote to all 211 member associations saying they would receive $40m (£30m) if they backed the plan.
Lars-Christer Olsson - a former chief executive of Uefa - told BBC Sport the "important" question was "what does he promise and what are the conditions, as he already did when he promised cash if the members supported his FFE project?"
How did we track Infantino's flights?
BBC Sport gleaned the information about where Infantino had been travelling to, and when, from postings on his social media accounts.
The reasons for his travels include holding meetings with football association presidents, opening pitches, meeting politicians and attending confederation gatherings.
The private jets he used are operated by Qatar Executive (QE) - a subsidiary of the Qatar Airways Group, which is one of Fifa's sponsors.
BBC Sport used flight-tracking records and the jet registrations of the Qatar Executive fleet to compile a detailed log of Infantino's flights, totalling at least 39 since the start of August. Fifa did not dispute the figure.
It said "all travel is in line with Fifa's regulations" and there are "rules which establish the framework for flights and travel by any Fifa official".
But Fifa declined to comment on how the use of QE flights impacts on the money available from the Qatar Airways sponsorship for the benefit of global football.
The governing body also declined to comment when asked when Infantino had last taken a commercial flight.
Olsson said: "What do these trips cost and who is paying, which are the implications for the total football community?
"Is he provided with transport in his private campaign with the idea of getting something back in return if he is elected? If Fifa is paying for private jets, would it not be better to invest this money in the member associations?"
Maduro said: "That's again a confusion between his role as president of Fifa and his role as candidate to Fifa presidency."
He said there were no regulations within Fifa on the "use of public money to support their campaign".
"There's no independent authority that controls that, there is no regulation of campaign funding," he said.
Infantino's trips included attending the Caribbean Football Union presidents' meeting and a junior football tournament in the Dominican Republic three weeks after FFE failed.
He then flew to Paris, where he attended the esports World Cup , alongside French President Emmanuel Macron and Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman.
On his Instagram account, Infantino said he had "pledged Fifa's support" for the Pakistan Football Federation president's development plans when he met him in the US in September.
A few days later, he referenced a "wonderful discussion" with the president of the Latvian Football Federation during a visit to Riga, describing him as "my dear friend".
During a visit to Indonesia in October for the final of the Fifa ASEAN Cup, he met presidents from the football federations of Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Brunei Darussalam, Cambodia, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Malaysia, Maldives, Mongolia, Myanmar, Pakistan, Philippines, Qatar, Singapore, Thailand and Timor-Leste.
He said: "Having your support and shared passion on this momentous occasion means a great deal and together we will continue driving this game forward."
And during a recent trip to Manila, he performed on stage as part of a quartet called the 'Backache Boys', alongside officials from the Asian Football Confederation, and the football federations of Malaysia and the Philippines.
1 of 3
Concern over sustainability

Drew Stevens kicks last-second field goal to lift Washington Commanders to surprise win over Joe Burrow's high-flying Cincinnati Bengals; watch an NFL Thanksgiving triple-header li
items.text:
NFL: Washington Commanders beat Joe Burrow's Cincinnati Bengals in upset after last-second field goal from Drew Stevens
Drew Stevens kicks last-second field goal to lift Washington Commanders to surprise win over Joe Burrow's high-flying Cincinnati Bengals; watch an NFL Thanksgiving triple-header live on Sky Sports NFL from 5pm on ThursdaySky Sports
Tuesday 24 November 2026 06:34, UK
Jayden Daniels connected with rookie Antonio Williams on two long pass plays, moving the Commanders 64 yards in 34 seconds to set up Drew Stevens' 26-yard field goal as time expired as the Washington Commanders stunned Joe Burrow and the Cincinnati Bengals 22-20 on Monday night.
After Evan McPherson put the Bengals ahead 20-19 on a 56-yard field goal, Washington got the ball back with 39 seconds left and no timeouts.
Daniels hit Williams over the middle for 22 yards, spiked the ball, then found him again for a 42-yard catch-and-run to the Cincinnati eight. The Commanders quarterback spiked it with five seconds left and Stevens did the rest.
Daniels finished with 283 yards passing, Williams had nine catches for 122 yards, and Stevens was five for five on field goals as Washington (4-5-1) remained in the NFC East race, two games behind the division-leading New York Giants.
- Recap on all the action, highlights and analysis from Week 11

- Get latest Sky Sports deals or stream with no contract
Burrow threw for 300 yards and two touchdowns for AFC North-leading Cincinnati (7-3), but the Commanders largely held in check a Bengals team that had won five straight, scoring 31 points or more each time.
Washington's defense forced Burrow to settle for checkdowns all night.
The dangerous Bengals receiving duo of Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins combined for just seven catches for 74 yards.
Washington coach Dan Quinn made another questionable late-game decision when he sent Stevens out on fourth-and-one to kick a 41-yard field goal with 2:26 left for a 19-17 lead. That left plenty of time for Burrow, who found Mike Gesicki for a 32-yard completion to move the Bengals into field goal range.
A sack pushed the Bengals back, but McPherson nailed the long kick with 46 seconds remaining.
The game got off to a slow start in rainy conditions but opened up in the second half as the teams traded scores throughout the third quarter.
Burrow's four-yard touchdown pass to Colbie Young put the Bengals ahead 17-10, and the Commanders rallied with three field goals by Stevens.
There was an unexpected stoppage early in the third when the stadium lights went out with the Commanders in the red zone. After a delay that lasted about four minutes, Stevens converted from 36 yards to tie the game at 10-all.
Washington held Cincinnati to three points on its first four drives before Higgins' 31-yard touchdown catch that made it 10-0.
Jacory Croskey-Merritt, activated off injured reserve earlier Monday, scored on a one-yard run for the Commanders with 12 seconds left before halftime.

items.text:
Dalton Smith: Paths align better for Shakur Stevenson unification than Adam Azim fight
Dalton Smith has had an outstanding 2026, winning and defending the WBC super-lightweight world title with wins over Subriel Matias and Alberto Puello; Smith believes he can headline at Hillsborough Stadium in his Sheffield hometown with American star Shakur Stevenson a potential opponent
Monday 23 November 2026 14:23, UK
Dalton Smith, the WBC super-lightweight champion, thinks he's more likely to fight Shakur Stevenson next than Adam Azim.
Sheffield's Smith has had an outstanding year, knocking out Subriel Matias in New York to win his world championship and defending the belt against Alberto Puello in his Sheffield hometown.
American star Shakur Stevenson secured the WBO's super-lightweight championship when he beat Teofimo Lopez in January.
Both Smith and Stevenson are looking for their next opponents and a unification between the pair would be an appealing match up.
"Boxing's business and if it makes good business on both sides it's definitely a fight that can be made. Obviously there's other champions, other belts. I just want to be part of the biggest fights," Smith told Sky Sports.
"It's a fight where the paths align a little bit better than me and Adam Azim right now. But like I said we'll see."
His advice to Azim is: "Be in world level fights.
"It's a fight what gets talked about a lot," Smith said of Azim. "I've got my own path I'm going on. I'm not just saying I'm doing. I think Adam needs to play his part as well.
"I'm not really concentrating on Adam. I'll let him do what he's doing.
"I'm concentrating on a big 2027 for me."
He would love to headline at Hillsborough Stadium in Sheffield next year.
"I'm in a position now to be part of some big, big fights," Smith said. "I'd love to have Hillsborough, I'd love to win more world titles.
"It's something I've dreamt of for years, I've always said it. People probably thought I was delusional at the time saying it, but I kept following the dream and I feel like it's very close. Possibly something we can get over the line next year. It'll just be big for Sheffield, big for the city and I'll be proud to say I've done it.
"I feel like I'm carrying that torch for the city now."

items.title: Weapons, war and wavering trust: Germans want to see more restraint in foreign policy
items.summary:
Majority of Germans oppose more weapons for Ukraine, poll shows
November 24, 2026
For decades, German foreign policy was never seen as particularly controversial at home. The country was firmly integrated into NATO and supported EU expansion and cooperation across Europe. It also advocated for multi
items.text:
Majority of Germans oppose more weapons for Ukraine, poll shows
November 24, 2026
For decades, German foreign policy was never seen as particularly controversial at home. The country was firmly integrated into NATO and supported EU expansion and cooperation across Europe. It also advocated for multilateral approaches to resolving conflicts around the world. All of this enjoyed broad public support. But all of this has also changed since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the wars in the Middle East. Now, Germany's foreign policy has become increasingly contentious and is fueling growing public anxiety.
Long-held assumptions are beginning to crumble, including the belief that the US would ultimately remain firmly on Germany's side. This is one of the central findings of a new survey by the Hamburg-based Körber Foundation.
In the foundation's latest poll on public attitudes on German foreign policy, 65% of respondents said they fear further military conflicts around the world. Meanwhile, 48% believe that Germany should adopt a more restrained approach to international affairs — a five percentage point increase from last year.
Growing numbers of Germans oppose international engagement
Since 2017, the non-profit Körber Foundation, established in the northern German city of Hamburg in 1959 by industrialist Kurt Körber, has conducted the annual surveys titled "the Berlin Pulse." For this year's study, the polling institute Forsa surveyed around 1,500 eligible voters in September.
The findings make one thing clear: The current government's approach under Chancellor Friedrich Merz — seeking to have a say in virtually every international conflict and drawing on Germany's position as the largest EU economy — is increasingly met with skepticism. Only 40% of respondents now favor greater international engagement, down from 48% in 2025.
Florian Bigge, who helped compile the study for the Körber Foundation, commented on the findings on Monday: "This is a significant decline, especially since we have been asking this question for years, with changes in the range of just two to three percentage points."
Meanwhile, 77% of respondents want Germany to focus primarily on diplomacy rather than military action.
No longer a majority in favor of military aid to Ukraine
The most dramatic shift in public opinion concerns the war in Ukraine. Germany's military support for the Eastern European country, including the delivery of billions of euros' worth of weapons, no longer has the backing of a majority of the population. In September 2026, only 46% of respondents supported continued military assistance, compared to 59% in the previous year's survey. Currently, a narrow majority of 53% want to halt weapons deliveries altogether.
As Jonathan Lehrer of "the Berlin Pulse" explains, opposition is particularly strong among supporters of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD).
"Eighty-eight precent of AfD supporters oppose military assistance to Ukraine," Lehrer said. "This is an interesting finding, especially considering political developments in Germany, including state elections in which the AfD gained support by campaigning against aid to Ukraine."
The AfD has recently overtaken the chancellor's conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) in nationwide polls.
Support for Ukraine was also the subject of a recent poll conducted by the opinion research institute Infratest Dimap. This study also found that public support for Ukraine is continuing to decline, with a majority now opposed to providing assistance (see graphic).
Overwhelming majority wants Germany to remain neutral between the US and China
One finding from the Berlin Pulse study is particularly alarming for politicians and experts committed to transatlantic relations. As the US and China are increasingly seen as rivals on the global stage, 83% of respondents believe that Germany should remain neutral. Only 15% would side with the US.
This may stem from the policies of US President Donald Trump. Florian Bigge of the Körber Foundation said of the widespread preference for neutrality: "This sentiment is strong among Germans across all age groups and political parties. In eastern Germany, support for neutrality is at 92%, compared to 81% in the west. We interpret this as a desire for security but also reluctant commitment: Germans do not want to take sides in this conflict between the great powers."
The picture becomes clearer when respondents are asked about Russia. Under President Vladimir Putin, 82% of those surveyed see Russia as a military threat. However, public opinion is more divided when Germany responds firmly to such threats, including hybrid attacks. For instance, after the attempted drone attack on Leipzig Airport in early May, Germany responded by closing the Russian consulate in Bonn. However, only 51% support such measures, while 46% favor a more restrained approach.
"The gap between external expectations and domestic support is the central challenge facing German foreign policy," said Sarah Pagung of the Körber Foundation.
Should Germany always stand by Israel? Now only a third agree
One issue that appears to cause relatively little concern among Germans is the conflict in the Middle East, despite the devastating situation in the Gaza Strip following Hamas's terrorist attack on Israel more than three years ago.
This may also have to do with changing public attitudes toward Israel. One question in the study asked: "Does Germany have a special historical and moral responsibility for Israel's security because of the Holocaust?"
The results were striking: 61% of respondents said no, while just 36% answered yes. Among those under 25, opposition to Germany's special responsibility toward the Jewish state was even higher, at 75%.
This article was originally written in German.

In a public notice, the hospital said the closure took effect at 5pm as part of an ongoing infrast
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 24 – Kenyatta National Hospital (KNH) has temporarily closed the front section of its International Trauma Centre (ITC) for renovation works expected to last approximately 120 days.
In a public notice, the hospital said the closure took effect at 5pm as part of an ongoing infrastructure improvement programme aimed at upgrading the facility.
The hospital said the renovation would improve safety, functionality and efficiency at the affected section to enhance service delivery for patients, healthcare workers and other users.
KNH, however, assured patients and the public that emergency and trauma care services would continue uninterrupted throughout the renovation period.
Patients requiring emergency treatment will be directed through designated alternative access points within the hospital.
The hospital has advised patients and visitors to follow directional signage and seek assistance from staff stationed around the affected area to help them access the appropriate service points.
“Arrangements will be made to minimize disruption and ensure continuity of emergency and trauma care throughout the renovation period,” the hospital said.
The improvements are expected to enhance the centre’s functionality and support the delivery of specialised emergency and trauma care.
Acting KNH Chief Executive Officer Dr Joel Lessan apologised for the short notice and any inconvenience caused, appealing to patients and members of the public for patience and cooperation during the renovation period.
The hospital did not indicate an exact reopening date but said the works would take approximately 120 days.

Premier League holders Arsenal face German giants Borussia Dortmund for the first time in more than a decade, as the Champions League returns for matchday five action.
Arsenal and their fans were left frustrated at the weekend despite opening up a six-point lead at the top of the Premier League with a 2-2 draw at Newcastle United.

Dortmund, too, have been impressive in their own ways. Unbeaten in Germany this season, they sit two points clear of defending champions Bayern Munich atop the Bundesliga table. Niko Kovac’s team are also on an eight-match unbeaten run.

The last time the two teams met in a competitive match was in the 2014-15 season.

items.text:
Russia downed almost 700 Ukraine drones overnight, defence ministry says
Russia said it had shot down nearly 700 Ukrainian drones overnight across a wide area that included the Moscow region and the annexed Crimean peninsula. 
"Overnight, air defence forces intercepted and destroyed 699 Ukrainian aerial-type drones," the Russian defence ministry said on Telegram. 
Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said 355 of the drones "were launched toward the Moscow region" and 63 devices "were destroyed as they approached" the capital.
Russian authorities have not reported any deaths or injuries.
                                    
                        Drone-hit Sparta II vessel has been towed to St Petersburg port, Russian transport ministry says
The Russian Transport Ministry said that the Sparta II cargo ship, which a drone attack had set on fire in the Gulf of Finland over the weekend, had been ‌towed to the port of St ‌Petersburg.
The Finnish military said the attack had probably been carried out by Ukraine, although Kyiv did not comment. All 16 crew were evacuated onto a Russian ship, one slightly injured.
                                    
                        Russian attack kills two people, wounds 22 in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia, official says
A Russian attack killed two people and wounded 22 more, including two children, in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia overnight, Ivan ‌Fedorov, co-head of the Zaporizhzhia Regional Defense Council, said on Telegram.
His Telegram account showed pictures of a damaged apartment building with the windows blown out and rubble spread ‌around.
Earlier, Mykhailo Semikin, the regional governor, said people might be trapped ‌under rubble after Russia struck the city, damaging apartments, private buildings, transport infrastructure and cars.
                                    
                        Russia says it struck cargo ship near Odesa and power substation in north Ukraine
Russia's Defence Ministry said its forces had struck ‌a cargo ship overnight that was allegedly carrying military supplies southwest of Ukraine's Black ‌Sea port of Odesa.
The ministry also ‌said Russian drones hit a power substation in Ukraine's northern Chernihiv region that supplied defence industry facilities.
                                    
                        Hegseth has yet to sign off on 60 Patriot interceptors for Kyiv, FT reports
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has yet to sign off ‌on 60 ‌Patriot air defence interceptors for Kyiv, including from European ‌arsenals, the Financial ‌Times reported, citing three people familiar with the matter.
                                    
                        Russian attack wounds 11 people in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia, governor says
A Russian attack wounded 11 people in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia overnight, leaving one ‌woman in serious condition, ‌regional governor Mykhailo Semikin said on Telegram.
He said that people ‌might be trapped under ‌rubble after Russia struck the city, damaging apartments, private buildings, transport infrastructure and cars.
Reuters could not independently confirm the report. Russia and Ukraine deny deliberately targeting civilians.
                                    
                        Russian military hits drone sites, Starlink terminals in Ukraine's Sumy region, Interfax reports
The Russian military has hit drone control sites, ‌Starlink satellite ‌terminals and other military assets in Ukraine's ‌Sumy region, Interfax ‌news agency quoted the Russian defence ministry as saying.
                                    
                        Russian drone briefly violated Polish airspace, Polish armed forces say
A Russian unmanned aerial vehicle briefly violated Polish airspace during Russia's nighttime attack on western Ukraine, ‌Polish armed forces said on X.
An authorization was ‌given to shoot down the object but after it changed its course to head east, "taking into account the potential ‌threat to civilians and the possible consequences of shooting down ‌the object," a decision was made to refrain from using weapons, the post said.
Three Russian Kh-101 missiles landed in Poland on Friday, prosecutors said, adding to fears that Russia's war in Ukraine could spill over into NATO territory. NATO will deploy an AWACS early-warning system aircraft to Poland as part of its response.
                                    
                        South Korea says Russian jets entered air defence zone
South Korean authorities said Wednesday several Russian military aircraft had breached its air defence zone, correcting an earlier alert that reported a North Korean plane had made an incursion.
A breach of South Korean airspace by a North Korean military plane would mark a significant escalation in tensions between the two Koreas, which remain technically at war.
The inaccurate alert came following heightened tensions along the heavily fortified border, after a recent mine blast that injured three South Korean soldiers in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ).
An emergency alert was issued on Ulleungdo in North Gyeongsang Province at 8 am Tuesday (2300 GMT Monday), saying a "suspected North Korean aircraft has left the danger zone".
"The air raid alert for Ulleung County was lifted at 7:58 am. Please resume normal activities," it added.
Around 40 minutes later, provincial authorities issued a correction.
"It was Russian aircraft that violated the airspace. We inform that it was Russian aircraft," they said, without explaining the cause of the error.

items.text:
India's 'cockroach' party leader says he was stopped from flying to UK
- Published
A leader of India's "cockroach" party has said that immigration officials at Delhi airport stopped him from flying to the UK, where he was set to attend a series of events.
Saurav Das said he was supposed to board a flight on Tuesday at 01:00 local time (19:30 GMT on Monday) but was told by immigration officers that his passport had been "flagged".
It is not clear yet why Das's passport was flagged. The BBC has reached out to the federal home ministry, Delhi police and airport officials for comment.
Das, who rose to prominence in India earlier this year after Gen Z-led protests, said that he had been invited by the Oxford Union to speak about the movement.
He said that he was also scheduled to speak at other universities in Cambridge and Edinburgh.
"Indian students put their heart and soul to organise the events but this anti-intellectual [government] was scared of me going to these prestigious institutions," he wrote on X.
A federal home ministry spokesperson directed the BBC to airport authorities and the Delhi police for comment on Das's allegations.
Ratna Singh, another leader of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), said in a post on X that she and Das had been invited by the Oxford Union but that her visa had been rejected a few days ago.
"The manner in which Saurav was not allowed to board today raises deeply troubling questions about the state of freedom of expression and the space being allowed for young voices in this country," she wrote.
Das, a former journalist, became one of the faces of the CJP - a Gen Z-led movement that began as satire but has since emerged as a youth-led pressure group.
In July, protests spearheaded by the CJP over exam paper leaks led to the resignation of India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan .
In October, CJP leaders including Das were among thousands of people detained by the police for trying to hold protests demanding the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls. Kumar and the Election Commission have denied wrongdoing.
The same month, Das and Ashutosh Ranka, another CJP leader, were jailed for seven days after being arrested for trespassing at a banned protest site in Delhi.
Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of CJP, wrote on X that if Das "had looted a bank or committed financial fraud", he may have been allowed to fly to London, referring to billionaire bank-loan defaulters who have left India.
There have been other instances in recent years of people being prevented from boarding flights.
In September 2025, Bhanu Tatak, an environmental and anti-dam activist from India's north-eastern Arunachal Pradesh state, was stopped from boarding a flight to Dublin.
In March 2022, Rana Ayyub, an investigative journalist and outspoken critic of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government, was also stopped from boarding a flight to London at the Mumbai airport. She was due to speak at different events on media freedom and the targeting of journalists.

Underground s
items.text:
Hundreds of flights have been cancelled and public transport severely disrupted across Belgium as a result of a strike against planned austerity measures.
All air traffic has been halted at Brussels Airport in Zaventem as well as at Charleroi, home to low-cost airlines such as Ryanair.
Underground services have also been halted in capital Brussels, where large numbers of people joined a protest march.
The protest comes as Prime Minister Bart De Wever continues talks with his coalition allies over a budget to cut borrowing costs. King Philippe declined his resignation earlier this month, giving De Wever more time to negotiate.
No flights are taking off or landing at Brussels Airport between 07:00 and 21:00 local time (06:00-20:00 GMT) as a result of the strike by air traffic controllers.
“In total, 404 flights today cannot be operated, which has an impact on more than 50,000 passengers,” Brussels Airport spokesperson Jeffrey Franssens said.
Reuters news agency spoke to Florence Faure, a French passenger who had arrived in Brussels from China’s capital, Beijing, only to find that her flight to Paris Charles de Gaulle airport had been cancelled.
“Since our luggage was supposed to go on to Paris Charles de Gaulle, we didn’t even collect it,” she said.
A similar situation has affected Charleroi, where all flights were shown as “scheduled”, regardless of the time of departure or arrival.
One passenger told Belgian broadcaster RTBF that she had received no warning and only discovered there were no flights when she arrived at the airport.
Philippe Naime, a teacher, was one of the tens of thousands taking part in the protest march in Brussels.
“Quite simply, no more money is being invested in education, and people are left to fend for themselves. But people do not have the means to do that,” he told Reuters.
Public transport, schools and other public services are also facing disruptions.
The Belgian prime minister leads a five-party coalition.
One of its members, the socialist Vooruit, has been refusing to endorse plans agreed by the other four. It wants to raise taxes on the rich and for there to be fewer cuts to pensions and the health sector.
De Wever met King Philippe on Monday for the third update since the impasse.
“While expressing regret over the lack of significant progress, the king encouraged the prime minister to persevere in order to reach an agreement as soon as possible,” the royal palace said in a statement.
The leader of one of the country’s main unions, FGTB, said the government had alternatives to “dismantling the social protection system”.
Bert Engelaar, head of the union, called for “a genuine wealth tax, fair taxation, and the elimination of tax loopholes”.
“Political responsibility is not about keeping a government afloat at all costs. It’s about knowing when to stop,” he added, praising the Vooruit party.
Another union leader, Ann Vermorgen of the CSC, criticised government plans to cut bank holidays when they fall on weekends.

items.text:
Pennsylvania reports ninth measles death in ongoing state outbreak
CDC and state figures on measles deaths differ as Pennsylvania faces escalating health crisis in 46 counties.
Pennsylvania health officials have reported another death linked to the ongoing measles outbreak, bringing the state’s death toll associated with the highly contagious viral disease to nine.
The state Department of Health confirmed on Monday the death of an unvaccinated resident of Centre County in central Pennsylvania who tested positive for measles.
Pennsylvania, the hardest-hit US state, has recorded 1,638 confirmed measles cases across 46 counties so far in 2026, including 330 hospitalisations.
The nine deaths were recorded across five counties, as Lancaster County accounted ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌for three deaths, while Jefferson County reported two.
Virginia recorded its first measles-related death in more than three decades on Friday, just days after the United States lost its hard-fought designation as having eliminated the highly contagious virus.
Meanwhile, Wisconsin has reported two deaths, and New York state has recorded one child death linked to the disease.
However, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has reported only six measles-associated deaths so far in 2026, without specifying the states where the deaths were recorded.
The discrepancy between state and federal tolls emerged earlier this year after the health agency, under US Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, began using National Center for Health Statistics mortality data instead of state figures.
The US Department of Health and Human Services said it was “saddened to hear of another death in Pennsylvania”, adding that the CDC has provided the state with nearly $4m in one-time emergency funding for response efforts in 2027.
A total of 5,838 measles cases were confirmed across the country this year as of November 19, according to CDC data. The figure is the highest number reported by the CDC since 1991.
Children below the age of five account for 18 percent of cases, while children between the ages of five and 19 make up 41 percent of cases.
The number of confirmed cases in November 2026 is more than double the 2,289 confirmed measles cases reported for the full year of 2025.

WHO chief visits Cuba as healthcare system deteriorates

The World Health Organization’s top official is in Cuba, as the island continues to suffer under an ailing healthcare system amid an economic crisis deepened by United
items.text:
WHO chief visits Cuba as healthcare system deteriorates
Analysts say fuel shortages blamed on US sanctions are worsening the crisis.
The World Health Organization’s top official is in Cuba, as the island continues to suffer under an ailing healthcare system amid an economic crisis deepened by United States sanctions.
WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus visited a paediatric cardiology centre in Havana on Monday alongside the country’s Public Health Minister Dr Jose Angel Portal Miranda.
“Hola, Havana!” Tedros wrote in a post on X during his tour. “Here for a visit to discuss Cuba’s health situation, challenged by sanctions, fuel and electricity shortages.”
The WHO leader arrived Sunday at the invitation of health authorities in the Caribbean nation for a three-day visit, the second time he has visited Cuba as WHO director-general.
Portal Miranda welcomed Tedros, saying it was an opportunity for him to see firsthand the reality of the Cuban healthcare system and the challenges that it faces.
Sharp decline
Cuba’s once-vaunted system of free universal healthcare has deteriorated sharply.
Analysts say the crisis has been compounded by fuel shortages that they blame on stricter US sanctions on the island’s energy sector, worsening an economy that already had been limping for years.
A government report released in June said that the survival rate for children with cancer had fallen to 65 percent from 85 percent, before the energy blockade began in January.
Hospitals across Cuba face shortages of supplies including syringes, gauze, vaccines and anaesthetics. They also lack spare parts to repair equipment such as haemodialysis and CT scan machines.
“The situation is shocking,” said Mario Cruz Penate, the Pan American Health Organization and WHO representative on the island.
He noted that Cuba has long enjoyed health indicators comparable to those of developed nations, including low mortality, high life expectancy, broad vaccination coverage and widespread prenatal care.

items.text:
India news: Nation deepens authoritarian slide under Modi — report
November 24, 2026
What you need to know
- Report warns against India's democratic backsliding under Prime Minister Narendra Modi
- Man injures nine police officer with knife, held after several gunshots
Here are the biggest headlines from India on Tuesday, November 24:
India deepens authoritarian slide under Modi — Report
Prime Minister Modi's Hindu nationalist government has "systematically weakened" institutions meant to protect human rights and democratic freedoms, a scathing new report by Human Rights Watch concluded.
In a 95-page report titled 'So What's This Democracy We're Talking About?: Modi's Authoritarian Playbook in India,' the watchdog found that the right-wing Bharatiya Janata Party-led (BJP) government is undermining parliamentary procedures, suppressing opposition and weaponzing investigative agencies for political ends.
It also found that the government has weakened constitutional and statutory bodies meant to protect democratic freedoms and the rights of the people.
'Authoritarian playbook'
"Over the past decade, the Modi government has been hollowing out India’s independent institutions that are critical to checking executive power and protecting civil liberties," said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch.
"The government has eroded the rule of law and promoted Hindu majoritarianism, rolling back human rights protections, undermining the rights of marginalized communities, and deepening India's authoritarian slide."
The report further claimed the Election Commission of India and the Supreme Court — both independent bodies — failed to uphold fundamental freedoms, pointing to the elimination of millions of voter names from India's electoral rolls in a controversial exercise.
"The Modi administration's actions over the past decade are not isolated institutional failures but mutually reinforcing elements of an authoritarian playbook," Human Rights Watch said.
"India's allies should press the Modi government to end its assault on independent institutions and restore checks on executive power," Pearson said.
The BJP or Modi's government is yet to comment on the report which was published Tuesday morning. However, both have dismissed similar criticisms in the past.
Welcome to our coverage
Hello! and welcome to DW's India blog.
This is Mahima Kapoor reporting from Studio Delhi. Even as the temperature is fast dropping in the national capital, Prime Minister Narendra Modi is facing a different kind of heat.
A new report by Human Rights Watch has raised concerns over India's deteriorating democratic institutions and growing authoritarianism under his leadership, putting the government's record on rights and freedoms back in the spotlight.
Incidentally, hours before the report was published, one of the leaders of India's cockroach movement claimed he was not allowed to board his overnight flight to the UK to deliver speeches at the universities of Oxford, Cambridge and Edinburgh and the London School of Economics.
In other news, a Delhi man reportedly injured nine police men during a stabbing spree after he was called in to a police station over a familial dispute.
Stay tuned for all of this and more!

items.title: Majority of Kenyans fear arrest, violence if they join protests, Afrobarometer survey finds
items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 24 – A majority of Kenyans fear intimidation, arrest or violence if they participate in public protests, with new Afrobarometer findings pointing to widespread concern over police conduct, government accountability and the protection of human rights.
The survey found that 57 per
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 24 – A majority of Kenyans fear intimidation, arrest or violence if they participate in public protests, with new Afrobarometer findings pointing to widespread concern over police conduct, government accountability and the protection of human rights.
The survey found that 57 per cent of respondents do not feel free to participate in demonstrations without fear of repression, while only 42 per cent said they felt somewhat or completely free to protest.
“A majority of Kenyans say they fear intimidation, arrest, or violence if they participate in public protests,” Afrobarometer said in its news release accompanying the findings.
The findings highlight a sharp contrast between freedom of expression and the exercise of the right to assemble, with 65 per cent of Kenyans saying they are free to express their opinions.
The research also found that 62 per cent of respondents consider police use of force to maintain order during protests unjustified, against 37 per cent who consider such force justified.
More than half of respondents, 53 per cent, believe violence during demonstrations is mainly caused by people hired to cause trouble, commonly referred to as “goons”. Another 29 per cent blamed the police, while 16 per cent pointed to protesters.
Views remain divided on whether demonstrations should be allowed even when they sometimes turn violent. While 51 per cent support citizens’ right to protest under such circumstances, 45 per cent disagree.
The survey further raises questions about the government’s responsiveness to public grievances, with only 37 per cent saying authorities take concerns raised through protests seriously.
The remaining 63 per cent believe the government gives such concerns little or no consideration, including 31 per cent who said it does not take them seriously at all.
The findings come against the backdrop of the 2024 Gen Z-led demonstrations against the Finance Bill, which appear to have influenced public attitudes towards protests. About 51 per cent of Kenyans said the demonstrations had changed their views on using protests to influence government decisions.
Human rights and accountability
Beyond protest participation, the survey found that 53 per cent of Kenyans believe the government is not committed to protecting human rights for all citizens, compared with 42 per cent who consider it committed.
There are also concerns over the conduct of security agencies, with 56 per cent saying police often or always use excessive force against suspects in custody.
On reported abductions, 66 per cent of respondents identified the police or other state security agencies as primarily responsible, while 26 per cent blamed criminal gangs.
An overwhelming 92 per cent said the government needs to do more to investigate and prevent abductions and extrajudicial killings. Of these, 68 per cent said it needs to do “a lot more”, while 24 per cent called for somewhat more action.
Confidence in access to justice for victims and their families was also low. Only 34 per cent said they were confident that victims of extrajudicial killings and their families could obtain justice in court, against 65 per cent who expressed little or no confidence.
Concerns over the state of democracy
The survey found that 53 per cent of Kenyans had been concerned in the previous five years that democracy was under threat in the country.
Among those expressing concern, 40 per cent said they had spoken to others or shared their concerns on social media, while 29 per cent had attended meetings where the issues were discussed.
One in five said they had participated in demonstrations in support of democracy, while 19 per cent had contacted elected leaders and five per cent had reached out to the media.
The proportion of Kenyans who consider the country “a full democracy” or “a democracy with minor problems” stood at 54 per cent, down from a high of 68 per cent in 2019.
Satisfaction with the way democracy is working in Kenya has also declined, with 46 per cent saying they were fairly or very satisfied, compared with 59 per cent in 2019.
About the survey
The findings are drawn from Afrobarometer’s Round 11 survey, a pan-African, nonpartisan research initiative that tracks public experiences and assessments of democracy, governance and quality of life.
In Kenya, the research was led by the Institute for Development Studies at the University of Nairobi, with researchers Paul Kamau and Karuti Kanyinga presenting the findings at the university on November 24, 2026.
The Kenyan team interviewed 2,400 adult citizens between September 1 and 20, 2026, using face-to-face interviews conducted in respondents’ preferred languages.
The sample was nationally representative, comprising 50 per cent men and 50 per cent women, with 64.7 per cent of respondents drawn from rural areas and 35.3 per cent from urban areas.
Afrobarometer says the sample size produces country-level results with a margin of sampling error of plus or minus two percentage points at a 95 per cent confidence level. The margin of error is higher for demographic subgroups because of their smaller sample sizes.
Afrobarometer, a pan-African survey research network, launched its round 11 surveys in May 2026, building on previous rounds conducted in Kenya bewteen 2003 and 2024.

items.title: Champions League Power Rankings before MD5: Who's No. 1?
items.summary: We're officially past the midway point of the UEFA Champions League league phase as the 2026-27 European season rumbles on, and the grind of the calendar is beginning to take its toll on the elite teams, with injuries starting to pile up. Harry Kane (Bayern Munich), Désiré Doué (Paris Saint-Germain)
items.text:
We're officially past the midway point of the UEFA Champions League league phase as the 2026-27 European season rumbles on, and the grind of the calendar is beginning to take its toll on the elite teams, with injuries starting to pile up. Harry Kane (Bayern Munich), Désiré Doué (Paris Saint-Germain) and David Raya (Arsenal) were all sidelined this weekend with issues of varying severity, and it's only going to get more grueling as we head toward the hectic festive period and, beyond that, the January transfer window.
So what has it done to the standings? Throughout the competition, we will be asking our writers, editors and other experts to rank the top 10 teams in the tournament in terms of who they think are the strongest and most likely to win it all. Here are your Champions League Power Rankings going into a fun week.
UCL Power Rankings before Matchday 5
1. PARIS SAINT-GERMAIN (no change)
- Previous rank: 1
- Games since MD3: defeated Lyon 2-0; defeated Le Havre 5-1; defeated Villarreal 6-0; defeated Troyes 1-0; defeated Nice 3-2
- MD5 opponent: vs. AS Roma (Wednesday)
Would anyone bet against them winning it all a third straight time? Our voters were nearly unanimous -- 15 of 17 -- in crowning the French champions and back-to-back Champions League winners as the best team in this competition, but there are tough tests to come.
PSG continue to look sharp and ruthless domestically, which isn't normally their rhythm at this time of year. (Folks will remember that they generally wake up, form-wise, after Christmas, at least in recent seasons.) Ferran Torres keeps showing why he was such a savvy summer signing from Barcelona, chipping in eight goals and an assist as an occasional starter, with the likes of Senny Mayulu -- one of 12 players to get on the score sheet in Ligue 1 this season -- also stepping up to contribute in the attacking third.
They were managing without Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, who tore his ACL in October and faces a lengthy spell on the sideline, but Saturday's season-ending knee injury suffered by Doué in this weekend's win over Nice will tax their reserves over the course of a grueling campaign. Up next is a potentially tricky midweek date with Roma who, despite losing to Man United in Matchday 4, have one of the stingiest defenses in Serie A (11 goals conceded in 12 games).
2. BARCELONA (no change)
- Previous rank: 2
- Games since MD3: lost 2-1 vs. Real Madrid; defeated Alaves 6-1; defeated Aston Villa 3-0; defeated Atletico Madrid 2-1; defeated Villarreal 3-2
- MD5 opponent: at Sabah FK (Wednesday)
The Spanish champions continue to be box-office entertainment every week. They simply do not believe in drawing games; every single one of their games this season has ended with a decisive winner and loser, with their back-to-back losses to PSG and Real Madrid surrounded by wins up and down the schedule. Since the Clasico setback it has largely been business as usual, with big wins over Alaves and Villa followed by a very different pair of comeback victories at Atletico and home to Villarreal. Sunday's win had the feel of a predator toying with its prospective dinner, as Villarreal scored twice in the opening seven minutes to daze Lamine Yamal & Co. early, only for the champs to respond with three goals in 10 second-half minutes and a three-point lead at the top of LaLiga.
Like PSG, they have a simmering injury concern to their defensive corps, with several front-line defenders in various stages of rehab or treatment: Andreas Christensen has managed just 30 minutes of game time since mid-September, Pau Cubarsí's health is being monitored after a hip injury on international duty, and Jules Koundé/Eric García are just coming back from absences of their own. Rodri's ongoing fitness is a worry too as the best choice to shield a vulnerable back line, but as long as they are scoring goals by the bucketload -- their 51 in 13 LaLiga games is more than the bottom four teams in the table combined -- it feels like a minor concern. That said, Hansi Flick's side will need to tighten up once we get into the business end of this competition.
3. ARSENAL (no change)
- Previous rank: 3
- Games since MD3: defeated Everton 2-0; lost 5-3 on penalties vs. Fleetwood Town (Carabao Cup); defeated Liverpool 1-0; defeated Slavia Prague 2-1; defeated Hull 1-0; drew 2-2 vs. Newcastle
- MD5 opponent: vs. Borussia Dortmund (Tuesday)
The Gunners already have a six-point lead atop the Premier League after just 11 games, which feels like business as usual for Mikel Arteta's side, but the manner in which they slumped to a draw at Newcastle on Saturday shows that this side isn't quite at the juggernaut levels it achieved last season. Their aggressive press yielded the opening goal, when Kai Havertz snagged the ball from Lewis Hall and teed up Eberechi Eze, but Noni Madueke whiffed before halftime to double their lead and Arsenal crumbled after the break, conceding twice. Noni Madueke eventually atoned by rifling in the equalizer, but the loss of control and absence of ruthlessness will have Arsenal's rivals on notice.
This week's visit of Dortmund has all the hallmarks of a trap game, considering BVB are having a superb season so far and Arteta will have one eye on next weekend's visit of Man City to the Emirates instead. Shrugging off Saturday's torpor and asserting dominance over Niko Kovac & Co. on Tuesday will be essential to demoralizing the chasing pack.
4. REAL MADRID (up 2)
- Previous rank: 6
- Games since MD3: defeated Barcelona 2-1; defeated Racing Santander 3-0; defeated AEK Athens 3-2; defeated Valencia 3-0; defeated Celta Vigo 2-1
- MD5 opponent: vs. PSV Eindhoven (Tuesday)
Since Jose Mourinho announced his return to the Bernabeu this summer, we've been wondering when things would start to come apart at the seams. Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, an alleged cartel leader known as “El Chapo Isidro”, will be tried in Mexico despite an extraditio
items.text:
Mexico to try ‘El Chapo Isidro’ despite US extradition request
Fausto Meza Flores faces drug trafficking and weapons charges after his capture in a violent Sinaloa operation.
Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, an alleged cartel leader known as “El Chapo Isidro”, will be tried in Mexico despite an extradition request by the US, in a move that could worsen already-strained relations between the two countries.
Attorney General Ernestina Godoy told reporters on Monday that Mexican authorities “are going to put him on trial in this country”.
Meza Flores, one of the FBI’s 10 most wanted fugitives, was captured after an hours-long firefight between Mexican forces and cartel gunmen on Friday at a compound in Guasave, in the northwestern state of Sinaloa. He was flown to Mexico City the following day.
He faces local charges for weapons offences and methamphetamine possession with intent to sell.
US involvement
Earlier on Monday, Security Minister Omar Garcia Harfuch said Washington had requested Meza Flores’s extradition after his capture in the northern state of Sinaloa.
President Claudia Sheinbaum said US authorities provided intelligence support but did not participate directly on the ground.
US surveillance drones were authorised to help track Meza Flores before the raid, authorities added, despite sensitivities over US anti-drug operations in the country in recent months.
Four Mexican soldiers and 16 alleged cartel gunmen were killed in the overnight operation, according to the Mexican Secretariat of National Defence.
Meza Flores is accused by US authorities of leading a major trafficking network that moved heroin, cocaine, methamphetamine, marijuana and fentanyl across the border.
The US Department of Justice said he faces six charges in the US that include running a continuing criminal enterprise, narcoterrorism, money laundering conspiracy and weapons offences.
His arrest is the latest in a series of high-profile anti-cartel operations by Mexico, including the February killing of Nemesio “El Mencho” Oseguera, as US President Donald ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌Trump presses ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌the Sheinbaum government to crack down on organised crime.

items.title: UN chief calls for world to agree on AI oversight within a year
items.summary:
UN chief calls for world to agree on AI oversight within a year
Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has become increasingly vocal about AI as end of term nears.
United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has called for measures to better manage the risks posed by artificial intelligence (AI) d
items.text:
UN chief calls for world to agree on AI oversight within a year
Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has become increasingly vocal about AI as end of term nears.
United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has called for measures to better manage the risks posed by artificial intelligence (AI) during a conference in Barbados.
“Today I call for member states to coordinate efforts and to develop within the next year a globally inclusive and principles-based multilateral framework for AI risk management, backed by independent and credible oversight,” Guterres said Monday.
Guterres, who is approaching the end of his term due in December, has become increasingly vocal about the need for safety measures around advanced technology to avoid a future in which “killer robots” are a reality.
‘Realities of today’s world’
Guterres said Monday at the Bridgetown Special Summit on AI Safety that “when one looks at different other institutions of global governance … they correspond to the reality of the world in 1945”.
“It’s clear that institutions need to be reformed in order to adapt themselves to the realities of today’s world,” he said.
“That applies to the UN, and that applies to the international financial architecture, that applies to the world trade system.”
Guterres said that he would advise his successor, due to take office in the new year but yet to be selected, that properly controlling AI would be necessary for “humanity to maintain control of our world”.
The AI race
International regulation of AI appears distant as the technology’s superpowers, the United States and China, continue to seek the upper hand in research and development breakthroughs.
Nonetheless, Guterres said that a starting point could be for countries to agree on shared safety measures, a testing regime and basic requirements for independent oversight.
In September, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX chief Elon Musk called for a slowdown in the development of AI.
Others, like Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, want to move full steam ahead.
Regulators in the US, where AI development has proceeded at the fastest pace, appear unlikely to immediately intervene.
In September, US President Donald Trump hosted a group of American tech executives who agreed to abide by a voluntary code of conduct on AI safety.

Amid Rising Consumer Fees, New Law Increases Price Transparency and Puts Money Back in New Yorkers’ Pockets
Governor Kathy Hochul today signed a bill restricting motor vehicle manufacturers and dealers from charging consume
items.text:
S.9348A/A.10411A Prohibits Car Companies from Charging for Built-In Features
Amid Rising Consumer Fees, New Law Increases Price Transparency and Puts Money Back in New Yorkers’ Pockets
Governor Kathy Hochul today signed a bill restricting motor vehicle manufacturers and dealers from charging consumers subscription fees after they purchase a vehicle. Amid rising consumer prices, the new law guards against a rising trend of car companies charging car owners fees to activate and use built-in features like heated seats, enhanced navigation, hands-free driving and entertainment options that do not present an ongoing expense for dealers and manufacturers.
“New Yorkers are already struggling with rising prices due to Trump’s affordability crisis, and we’re not going to let harmful business practices increase the cost of living even more,” Governor Hochul said. “People spending their hard-earned money on a car shouldn’t have to fork over even more money for features that should automatically come with the car. My message to car companies is clear: this kind of deceptive business model isn’t going to fly in New York State. Keep your hands out of New Yorkers’ wallets.”
S.9348A/A.10411A prohibits motor vehicle manufacturers, dealers or third-party service providers from adding subscription services or charging post-purchase fees for any motor vehicle feature that uses pre-installed components or hardware that do not have an ongoing cost. As vehicles become more advanced, the new law aims to establish clear rules preventing exploitative practices and prevent post-purchase fees as a future automotive business model.
New York Attorney General Letitia James said, “No one should have to pay recurring fees just to use features in a car they already bought. My office has secured millions of dollars for New Yorkers throughout the state who were charged illegal junk fees when purchasing a car. Unfair fees are fueling rising costs, and I am proud to work with Governor Hochul and the legislature to bring costs down.”
State Senator James Skoufis said, “People ought to know they’re able to use their already-installed remote start or heated seats during the winter without a monthly subscription. This new law will simply and clearly prohibit car manufacturers from ripping off New Yorkers who already paid for vehicle features when they purchased their car. It’s a common sense law and I’m grateful for the Governor and Assemblymember Magnarelli for their partnership enacting this legislation."
Assemblymember William B. Magnarelli said, "I thank Governor Hochul for recognizing the importance of this legislation, particularly as technology continues to evolve at a rapid pace. This law will help protect New Yorkers from unfair fees and ensure consumers aren’t paying extra for features already built into their vehicles.”
The law will take effect in 90 days on February 27, 2027.
This new law is the latest in Governor Hochul’s ongoing commitment to help address the cost of living by putting money back in the pockets of New Yorkers statewide. Under Governor Hochul’s leadership, she has:
- Secured reforms to lower auto insurance premiums for New Yorkers, battling fraud, limiting damages paid out to bad actors, and ensuring consumers, not insurance companies, are prioritized.
- Signed legislation requiring businesses to notify consumers of upcoming renewals and price changes as well as provide clear instructions on how to cancel subscriptions.
- Cut middle-class taxes to their lowest rates in 70 years.
- Tripled the Child Tax Credit, providing families up to $1,000 per child under the age of four and up to $500 for school-aged children, beginning in 2026.
- Made school meals free for every student, saving families $1,600 per child every year.
- Sent Inflation Refund checks to 8.2 million New Yorkers — up to $200 for individuals and up to $400 for families.
- Increased the maximum weekly unemployment benefit by $300 a week.

Intelligence reports about a possible lau
items.text:
Nato chief vows defence against space threat after Russian nuclear satellite reports
- Published
Nato chief Mark Rutte has said the alliance will defend against any threats in space after reports that Russia was preparing to launch a nuclear-armed satellite.
Intelligence reports about a possible launch in the next 60 days had been shared among Nato countries this month, according to German media outlets. It was not clear which country had authored the reports.
Asked about the reports, Rutte said: "We will always make sure we defend every inch of Nato territory, and that includes making sure we are safe when it comes to the space element."
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he hadn't seen the latest reports but dismissed reports citing "unknown sources" as "hardly worth taking seriously".
The Russian embassy in Berlin told German media it rejected what it called "unfounded allegations" and said the reports were part of a "propaganda campaign".
Rutte told the press conference in Berlin that Nato had a variety of response options.
"When it comes to the military domain, we will always make assessments of our deterrence and defence and make updates where necessary," he said.
Citing anonymous German military and intelligence sources, the reports by broadcasters NDR and WDR, and newspaper Sueddeutsche Zeitung, said the Russian satellite was dubbed "Sputnik-S" and was equipped with a nuclear warhead. It could be used to disrupt or destroy other satellites, including important communication and observation satellites.
Standing alongside Rutte, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz did not confirm or deny the reports of Russia's plans, but said they "reveal the level of escalation Russia is evidently prepared to pursue".
"Reports that Russia is planning to introduce nuclear weaponry into space are not new, yet they remain no less shocking," he said.
A German government spokesman earlier also did not confirm or deny the reports, but said it was taking the reports "very seriously", AFP reported. The spokesman, however, warned against causing "excessive nervousness regarding hypothetical dangers".
Josef Aschbacher, the head of the European Space Agency, said having nuclear weapons in space was "the ultimate nightmare scenario", German paper Handelsblatt reported.
Russia is a signatory to the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which bans weapons of mass destruction from orbit. Other countries, including the US and China, have deployed or plan to deploy other weapons in space, exploring other capabilities outside of the treaty, such as targeting rivals' satellites - which are key for military communications, surveillance and navigation.
In 2024 the US claimed Russia was developing a "space-based" anti-satellite weapon armed with a nuclear warhead. Russia denied the accusation.
"Our position is clear and transparent. We have always been categorically against the deployment of nuclear weapons in space and we are still against it," President Vladimir Putin said at the time.
In September the US Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said the US had "on-orbit, space-control weapons" circling the planet, but did not provide specifics. In response to the announcement, the Kremlin's Peskov told Russian media that space "must be free of any weapon".
